Which sale routes suit a Chicago owner who wants speed?

Three routes exist: work with a broker, sell it yourself, or accept money from a cash purchaser. A two-flat, a bungalow and a high-rise condo each point toward a different choice, so start with the building's condition and your deadline.

  • Broker listing. Showings come first, then a buyer whose lender sends an appraiser. Inspection findings turn into repair credits or price cuts.
  • Sale by owner. You save the commission and take on pricing, showings and the paperwork, usually with an attorney reviewing the contract.
  • Cash purchase. The purchaser accepts the building as it stands. Expect a lower figure than a polished retail sale and compare it with your net after repairs and carrying costs.

Every route ends with the same public filings: a transfer tax declaration, a recorded deed and a seller disclosure report.

What does Chicago look like in the Census numbers?

Chicago is a very large city made of many separate housing markets, so a street-by-street view matters more than the citywide average. Estimates for mid-2025 put the population at 2,731,585 within 227.73 square miles of land, or about 12,060 people per square mile in the 2020 count.

Chicago received its city charter on March 4, 1837 and rebuilt after the fire of October 8, 1871, which burned an area about four miles long and a mile wide. It sits on the southwestern shore of Lake Michigan and is the seat of Cook County. University of Chicago sociologists divided it into community areas in the late 1920s, and the city now recognizes 77 of them, containing more than 200 informal neighborhoods.

The 2020 to 2024 Census housing figures show how mixed the stock is. Only 46.0 percent of Chicago households own their residence. The middle owner-occupied value is $334,100 and the middle gross rent is $1,440. There are 1,160,205 households averaging 2.29 people.

How much transfer tax does a Chicago sale carry?

Three layers of transfer tax can apply to a Chicago sale: a state tax, a city tax and a surcharge for the Chicago Transit Authority. At the state level, Section 31-10 of the Property Tax Code taxes a transfer at fifty cents per $500 of the value stated in the declaration, or fraction of $500.

The City of Chicago adds its own real property transfer tax. Its Department of Finance prints the rate as $5.25 per $500 of transfer price, made up of a $3.75 city portion and a $1.50 CTA portion. In general the buyer owes the $3.75 and the seller owes the $1.50. Section 3-33-060 of the municipal code lists the exemptions, and the page says none applies unless the declaration describes supporting facts and attaches documents.

Where each piece of Chicago transfer paperwork goes
ItemWhere it is handled
Transfer tax declarationFiled online through MyDec; the city does not take declarations by mail
Transfer stampsDepartment of Finance counter at 121 N. LaSalle, Room 107, or a registered title company
Deed recordingCook County Clerk, Recordings Division
State transfer taxFifty cents per $500 of declared value

One break is worth knowing about. The city page describes a refund of the CTA portion for a buyer who is at least 65, lives in the home for a year or more and paid $250,000 or less. Have the title company confirm which lines apply to your contract, since the buyer and seller can agree to split charges differently.

Who records a Chicago deed, and what happens at the filing?

Recording belongs to the Cook County Clerk's Recordings Division, not to City Hall. Its public search finds recorded land documents by property index number and party name.

The counter keeps nine-to-five hours and stops taking customers at 4:45 pm. The Clerk's site also lists a Property Fraud Unit for owners who spot a questionable filing against their home.

At most closings the title company or attorney prepares the declaration, buys the stamps and sends the deed, so a seller seldom needs to go downtown in person.

Which Cook County tax exemptions affect a Chicago house?

Missing exemptions are a common reason a Chicago bill runs high. The Homeowner Exemption subtracts $10,000 from equalized assessed value, continues each year once granted, and the Assessor puts its average saving near $950 a year.

  • Senior Exemption: a further reduction for owners 65 and over who live in the home.
  • Senior Freeze: household income at or under $65,000 for 2024, refiled yearly.
  • Long-Time Homeowner Exemption: about 2 percent of owners qualify, and the Assessor mails applications to likely candidates.
  • Home Improvement Exemption: applied without an application for up to $75,000 of added value, for four years at most.

The second installment bill lists the exemptions applied. If one was missed, a Certificate of Error can recover savings for tax years 2021 through 2025. The 2025 second installment bills were mailed September 1, 2026 and were due October 1, 2026. Mention any pending certificate to whoever runs your closing.

What must a Chicago seller disclose under Illinois law?

A written disclosure report must reach the buyer before a contract is signed. Section 20 of the Residential Real Property Disclosure Act sets the duty and Section 35 prints the form.

Questions on the form that matter in older Chicago housing include basement or crawl space leakage, foundation and roof defects, outdated electrical or plumbing, radon, asbestos, and lead paint or lead service and plumbing pipes. Termites, buried fuel tanks, boundary disputes and open violation notices appear too.

The seller answers from actual knowledge, may still sell as-is, and must update the report if conditions change before closing.

Sell as-isNo repairs, no cleaning and no showings. We buy Chicago houses in any condition.See My Cash Offer →

How do Chicago winters and older buildings affect a quick sale?

Four distinct seasons shape Chicago houses: hot, humid summers and winters with real cold and snow. The normal winter high from December through March is about 36 degrees Fahrenheit, and measurable snow can continue into the first or second week of April. Summer heat waves are frequent, though lake breezes keep the shoreline cooler.

Lake Michigan moderates temperatures, so waterfront neighborhoods run slightly warmer in winter and cooler in summer than inland ones. The disclosure form asks directly about basement leakage and roof, wall and foundation defects, so expect buyers to start there.

Before taking any offer, list what an inspector would flag and estimate each repair. A long list favors a buyer who takes the property as-is over a retail listing that may stall on repair credits.

What belongs in a side-by-side check of Chicago offers?

Compare what each offer leaves in your bank account after every cost. Request each proposal in writing with a closing date and a list of who pays what.

  • Which side covers each transfer tax portion, and whether the contract departs from the usual split.
  • Whether open city violations travel with the building.
  • How leases are handled in a multi-unit property.
  • How leftover property tax installments and water balances are settled.
  • Whether the purchaser waives a mortgage contingency and appraisal.

A second offer or a broker's price opinion gives you something to measure against.

Frequently asked questions

How fast can a house sell in Chicago?

Title work, tenants and the speed of the declaration and deed filings set the pace. A cash purchaser removes the lender and appraiser from the timeline.

Who pays the Chicago transfer tax?

Per the Department of Finance, the buyer generally owes $3.75 per $500 and the seller $1.50 per $500. The state tax is separate and the contract may shift either piece, so confirm with your title company.

Do I need to repair my Chicago house before selling?

No. An as-is sale is allowed, but the disclosure report still has to be delivered first. A purchaser who takes the house as-is will price the needed work into the figure.

Where does the deed get filed after a Chicago closing?

The Cook County Clerk's Recordings Division records it, usually through the title company along with the MyDec declaration.

Can I sell a Chicago house that has tenants in it?

Yes. Hand the buyer the leases and rent records, and ask your attorney about deposits and lease handling at closing.

Selling in Aurora?

How big is Aurora, and which counties does it cover?

Aurora straddles the Fox River in northeastern Illinois and ranks second in the state by population, behind only Chicago. The 2020 census found 180,542 residents, and the July 2025 Census estimate is 181,505. No other Illinois city this large lacks a county seat.

It began in Kane County and has since spread into DuPage, Kendall and Will, one of three Illinois cities spanning four counties. For a seller, that decides which recorder files the deed and which treasurer sends the tax bill, so start with the parcel number.

Aurora in the numbers: Census Bureau data on homes, rent and income
MeasureAurora
Households, 2020-202461,317
Share of homes occupied by owners66.4%
Midpoint home value, owner-occupied$274,800
Midpoint monthly cost for mortgaged owners$1,995
Midpoint gross rent$1,596
Midpoint household income$93,633
Land area45.02 square miles

What are the West Side, East Side and Far East Side?

The river splits the city, and each bank has its own story. East Aurora incorporated in 1845 and West Aurora was organized in 1854, and the two merged into one city in 1857. Because neither side would yield, public buildings went up on Stolp Island, in the river itself.

  • The West Side is everything west of the Fox River.
  • The East Side runs east from the river to the DuPage County line.
  • The Far East Side is the part of Aurora beyond that line.

Ten wards divide the city, and the three regions also track police boundaries and school districts. When you describe a house to a buyer, name the side of the river: it signals the school district and often the county in one phrase.

What kinds of older houses does Aurora have?

The Chicago, Burlington and Quincy Railroad kept its roundhouse and locomotive shop in Aurora and was the largest employer until the 1960s. Luxembourgers arrived in numbers between 1850 and 1870, and later waves from Ireland, Britain, Scandinavia and elsewhere filled the neighborhoods near the East Side factories.

Near downtown you find Italianate and Queen Anne houses, with Prairie School homes in the neighborhoods beside the core. The city also counts over 50 Sears Catalog Homes and seven Lustron all-steel houses. Owners of those, or of any pre-1950 house, will hear buyer questions about old wiring, lead paint, aging plumbing and settling foundations.

A cash offer for such a house is usually priced with the repairs in mind, while a listing buyer tends to raise them after the inspection.

Free, no-obligation offerTell us about your Aurora house and get a written cash offer within 24 hours.Get My Cash Offer →

Why is Aurora called the City of Lights?

In 1881 Aurora became one of the first American cities to light its streets entirely with electricity, and it adopted the City of Lights nickname in 1908. Downtown centers on Stolp Island, where the Paramount Theatre and the Leland Tower, a former hotel that was once the tallest building in Illinois outside Chicago, are both on the National Register of Historic Places.

The Aurora Public Library got its start with a Carnegie grant in 1901, and its main building, the Santori Public Library, opened in June 2015. Museums include the Aurora Regional Fire Museum, the David L. Pierce Art and History Center and the Schingoethe Museum of Native American Culture. Buyers who like a downtown with architecture by Frank Lloyd Wright and Ludwig Mies van der Rohe nearby will ask how close your house is to the island.

Which school districts serve Aurora houses?

The answer changes with the address, because several systems share the city.

  • West Aurora District 129 covers the west bank.
  • East Aurora District 131 covers the east bank.
  • Indian Prairie District 204 covers the far eastern portion in DuPage County.
  • Oswego District 308 runs four schools within Aurora's limits, while parts of the far north end go to Batavia schools and a southwestern corner to Kaneland.

The Illinois Mathematics and Science Academy, a state-funded residential school for grades 10 to 12, is in the city, along with Aurora University and two Waubonsee Community College branches. Across the districts, the city has 46 public schools.

Does Aurora's weather and flood history affect a house sale?

It can. Aurora's climate is humid continental, with annual precipitation near 40 inches. A storm on July 17 and 18, 1996 dropped a state-record 16.94 inches of rain in one day, and floodwater reached nearly every low spot and the neighborhoods along the Fox River.

Buyers near the river therefore tend to raise basement moisture, sump pump age and flood insurance. Keep repair invoices handy and answer honestly about past water. Your insurer or the city's engineering staff can tell you whether your parcel sits in a mapped flood zone.

Sell as-isNo repairs, no cleaning and no showings. We buy Aurora houses in any condition.See My Cash Offer →

What drives the Aurora economy and housing demand?

Manufacturing built the city, and it still sits at the edge of the Illinois Technology and Research Corridor. Caterpillar, Western Electric and Lyon Workspace Products are among the names on its industrial list, and the railroad shops once employed much of the East Side.

The 2022 Economic Census shows $3.12 billion in retail sales and $1.42 billion in health care receipts, and workers spend 27.2 minutes on average getting to their jobs. Downtown has the Paramount Theatre and the Hollywood Casino, and Phillips Park Zoo is also in the city.

  • 72.1% of people 16 and older are in the labor force.
  • 46.4% of residents age 5 and up use another language at home.
  • 26.4% of residents were born outside the United States.

Buyers range from first-time families to investors, so a tidy house on a quiet street draws different interest than a fixer on a busy corner.

What does Aurora's rental licensing mean if my house has tenants?

Each non-owner-occupied unit needs a license and gets inspected once a year, inside and out. The program dates to June 1, 1982, when the city council adopted its Property Maintenance Code. Renewals fall due by August 31, and the Property Standards Division mails renewal forms and schedules inspections by letter.

When a licensed building sells, the code asks for the new owner to be reported to the Operations Department within 3 working days. Property Standards is at 77 S Broadway, 1st Floor, and the licensing line is 630-256-3770. The division also handles high weeds, junk and trash, unsafe stairs, illegal basement apartments and unregistered landlords, and it runs vacant property licensing.

An empty inherited house, or a rental whose tenant has left, can draw a violation notice, so clear those items first.

How are the deed and transfer tax handled on an Aurora sale?

The state's transfer tax is collected as revenue stamps through the recorder of the county where the parcel lies, and the Illinois Department of Revenue notes the same stamp can show payment of a county tax. Buyer and seller sign Form PTAX-203 for filing at that county.

Since Aurora touches four counties, ask the title company which recorder handles your address before you set a signing date, and ask whether any home rule charge applies.

You pick the closing dateClose in as little as 7 days or on the date that works for you, with no fees or commissions.Get My Cash Offer →

Frequently asked questions

Which county is Aurora in?

Parts of four: Kane, DuPage, Kendall and Will. The parcel number on your tax bill tells you which one holds your house, records the deed and sends the tax bill.

Does a tenant-occupied house need a license to sell?

The license belongs to the owner who rents the unit and is renewed by August 31 each year. Report the new owner to the Operations Department within 3 working days after a sale, and call Property Standards at 630-256-3770 with account questions.

Will past flooding hurt the sale?

It can, mainly because buyers worry about repeat water. Tell them about past problems, keep repair records, and mention any sump pump or drainage work. Near the Fox River, expect flood insurance to come up.

Can a house with open code violations be sold?

Yes, and many buyers take houses as-is. Still, find out what is open at your address before you sign anything. Property Standards can explain what it takes to close a case.

Listing or cash offer: how do I decide?

Compare take-home money and timing. A listing may reach a higher price but adds repairs, showings and loan risk, while a cash purchase trades some price for a faster, steadier closing.

Selling in Naperville?

Where is Naperville and what does that mean for a seller?

Naperville is a city about 28 miles west of Chicago on the DuPage River, and it sits in two counties, DuPage and Will. Census estimates for July 1, 2025 show 153,114 residents, a 2.4% rise since the April 2020 count, spread over roughly 39 square miles of land.

The settlement began in 1831 as Naper's Settlement, became a village in 1857 and was reincorporated as a city in 1890. It served as the DuPage County seat from 1839 until Wheaton took that role in 1868. Growth then came in a rush: the census counted 12,933 people in 1960, 85,351 in 1990 and 128,358 in 2000. A house here can therefore be a downtown property older than that boom or a subdivision home from the 1980s and 1990s, and buyers and appraisers treat those two groups differently.

The city spreads across six townships. Winfield, Milton, Naperville and Lisle are on the DuPage side, while Wheatland and DuPage townships are on the Will side. Several enclaves are cut out of the city limits, including the unincorporated Tamarack neighborhood in the southwest, so a Naperville mailing address does not always mean the property is inside city limits.

Which county records a Naperville deed, DuPage or Will?

It depends on which side of the county line the parcel is on, and your tax bill or your last recorded deed shows the county. DuPage parcels go to the DuPage County Recorder, and Will parcels go to the Will County Recorder of Deeds in Joliet.

The two offices publish different fee schedules for the same kind of document:

OfficeStandard deed or document feeWhat the schedule says it includes
DuPage County Recorder$86.00Recording, document storage ($10), GIS ($31), real property ($1) and Rental Housing Support Program ($18)
Will County Recorder of Deeds$90.00 (effective October 1, 2025)A $19.00 Rental Housing Support Program surcharge, which is dropped for government filers

Sources: the DuPage County Recorder forms and fee schedules page and the Will County Recorder fee notice effective October 1, 2025. The DuPage page states that its fees can change without notice, so ask the recorder for the current figure before closing.

For questions about the state transfer declaration, the DuPage page points filers to the Illinois Department of Revenue MyDec help line at 844-445-1114. On the Will side, the recorder's guidelines list what a deed needs: preparer and return addresses, the permanent index number, a legal description, a notarized original deed, the grantee name and address, a tax bill name and address, and a completed transfer declaration or exemption.

How does Naperville's real estate transfer tax stamp work?

Under the city ordinance, the buyer of a residential or commercial property inside incorporated Naperville buys the transfer tax stamp. The city's page prints the rate as $1.50 per $500 of purchase price, rounded up to the next $500 step.

The stamp applies only to incorporated property. The city points owners to its Your Place application, under Planning/Zoning Info, to check whether an address is inside the limits. The Will County Recorder's deed checklist also names Naperville among the municipalities whose transfer stamps must be on a deed.

The paperwork the city lists for a stamp is short:

  • A Statement of Open Account letter, requested online no later than seven business days before closing.
  • A sales contract, a PTAX (MyDec) form or a sheriff's receipt that carries both buyer and seller signatures.
  • A copy of the deed that will be recorded with the county.

Plan for up to seven business days of processing whether you apply online or drop a packet at the Finance Department. The Customer Care Center at 630-420-6059 answers questions Monday through Friday, 7 am to 7 pm. Because the open account statement has its own seven business day lead time, a closing date set only a week out leaves no slack.

When does a Naperville deed need an exempt stamp instead?

An exempt stamp is required when a deed changes on property you already own and no sale price is involved. There is no fee for it, and it covers properties inside the city limits only.

The city's list of examples is:

  • Moving the property into or out of a trust.
  • A divorce, or removing a name.
  • A marriage, or adding a name.
  • A legal name change.
  • A refinance.
  • A foreclosure where the sheriff's deed puts the property in bank ownership. If an individual buys at the sheriff's sale, that buyer purchases a regular stamp.

The exempt packet needs the open account statement, a Certificate for Exemption (mailed and in-person applications only) and a copy of the notarized deed. Anyone moving a house between names ahead of a sale, such as out of a trust or after a divorce, should start with this packet.

Which Naperville permits should a seller check before listing?

Start with any work done after you bought the house. Naperville's permit list includes separate entries for decks, patios and sheds, driveways, fences, generators, lawn sprinkler systems with an RPZ backflow preventer, plumbing, electrical work, swimming pools and residential room additions or alterations.

If you cannot find paperwork for a finished basement, a deck or a sprinkler system, call the city and ask whether a permit was issued for that address. It is easier to learn the answer before a buyer's inspector or attorney raises the question.

If the house has unfinished work you do not want to complete, a buyer paying cash can take it as it stands and handle permits afterward.

How do floods and weather affect a Naperville house sale?

The flood record matters more than the snow. The area took 14 inches of rain in under 24 hours in 1996, DuPage County was declared a disaster area, and damage topped $30 million. A second major flood followed in 2013.

Much of the land along the West Branch of the DuPage River is owned by the Forest Preserve District, which keeps development out of the floodplain and reduces overbank damage. Even so, ask your insurance agent about your parcel before you list, since buyers' lenders will ask the same question about flood zones.

Winters are cold and snowy and summers are hot. The recorded extremes are 105 degrees Fahrenheit and minus 29. Average precipitation runs about 37.7 inches a year, which makes sump pumps, gutters and grading the items buyers examine first on older homes.

Sell as-isNo repairs, no cleaning and no showings. We buy Naperville houses in any condition.See My Cash Offer →

How expensive are Naperville homes, and who lives in them?

Census estimates for 2020 to 2024 paint Naperville as a high-priced, owner-heavy market:

  • Homes lived in by their owners: 74.8%.
  • Typical home value: $540,200 (median, owner-occupied).
  • Median selected monthly owner costs: $3,154 with a mortgage and $1,305 without.
  • Median gross rent: $1,885.
  • Households: 54,847, at 2.70 persons per household.
  • Median household income: $155,105, and 72.5% of adults over 25 have finished a four-year degree.
  • Average commute: 30.5 minutes each way.

Roughly 22.5% of residents were born abroad, and 26.9% of those age 5 and up speak another language at home.

Which schools, roads and employers anchor Naperville neighborhoods?

Two school districts cover most of the city. Naperville Community Unit District 203 serves central and northern Naperville and runs Naperville Central and Naperville North high schools. Indian Prairie School District 204 serves much of the rest. Small areas fall in District 200 on the DuPage side, and Plainfield District 202 and Valley View District 365U on the Will side.

Interstate 88, the Reagan Tollway, crosses the north end, and Illinois Route 59 meets it at a diverging diamond interchange that opened in 2015. Ogden Avenue is US 34. Metra and Amtrak both stop in Naperville on the BNSF line.

The city's 2020 financial report, as summarized by Wikipedia, listed Edward Hospital with 4,500 employees, District 204 with 3,071 and Nokia with 2,750 as the largest employers. North Central College, on a 59-acre campus downtown, has been in Naperville since 1870.

Frequently asked questions

Can I sell my Naperville house without fixing it up?

Yes. Whether a buyer takes the property in present condition is a term of your contract. The city side of the closing is the transfer stamp packet and the statement of open accounts, and neither of those asks you to make repairs first.

Who pays the Naperville transfer tax stamp?

The buyer does. The city's ordinance requires buyers of residential or commercial property inside incorporated Naperville to purchase the stamp, at the rate of $1.50 per $500 of purchase price printed on the city's page.

How early should I start the Naperville paperwork before closing?

At least seven business days early. The city asks for the Statement of Open Account request no later than seven business days before closing, and stamp processing itself can take up to seven business days.

Does it matter if my Naperville home is on the Will County side?

It changes where the deed is recorded and the fee. Will County parcels record with the Will County Recorder of Deeds, whose standard document fee is $90.00 from October 1, 2025, while DuPage County lists $86.00. The city's own stamp rules are the same on both sides.

Which deed changes in Naperville need an exempt stamp?

Any change of name on a house you already own, such as adding a spouse, removing a name after a divorce, moving the property into a trust or refinancing. A sheriff's deed that puts the property in bank ownership also qualifies, with no fee for the exempt stamp.

Where is Joliet, Illinois, and how is the city laid out?

Joliet serves as Will County's seat of government, about 40 miles southwest of Chicago, and a small part of the city lies in Kendall County. The 2020 census counted 150,362 people, which made it the third most populous city in Illinois, and the Census Bureau's July 1, 2025 estimate is 152,241.

The city has an irregular, sprawling shape that reaches into nine townships, more than any other Illinois city: Joliet, Plainfield, Troy, New Lenox, Jackson, Channahon and Lockport in Will County, and Na-Au-Say and Seward in Kendall County. It grew along the Des Plaines River, and locals speak of an east side and a west side relative to the river, plus a far west side that includes the Kendall County land.

That patchwork has a practical result. Your address may sit in a different school district, assessor's office and tax bill from a neighbor a few blocks away, so check the parcel before assuming anything.

What is Joliet's history, and what does it mean for older houses?

Joliet was settled in 1833 and reincorporated as a city in 1852. Joliet Iron and Steel Works ran from 1869 to 1936 and was once the second largest steel mill in the country. The old prison, completed in 1858 from local limestone, closed in 2002 and has offered tours since 2018. U.S. Route 66 runs through town, and the first Dairy Queen opened here.

Housing history left its mark. During the 1930s many owners could not keep up their large houses, and in the 1940s big Victorian homes were divided to house several families. Absentee landlords and deferred maintenance followed, and heavy use of vinyl siding changed several historic limestone buildings. The Joliet East Side Historic District, created in 1980, and the Upper Bluff Historic District, created in 1991, are both listed on the federal historic register.

  • If your house stands in one of those districts, ask the city's Planning and Zoning staff what review applies before you plan repairs.
  • If a large older house was ever split into units, bring any records of that conversion.
  • Buyers of pre-war houses commonly ask about foundations and wiring, so have repair records ready.

What do the Census numbers show for Joliet homeowners?

QuickFacts for 2020 to 2024 shows 73.7 percent of homes owner-occupied, with a median home value of $265,800 among them, and 51,055 households averaging 2.89 people. Median gross rent is $1,276, the median household income is $92,201, and 11.1 percent of residents are in poverty. About 91.1 percent had not moved in the past year, and the mean commute is 28.8 minutes.

Homeowners with a mortgage had median monthly owner costs of $1,960, compared with $819 for owners with no mortgage.

  • About 26.3 percent of homes are not owner-occupied, so landlords and tenants figure in many Joliet sales.
  • Only 11.5 percent of residents are 65 or older, and 24.4 percent are under 18.
  • With 34.2 percent Hispanic or Latino residents and 28.8 percent speaking another language at home, bilingual paperwork can be useful.

What jobs, schools and roads shape the Joliet housing market?

Joliet has moved from a steel and manufacturing town to a commuter city. Downtown draws on the Rialto Square Theatre, the Joliet Slammers' ballpark and two casinos, and the largest employers in the city's 2017 financial report included Amazon, a Joliet hospital, Will County, Joliet Junior College and the public school districts.

The motto Crossroads of Mid-America on the city seal points to the meeting of I-80 and I-55 near Channahon. US 6, US 30, US 52 and US 66 also cross the city, as do Illinois Routes 7, 53, 59 and 171. The Joliet Transportation Center is the final stop for the Metra Heritage Corridor and Rock Island District lines, and Amtrak stops at Joliet Union Station. Pace buses leave a downtown terminal about once an hour, six days a week.

Schools vary by address. Joliet Public School District 86 and several smaller districts feed Joliet Township High School District 204. Other parts of the city fall in Plainfield District 202, New Lenox District 122 and, in Kendall County, Minooka and Oswego districts. Joliet Junior College and the University of St. Francis are the local colleges.

What does the City of Joliet require before a house sells?

The seller of residential or commercial property inside city limits buys the transfer tax stamp. The city prints the cost as $3.00 per $1,000 of purchase price. The stamp applies only to incorporated Joliet, and the city offers an address verification map and a phone line for borderline addresses.

  • A completed water and lien letter must reach the city at least four business days before closing. Forms received later may not be processed before the closing date.
  • An exempt stamp, with no charge, is needed on any deed change inside city limits, such as adding or removing a name, moving a property into or out of a trust, or a divorce.
  • Exempt stamps require the original signed and notarized deed, not a copy, with exempt language on it or a completed city exemption form.
  • Start or stop water service through Customer Service at 815-724-3820, option 2.

Questions about stamps go to the Customer Service real estate transfer stamps desk at 815-724-3902. Joliet's FAQ also says most exterior projects, including fences, decks, pools, patios, garages, additions and concrete work, need a building permit and a plat of survey, so look for those before you list.

How is a deed recorded in Will County, and what does it cost?

The Will County Recorder of Deeds is at 158 N. Scott Street in Joliet, phone 815-740-4637. Its fee schedule effective October 1, 2025 lists $90.00 for a standard document and $118.00 for a non-standard one. A standard document stays within up to five property index number references and up to five related document references.

The Recorder's guidelines list what a deed needs: a notarized original deed, grantee name and address, a tax bill-to name and address, a property address, a permanent index number, the real estate transfer tax declaration or exemption, and the municipal transfer tax stamp. Joliet is one of nine Will County municipalities that require that stamp.

Which Joliet property tax and rental rules should a seller know?

Joliet's FAQ sends Will County owners to the Will County Treasurer's Office or the Supervisor of Assessments for tax bills, homestead exemptions and appeals, and Kendall County owners to the Kendall County Treasurer and Assessment Office. The back of your property tax bill lists your township assessor's contact.

If the house is a rental, the city runs a Rental Inspection Program with an owner registration form, a landlord checklist and a fee schedule. Ask Neighborhood Services at 815-724-4090 whether the property is registered before you tell a buyer anything about it.

The city also bans parking on streets automatically when 2 inches or more of snow falls within 24 hours, under City Code Sec. 19-142, and prohibits boats, RVs, trailers and trucks over 8,000 pounds on streets and in residential parkways. Buyers who own a trailer or boat will ask about both.

What are the realistic ways to sell a Joliet house fast?

Each option suits a different situation.

  • List with an agent. A house in good repair does well on the open market.
  • Sell on your own. You handle the contract, the city stamp and the water and lien letter yourself.
  • Accept a cash offer. It can fit an inherited house, a rental with tenants or a property with a failed inspection, and closing can follow the schedule you need.

Work backward from closing. The water and lien letter is due four business days ahead, the stamp must be bought before recording, and the deed must be the original. Missing any one of them can push a closing back.

What is the population of Joliet, IL?

The Census Bureau estimated 152,241 residents on July 1, 2025. The 2020 census counted 150,362.

How much is the Joliet transfer stamp?

The city prints $3.00 per $1,000 of purchase price, and the seller buys the stamp. Exempt stamps carry no charge.

How early must the water and lien letter reach the City of Joliet?

At least four business days before closing. Forms received later than that may not be processed before the closing date.

Where do I record a deed for a Joliet house?

Joliet is the Will County seat, so deeds go to the Will County Recorder of Deeds at 158 N. Scott Street. The fee schedule effective October 1, 2025 lists $90.00 for a standard document.

Does a Joliet house in Kendall County use a different office?

Yes. A small part of Joliet is in Kendall County, so that parcel's tax bill and deed run through Kendall County offices. The city's address verification map and the tax bill show which county applies.

Which sale route fits a Rockford homeowner?

Rockford owners can hire an agent, try a sale without one, or deal directly with a buyer who pays cash and takes on the repairs. Your pick depends on what shape the house is in, what you still owe, and how quickly you must relocate.

Rockford is the biggest city in Illinois outside the Chicago area, and with 61,324 households and a large rental share, its buyers range from owner-occupants to investors with very different budgets and expectations. Ask yourself which of these fits:

  • The structure is sound and you can sit through showings and a buyer's loan approval.
  • A failing roof, tired mechanicals or code citations make a pre-sale renovation unappealing.
  • The property is a rental, either with a tenant in place or sitting empty and costing you money.
  • You inherited it, or you live elsewhere and cannot babysit a long listing.

Selling for cash avoids the lender's appraisal, a frequent source of delay. Weigh any offer against what a listing might really produce, and obtain the terms in writing.

What does the Census show about Rockford housing?

Renters make up a big part of Rockford. Only 54.9 percent of occupied units are owner-occupied in the five-year survey that ends in 2024, so investors and landlords drive a lot of the demand.

The city counted 152,871 residents in 2010 and 148,655 in 2020, and the Census estimate for 2025 is slightly lower again. With a median home value near $129,000, repair costs weigh heavily against a sale price, which is one reason owners of older houses look at as-is sales.

How do Rockford's geography and weather affect a house?

Rockford spreads along the Rock River in far northern Illinois, about 90 miles west-northwest of downtown Chicago and 70 miles south-southeast of Madison. The city sits mostly in Winnebago County, with a sliver reaching into Ogle County. The Kishwaukee River joins the Rock at the southern end, and Spring, Keith and Kent creeks feed it from the east and west.

Weather matters to sellers. Violent thunderstorms are common from March through June, and one on July 5, 2003 left about 70,000 people without power, some for a week. Winters bring blizzards, and annual precipitation averages about 37 inches. Buyers and their inspectors therefore look closely at:

  • Roof age and shingle condition after hail and wind events.
  • Basement moisture near the river and creek corridors.
  • Furnace age, since January highs average only about 29 degrees.
  • Trees, which give Rockford its Forest City nickname but can damage roofs and sewer lines.

Fixing or documenting these items before a showing helps, and it also helps you fill out the state disclosure report accurately.

What is Rockford's background, and which roads do buyers use?

The city began in 1834 as the settlement of Midway, named for its position about halfway between Lake Michigan and the Mississippi River. It later became known for heavy machinery and furniture, and it carries the nickname Forest City for its tree-lined residential streets. Landmarks include Anderson Japanese Gardens, Klehm Arboretum, Tinker Swiss Cottage and the Burpee Museum of Natural History.

Highways define how buyers get around. Interstate 39 and Interstate 90, the Jane Addams Memorial Tollway, serve the region, along with U.S. Routes 20 and 51 and Illinois Routes 2, 70 and 251. The Rockford Mass Transit District runs 17 fixed routes with about 40 buses to Rockford, Loves Park and Machesney Park. Chicago Rockford International Airport lies at the southern edge of the city. Rockford University and Rock Valley College are among the post-secondary schools in the city.

Who employs Rockford residents, and which schools serve the city?

As of January 2024 the ten largest employers in Rockford were Rockford Public School District 205 with 4,075 employees, UW Health's SwedishAmerican Hospital with 3,780, Mercy Health with 3,000, OSF Saint Anthony Medical Center with 2,200, and UPS, Collins Aerospace and Woodward with about 2,000 each. Amazon, Walmart and the Stellantis Belvidere Assembly Plant follow.

The region leads Illinois in aerospace production employment, and Chicago Rockford International Airport is one of the faster-growing cargo airports in the country. After a long decline in heavy machinery and furniture manufacturing, healthcare, aerospace and logistics now give the area a more varied job base.

Most of the city sits in Rockford Public School District 205, which has 41 schools and about 27,700 students. The district's high schools are Auburn, East, Guilford and Jefferson. Small parts of the city fall in Winnebago Unit District 323, Harlem District 122 and Meridian District 223, and the Ogle County portion is in Meridian. Call the district to confirm yours before you describe the house to anyone.

What city rules apply to Rockford rentals and property standards?

Rockford keeps a Rental and Short-Term Rental Registry that supports its Residential Quality Support Ordinance and its Short-Term Rental Ordinance. The goal is less chronic nuisance activity through better communication between the city and landlords, who register and update their details on the registry website.

The city's Property Standards division inspects exteriors and interiors for code and ordinance violations. A few of the items it lists would also come up in a buyer's inspection:

  • Roofs must be sound, and a tarp is not a repair. A roofing permit is required for any roofing work.
  • Heat must be supplied from October 1 to April 1 and maintain at least 68 degrees in habitable rooms.
  • Insect screens are required from April 1 to October 1 on doors, windows and other openings.
  • Smoke detectors must be outside each sleeping area, and carbon monoxide alarms must be within 15 feet of every room used for sleeping.
  • Property addresses must be visible from the road.

The city does not inspect for mold. If a buyer's inspector flags it, you would need a private specialist. Before listing, ask Property Standards whether an open case exists at your address.

How does a Rockford sale get recorded in Winnebago County?

Deeds and mortgages for Rockford parcels are indexed by the Winnebago County Recorder's Office at 404 Elm Street, Room 405. The fee schedule dated January 1, 2025 shows $54.00 for a standard document and $66.00 for a non-standard one. A standard document uses white 8.5 by 11 inch paper, black ink, margins of at least a half inch, and a blank 3 by 5 inch space at the top right of page one. The office takes no copies, and every document needs a return-to name and address.

E-recordings are processed daily, with the last review at 2:30 p.m., and later submissions wait for the next business day. If timing matters at closing, tell whoever handles your title work. The deed must also carry the state transfer declaration or an exemption statement.

A county notice dated June 1, 2026 said that Illinois counties must adopt a review process for deeds that look fraudulent and keep a property fraud alert system, with the review expected to begin on or after September 8, 2026. Owners can sign up free online for alerts about suspicious filings against their property.

Frequently asked questions

Does a landlord have to be on the Rockford rental registry?

The city runs a Rental and Short-Term Rental Registry for landlords, so make sure your entry is up to date before a sale. A buyer or title company may ask whether the property is registered.

What does it cost to record a deed in Winnebago County?

The schedule dated January 1, 2025 shows $54.00 for a standard document and $66.00 for a non-standard one. Check with the Recorder's Office before closing, since schedules change.

Will Rockford inspect for mold before I sell?

No. The Property Standards page says the city does not inspect for mold, so a worried buyer would need a private specialist.

Is Rockford in one county or two?

Rockford is mostly in Winnebago County, with a small portion extending into Ogle County. Check the parcel number on your tax bill to see which county records your deed.

How large is Rockford?

The 2025 Census estimate is 147,384 people, slightly below the 148,655 counted in 2020. Rockford is the Winnebago County seat and ranks fifth among Illinois cities by population.

How do I sell a house fast in Elgin, IL?

Selling quickly in Elgin generally means either a cash buyer or a listing that is ready on day one, and condition plus your calendar usually decide between them. Elgin is a large city, with 115,476 residents estimated for July 1, 2025, so buyers and investors are active, but permits, rental licensing and Kane County or Cook County paperwork still decide how smoothly a closing runs.

Elgin straddles two counties, Kane and Cook, so recording and tax bills depend on which county holds your parcel. Check the county named on your tax bill before you contact a recorder.

  • Confirm the parcel number, the county and the township that assesses your home.
  • Request a mortgage payoff figure and look for liens or judgments.
  • Pull permit records for roofs, windows, water heaters and furnaces.
  • If the house is rented, learn how the city's rental license treats a sale.

What makes Elgin different from other Chicago suburbs?

Elgin sits about 35 miles northwest of Chicago along the Fox River and was the sixth most populous city in Illinois at the 2020 Census, with 114,797 residents. The Gifford brothers founded it in April 1835 on the Chicago to Galena stagecoach route. Gail Borden opened a condensed milk factory here in 1866, and the Elgin Watch Company later employed three generations of residents until its factory stopped production in 1965.

Older housing is part of Elgin's character. The city has Queen Anne homes built for watch company executives, Sears catalog kit homes from 1908 to 1940, and early cobblestone houses, with two districts listed in the federal register of historic places. Newer housing sits on the west and southwest sides. The Grand Victoria riverboat casino opened in the 1990s and became a major source of city income, and downtown has gained townhouses, lofts and condo towers since then.

The Fox River Trail, Lords Park (112 acres) and Wing Park (121 acres) give the city parkland that appears in many listings.

What do Census numbers show about Elgin homes and owners?

The Census Bureau lists 39,317 Elgin households for 2020 to 2024, with 2.88 people per household and a 71.9 percent owner-occupied rate. Owner-occupied homes had a middle value of $273,000, and rent at the midpoint was $1,361 per month. Roughly half of residents age five and up, 48.1 percent, speak another language at home, which makes Elgin one of the more multilingual cities in the area.

Which school districts and commute routes matter when selling in Elgin?

Five public school districts serve Elgin. Elgin Area School District U-46 covers most of the city, ranks as the second largest district in Illinois and enrolls close to 40,000 children across Cook, DuPage and Kane counties. Elgin High School and Larkin High School are its two high schools in the city. Community Unit School Districts 301, 300 and 303 serve western and northwestern pockets.

Commute access is a selling point. Interstate 90 and U.S. 20 cross the city, along with Illinois Routes 19, 25, 31, 47, 58, 59 and 72 and Randall Road. Metra's Milwaukee District West Line has three Elgin stations, National Street, Elgin and Big Timber Road, with service to Chicago Union Station. The Pace bus system meets at the Elgin Transportation Center at 102 West Chicago Street.

Describe the district and nearest station in a listing, since buyers filter on both. A house in a western pocket may report a different district than one near downtown.

What permits and historic rules apply to an Elgin house?

Elgin's Community Development Department, at 150 Dexter Court, issues building permits. The city's permit page says review takes about 3 to 5 business days for quick permits such as roofs, windows, water heaters and furnaces, 7 to 10 business days for projects needing planner review such as sheds, fences, patios and driveways, and 10 to 15 business days for plans examiner review such as basement remodels, in-ground pools and decks larger than 100 square feet. Applications go to permits@ElginIL.gov.

The same page warns that work started without a permit can draw a stop-work order and fines, and that unpermitted work may have to be removed if it does not meet requirements. If the property is a designated landmark or lies in a historic district, exterior changes require a Certificate of Appropriateness. Elgin keeps an interactive historic property map so you can check an address.

Fixing permit gaps before you list helps, and for houses with several unpermitted changes, a buyer who purchases as-is can take them on directly. Call 311, or 847-931-6001 from outside the city, to find out whether a past project needs a permit record.

What happens to an Elgin rental license when the property sells?

Elgin requires a rental license for any residential property occupied by someone who is not a blood relative. The city states that licenses are not transferable and are voided automatically when the property sells, and the new owner has 30 days from closing to apply. Operating without one can bring a $500 citation from Code Enforcement.

Fees depend on unit count. The city's schedule lists $149.00 for one to five units, with one unit inspected. A license lasts one year, and a property that passes its initial inspection with landlord training completed receives a two year extension. For single-family rentals, inspectors review the entire interior and exterior, and any code violation found must be corrected within 30 days or the license can be suspended or revoked.

  • Sellers of occupied rentals should tell the buyer about the 30 day licensing window.
  • Unpermitted changes found in an inspection are subject to enforcement no matter who made them, which concerns buyers.
  • Short-term rentals through Airbnb or VRBO also need the license, according to the city's FAQ.

How do recording, taxes and utilities work at an Elgin closing?

On the Cook side, the Clerk's schedule shows .50 per $500 going to the state and .25 per $500 to the county, and it names the seller as the liable party. The Clerk's schedule effective April 1, 2024 prices a deed at $107. For parcels in Kane County, ask the Kane County Clerk's office for the current transfer declaration and recording fee instructions. Your title company normally manages submissions in both counties.

Kane County's treasurer guide explains that a tax bill follows the property regardless of who owned it during the billing year, so check your closing statement to see whether the seller credits the buyer. A Kane County assessment complaint has to reach the Board of Review within 30 days of the township's published assessment notice. Elgin Township has its own assessor.

For a final meter reading, call Elgin's 311 line. The city's rental page says a Citizen Advocate at 311 schedules a final meter reading for the owner's account. Ask the city at the same time whether any balance must be settled before closing.

Frequently asked questions

Does Elgin charge a transfer tax on home sales?

Cook County's Clerk shows the state at .50 per $500 and the county at .25 per $500 for parcels on the Cook side. Ask Elgin's Finance Department whether any city-level stamp applies to your sale, and ask your title company to confirm the full charges before you close.

Is my Elgin rental license transferable to a buyer?

No. The city states that licenses cannot be transferred and are voided automatically when the property is sold. The buyer has 30 days from closing to apply for a new license, and the first license year carries an inspection.

How long do Elgin permit reviews take?

Quick permits such as roofs, windows, water heaters and furnaces take about 3 to 5 business days. Planner-review projects take 7 to 10 business days, and plans examiner reviews take 10 to 15. Contact permits@ElginIL.gov for the status of a specific application.

Which county records an Elgin deed?

It depends on where the parcel sits, because Elgin lies in both Kane and Cook counties. The tax bill names the county, and the title company files with that county's office.

Can I sell an Elgin house that has unpermitted work?

Yes, but disclose it and expect questions. Elgin says unpermitted work can be ordered removed if it fails requirements. Many sellers close permit gaps first, while an as-is buyer may take on the work and the risk for you.

Which selling path suits a Springfield homeowner?

Springfield homeowners usually weigh a brokered listing, a do-it-yourself sale and a cash purchase of the house exactly as it stands. Price, speed and repair work set them apart, and the best fit follows from the condition of the property and your move-out date.

  • Brokered listing: works for a sound house when you can wait out showings and a buyer's mortgage approval.
  • Do-it-yourself sale: you control price and buyer pool, and you arrange the paperwork yourself or through counsel.
  • Cash purchase: fits an estate house, an empty house or one with deferred upkeep, because no mortgage underwriting is involved.

At a median owned-home value of $162,100, every month of utilities, insurance and mowing on a vacant house eats into a slow listing. Weigh the amount you keep after repairs and carrying months against the asking figure.

What kind of city is Springfield for a home seller?

Springfield is the capital of Illinois and the Sangamon County seat, in the central part of the state. The city lies about 80 miles northeast of St. Louis, 40 miles west of Decatur and roughly 200 miles southwest of Chicago. Its land area is 61.14 square miles.

The ground is flat glacial till, with relief of no more than about 20 feet across most of the plain. Lake Springfield, a 4,200 acre reservoir created in 1935 by damming Lick Creek, supplies the city's drinking water. Numbered streets run from First Street to 32nd Street in the far east, and the city lists at least twenty neighborhoods, including Enos Park, Aristocracy Hill, Harvard Park, Lincoln Park and the Medical District.

The housing stock spans more than a century. The Dana-Thomas House, a Frank Lloyd Wright design built in 1902 and 1903, stands in the city, and historic Route 66 passes through it. A house from an earlier era may have older wiring or plumbing, and buyers price that in. A cash purchase can sidestep that negotiation.

Four separate municipalities, Jerome, Leland Grove, Southern View and Grandview, sit entirely inside Springfield's borders. If your mailing address says Springfield but the village differs, the permit, tax and transfer rules of that village apply instead.

What do Census figures show about Springfield housing?

Springfield's housing costs sit well below the Chicago region, and renters make up more than a third of households. Figures come from the 2020 to 2024 American Community Survey period.

Which school districts and local institutions affect Springfield buyers?

District 186 covers most of Springfield, with 24 elementary schools, five middle schools and the high schools Lanphier, Springfield and Southeast. Fringe areas belong to Ball-Chatham 5, Rochester 3A, Riverton 14, Williamsville 15, Pleasant Plains 8 and Unit 16.

Buyers who work for the state or a hospital often search by commute and district, so name both in any listing or offer conversation.

How does Springfield weather affect a house on the market?

Hot, humid summers and cold winters are normal here, and the city sits at the far edge of Tornado Alley. Two F2 tornadoes crossed Springfield on March 12, 2006, damaging hundreds of buildings. Annual precipitation averages about 38 inches, and snowfall averages 21.8 inches.

Inspectors for a buyer typically look at roof age, gutters, sump pumps and basements. Hold on to storm repair receipts and any claim paperwork, because a buyer's insurer may ask for them. A cash buyer purchasing as-is will still want to see the roof and foundation, and the negotiation stays between two parties.

What does Springfield require for permits, code orders and vacant buildings?

The city's Building and Zoning Department, located in Municipal Center West at 300 S. 7th Street, handles building permits. Its registration form for vacant buildings quotes a rule from the International Property Maintenance Code: an owner who has received a compliance order or notice of violation may not sell, transfer or mortgage the building until the order is complied with, unless the buyer gets a copy and signs a notarized statement accepting responsibility for the corrections.

The form adds that a certificate of occupancy must be obtained before a vacant building is occupied again. A vacant house with two or more violations calls for a written plan with a repair schedule or a demolition plan. Ask the department for current fees and forms before you register or sell a vacant house.

The city's public works page also notes that basement backups caused by private sewer laterals are not counted as city sanitary sewer overflows. If your house has flooded, say so plainly to buyers and keep plumbing records.

How are Springfield property taxes assessed and paid?

Springfield sits in Capital Township, and Sangamon County's Supervisor of Assessments keeps ownership, sales and assessment records for every parcel. The county says non-farm property is reassessed once every four years, and an assessed value is one third of market value before a multiplier is applied.

  • A value dispute begins at the township assessor's desk and moves to the county Board of Review, which usually takes filings from July 1 through September 10.
  • Unhappy with that ruling, you get 30 days from its mailing to go on to the state Property Tax Appeal Board.
  • Exemption forms and mailing address changes: Supervisor of Assessments, 217-753-6805.
  • Bill copies and payments: County Treasurer, 217-753-6800.

The 2025 bills, payable in 2026, came due June 5 and September 4, 2026. Payments were accepted through November 5, and the annual tax sale followed on November 6. The county's FAQ explains that taxes paid in a year are for the prior year, and that closing papers normally give the new owner an allowance for the months the seller held the house.

After the deed is recorded, the county says it takes about four to six weeks for the ownership record and the tax bill address to change, so a buyer should confirm where the next bill is going.

What does recording a deed in Sangamon County cost?

Sangamon's recorder charges $64 to file a standard real property document, meaning letter-size paper with a 3 by 5 inch blank area at top right. Anything outside that format costs $84. The office's number is 217-535-3150.

Deeds can also need transfer stamps, which the same fee page prices at 50 cents per $500 for the state and 25 cents per $500 for the county. Any city charge or final utility step is a question for your title company, and each item will show on the settlement statement.

Is a Springfield house with open code violations sellable?

Yes, with conditions. The property maintenance rule on the city's form requires either that the violations be corrected first or that the buyer receive the notice and sign a notarized statement accepting the repairs.

What transfer stamps apply to a deed in Sangamon County?

The recorder prints 50 cents per $500 for the state and 25 cents per $500 for the county. Your title company can say whether anything further applies.

Who do I call to change the tax bill address after a sale?

Send the request in writing, by fax or in person to the Supervisor of Assessments, whose number is 217-753-6805. The county does not take address changes by phone, and the owner is responsible for sending the new address.

How often is a Springfield house reassessed?

Sangamon County states that non-farm property is reassessed every four years, though individual parcels can change sooner when there are physical changes or corrections.

What is Springfield's population?

About 112,989 people lived in Springfield on July 1, 2025 by Census Bureau estimate, down from the 114,394 counted in 2020.

What is Peoria's history and layout?

Peoria was the earliest permanent European settlement in what became Illinois. French explorers built Fort Crevecoeur here in 1680, Fort Clark followed in 1813, and the town took the name Peoria when the county was organized in 1825. It became a village in 1835 and a city in 1845.

The city covers about 48 square miles of land, and its neighborhoods include Downtown, the East Bluff, the West Bluff, the Uplands, Moss-Bradley, North Valley, Northwest Peoria, the Heart of Peoria, University East, and the Glen Oak-Flanagan and Randolph-Roanoke historic districts. Several of those areas, such as Averyville and El Vista, began as separate unincorporated towns that the city absorbed, so a Peoria sale can look very different from one neighborhood to the next.

How big is the Peoria housing market, and who lives there?

The Census Bureau counted 113,150 residents in 2020 and estimated 110,920 for July 2025, a drop of 2.0 percent from the 2020 base. Pekin, across the river, has about 31,000.

What jobs and hospitals drive demand in Peoria?

Health care leads. OSF HealthCare has been the top employer since 2021 and moved its headquarters into a renovated downtown building in 2022. It opened a $250 million cancer institute in February 2024. Carle Health completed its purchase of Methodist and Proctor hospitals from UnityPoint in 2023 and is the third-largest employer.

Industry still matters:

  • Caterpillar Tractor Co. was formed in 1925, kept its world headquarters in Peoria for over 110 years, and remains the second-biggest employer even though the headquarters moved to Deerfield after a late 2017 announcement.
  • Komatsu America builds off-highway trucks in Peoria and announced a new office building in September 2024.
  • Bradley University, Methodist College, the OSF St. Francis College of Nursing, the University of Illinois College of Medicine at Peoria and Illinois Central College's north campus are based in the city.

The hospitals cluster in a medical district near Interstate 74 and Knoxville Avenue, southeast of downtown.

Which roads and school districts matter for a Peoria address?

Interstate 74 runs through downtown and crosses the river on the Murray Baker Bridge. Interstate 474 forms a southern bypass, and Interstate 155 runs south from Morton toward Lincoln. Illinois Routes 6, 8, 29 and 40 and U.S. Route 150 serve the city itself.

Several school districts cover the city:

  • Peoria Public Schools District 150 serves most of it, with Richwoods, Manual and Peoria High School, the oldest high school in Illinois.
  • Dunlap Community Unit School District 323 serves the far north and northwest.
  • Pleasant Valley School District 62, Limestone Community High School District 310, Peoria Heights District 325 and Illinois Valley Central District 321 cover edge areas.

Because a few blocks can change a child's district, give buyers the district name that matches the address.

How does Peoria's weather affect older houses?

Peoria has a humid continental climate. Precipitation averages about 36 inches a year and snowfall about 26.3 inches. The recorded extremes run from minus 27 degrees in January 1884 to 113 degrees in July 1936, and the 1991 to 2020 normals put July afternoons near 86 degrees and January afternoons near 34.

Swings that wide are hard on older roofs, flashing, chimneys and basement walls. A buyer's inspector will ask how old the roof, chimney and basement walls are and when they were last repaired. Collect receipts and permit records before you list.

What must you do with a Peoria rental or vacant property?

The city requires registration of rental properties, vacant residential properties and any dwelling the owner does not live in. Owners renew by February 28 each year. A new registration is due within 30 days after closing or after the home becomes non-owner occupied.

Fees listed by the city:

  • Renewal for a single-family home is $75; a multi-family property pays $75 for the first unit and $20 for each additional unit.
  • New single-family registrations cost $75 from January 1 to September 30 and $50 from October 1 to December 31.
  • A late registration fee of $150 per property applies after February 28 or more than 30 days after purchase.

You can register as exempt when the property is vacant and for sale, with an MLS or other listing as proof, when it is in probate or estate settlement, when an immediate family member lives there, when it holds a city Mothball Permit, or when an owner-occupied home is temporarily vacant for up to six months. Owners who live outside Peoria, Tazewell and Woodford counties must appoint a local property manager. Tell the city if you sell or buy a property, and use the Change of Status form to deactivate a sold property's registration.

What does the Peoria transfer declaration require at closing?

The City of Peoria's real estate transfer declaration prints a tax of $2.50 per $1,000 of consideration or part thereof. It also asks you to check whether the property will be owner occupied or non-owner occupied. If the non-owner box is checked, section 5-522(a) of the city code requires the property to be registered as non-owner occupied at the time of closing.

The form lists exemptions, including deeds where the actual consideration is less than $100, tax deeds, deeds that only confirm or correct a prior recorded deed, and deeds to or from governmental bodies. The county side runs separately: Peoria County takes part in the state MyDec system, which allows the PTAX-203 to be submitted electronically before the deed is recorded. Ask your closing attorney or title company to prepare the city form with the county filing so nothing holds up the recording.

How can you sell a Peoria house fast?

With a median value of $156,200 and a large rental share, a house that needs work often sells to an investor. Those buyers pay cash, close on your schedule and buy as-is, while a listed sale usually means repairs, showings and a lender's appraisal.

  • Decide whether the house is owner occupied, vacant or rented, since that sets the registration steps.

How much is the City of Peoria real estate transfer tax?

The city's transfer declaration prints $2.50 per $1,000 of consideration or part thereof. The form includes a list of exempt deed types. Ask your closing attorney to complete it with the PTAX-203 filed through the county.

Do I have to register a Peoria house I am selling?

Only if it is not owner occupied. Vacant homes listed for sale qualify for an exempt registration when you give the city an MLS or other listing as proof. After a sale, tell the city and use the Change of Status form to deactivate the registration.

When is Peoria's non-owner-occupied registration due?

Renewals are due every year by February 28, and new properties must be registered within 30 days after closing or after becoming non-owner occupied. A $150 late fee applies after those dates.

Which school district is my Peoria house in?

Most of Peoria is in District 150, but Dunlap District 323, Pleasant Valley District 62, Limestone District 310, Peoria Heights District 325 and Illinois Valley Central District 321 cover other parts. Check the address with the district before you list.

Is Peoria a good market for a quick cash sale?

A cash sale is an option for many houses. Only 57.5 percent of units are owner occupied, so investors and landlords are part of the buyer pool. Compare any offer against a listed sale after repairs, fees and carrying costs.

Where is Champaign and why does the university matter to home sellers?

Champaign is a city in Champaign County in east-central Illinois, and it shares the main University of Illinois campus with its twin city, Urbana. The 2020 census counted 88,302 residents, making it the tenth most populous municipality in the state and the fourth largest outside the Chicago area.

The university is the biggest fact in the local housing market. The University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign enrolls more than 50,000 students a year, and Parkland College adds about 9,000. Whether a house sits near campus, near Parkland on the northwest side or out toward the newer southwest subdivisions changes who the likely buyer or tenant is.

How did Champaign begin?

The city dates to 1855, when the Illinois Central Railroad laid its track two miles west of downtown Urbana. The new town was first called West Urbana and took the name Champaign when it received a city charter in 1860. The name comes from Champaign County, Ohio, which took it from a French word for open, level country.

The flat prairie location matters for houses in the city. Champaign sits on relatively high ground for the region, and downtown drains toward Boneyard Creek. Ask your insurer or the city about drainage if your street is near the creek, since a buyer's inspector will notice a wet basement.

What are Campustown and downtown Champaign like for property owners?

Campustown, along Green Street, is the retail and entertainment district for students. Streetscape work finished around 2002 and was followed by high-rise apartment buildings, including the 18-story Burnham 310 and the 24-story 309 Green, both opened in 2008, and a 14-story complex finished in 2014 at Sixth and Green.

Downtown Champaign is a separate district around City Building and the Virginia Theatre, a restored 1,463-seat theater that opened on December 28, 1921. In the 1980s a section of Neil Street was closed to cars as a pedestrian mall, but business declined and the experiment ended. Later mixed-use buildings and a city-funded parking deck helped revive the area. A single-family seller a few blocks from either district should expect buyers to ask about parking, noise and nearby rental density.

How do Champaign winters and summers affect an older house?

Champaign has a humid continental climate with hot summers and cold winters. The city averages 40.92 inches of precipitation and 20.8 inches of snow a year. Temperatures top 90 degrees on about 24 days a year and fall below zero on about six nights.

  • Record high: 109 degrees in 1954; record low: minus 25, hit on four separate occasions
  • Wettest months: May and June, at about 4.8 and 4.6 inches of rain
  • Snowiest months: January, 6.5 inches, and February, 5.8 inches

Those swings put stress on roofs, gutters, sump pumps, furnaces and air conditioners in the same year. Buyers' inspectors in Champaign tend to look at all four, so a seller with an aging system can expect the issue to surface in negotiations. A cash buyer purchasing as-is usually prices that in directly.

Champaign Unit 4 School District serves the city and runs Champaign Central High School and Champaign Centennial High School. Parkland College, in northwestern Champaign, is part of the Illinois Community College System. Homes near Parkland or the university draw a different group of buyers than homes inside the Unit 4 attendance areas, so check the attendance boundary before you advertise a school connection.

What roads, rail and airport serve Champaign?

Interstates 57, 72 and 74 all meet at or near Champaign. I-57 and I-72 meet in a cloverleaf, I-72 heads toward Decatur and ends at University Avenue on the southeast side, and I-74 leads to Indianapolis. U.S. 45 and U.S. 150 also serve the area.

Illinois Terminal, opened in 1999, is the intermodal hub for Amtrak, intercity buses and the local Champaign-Urbana Mass Transit District. Amtrak stops here with the City of New Orleans, the Saluki and the Illini. The university also operates Willard Airport. Houses near a bus line to campus are easy to describe to investors and to students' parents.

What does the City of Champaign require for building work and rentals?

Permits are needed to build, enlarge, alter, repair, move or demolish a building, or to install or replace electrical, gas, mechanical, plumbing, sprinkler or fire alarm systems. Sheds up to 120 square feet, fences (zoning rules still apply), playground equipment and minor repairs are exempt. Since January 1, 2025, applications go through an online portal. The city adopted the 2021 International Codes on January 9, 2024.

The Neighborhood Code Compliance Division enforces property maintenance, nuisance and blight rules, and residents can file a complaint with the city. The city's rental registration page describes a proposed registry of residential rentals and vacant commercial buildings meant to give the city current owner and agent contact information. If you own a rental, ask the Neighborhood Services department whether registration has taken effect.

Downtown property owners should know about the snow rule. When public works declares the ordinance in effect after more than two inches of snow, owners in the designated areas have 24 hours to clear sidewalks, or the city clears them and bills the owner plus an administrative fee.

What do the state and county require when I sell a Champaign house?

Illinois imposes a transfer tax of 50 cents for each $500 of value or fraction of $500 stated on the declaration (35 ILCS 200/31-10). The declaration is filed through the state's MyDec system, whose customer service line is 844-445-1114.

The deed is recorded with the Champaign County recorder. Ask the county recorder, the City of Champaign and your title company whether any local transfer or utility requirement applies to your property before the closing date is set.

A listing usually fits a well-kept house that can wait through a school-year showing schedule. Sheds up to 120 square feet and fences are exempt from building permits, but zoning rules still apply to fences. Ask the Building Safety Division before you build.

How do I report a property maintenance problem?

File a complaint with the Neighborhood Code Compliance Division of the City of Champaign. The division enforces property maintenance, nuisance and blight rules.

The state rate is 50 cents for each $500 of value or fraction of $500 stated in the transfer declaration. The declaration is completed in the state's MyDec system.

The city's FAQ is blunt about exceptions: its ordinance lists none, so foreclosure and tax-sale transfers need the same documents. Each parcel number in a sale needs its own closing letter, and a missing number can hold up the closing.

  • Buyer side, once you have one: a driver's license number for the water account transfer, receipts for any city amounts already settled, and a notarized affidavit.
  • Utility side: call the Water Department at least five business days before closing to schedule the final meter reading (847-360-0535).

What does a Waukegan sale cost and require, step by step?

The table pulls the city and county items together. Everything in it comes from the Waukegan and Lake County pages named in the last column.

Recording a standard deed$70 flat fee, plus any transfer tax dueLake County Clerk recording fee page

The closing letter is issued only after the fees and the final water bill are paid. Any liens on the property are disclosed in the record, and the payoff statements can be settled at closing.

Is an as-is sale allowed in Waukegan?

Yes, with conditions. The city's FAQ allows an as-is sale when the zoning certificate inspection is done and the buyer signs a notarized affidavit. The city does not provide a template, so the affidavit has to carry a date, the buyer's address, phone number and email, a list of the items the buyer takes on from the inspection report, the buyer's signature and the notary's confirmation.

That matters for a fast sale. A cash buyer who agrees to take the inspection items does not hold the closing up for repairs, though the inspection itself still has to happen. Sellers who wait until a contract is signed to apply risk running into the 30-day window.

State law adds a separate duty: residential sellers give the buyer a completed disclosure report before signing (765 ILCS 77/20). Transfers from an estate fiduciary, by court order or in lieu of foreclosure are among the exempt ones listed in Section 15.

What do Waukegan homes and households look like on paper?

Five-year survey results show a city split almost evenly between owners and renters, with values well under those in suburbs to the south.

  • Owners occupy 50.2% of homes
  • Middle value among owned homes: $190,900
  • Middle monthly rent including utilities: $1,205
  • 32,042 households of about 2.72 people
  • Midpoint household income $71,919; 15.3% of residents in poverty
  • Bachelor's degree or above, adults 25 and up: 20.9%

The city's roots are industrial. Its harbor, a railroad through town by 1855 and later plants such as a sugar refinery and a barbed-wire maker drew workers from Sweden, Finland, Lithuania and elsewhere. The 2023 annual financial report lists Lake County, Southwire, Vista Medical Center East, Lake Behavioral Hospital and Medline Industries among the largest employers. The city has also pursued a lakefront plan to replace much of the old industrial shoreline with residential and recreational space.

What do Waukegan schools, roads and transit mean for a listing?

Most of Waukegan belongs to Waukegan Community Unit School District 60, which serves about 17,000 students from preschool through grade 12. Waukegan High School runs on two campuses, Brookside for grades 9 and 10 and Washington for grades 11 and 12. Pieces of the city fall inside Gurnee School District 56 with Warren Township High School District 121, and a small section sits in Beach Park District 3 and Zion-Benton District 126, so look at the district named on the tax bill before you describe schools in a listing.

Buyers who commute will look at the Metra Union Pacific North line, the Pace bus hub at Sheridan Road and Washington Street, the Tri-State Tollway and the Amstutz Expressway. The Robert McClory Bike Path crosses the city, and Waukegan National Airport handles general aviation. The lake also tempers the climate, cooling summers and warming winters.
