Which school districts serve Hoffman Estates?

Several districts overlap here, so the assigned school follows the street address.

  • North of Interstate 90, Township High School District 211 serves high school students.
  • In that northern area, Community Consolidated School District 15 (K to 8) serves addresses east of Huntington Boulevard.
  • Barrington School District 220 (K to 12) serves addresses west of Huntington Boulevard in the same area.
  • Residents west of Barrington Road primarily attend Elgin Area U46.

Most of the village is in Harper College Community College District 512. Libraries that serve residents include the Schaumburg Township District Library, the Barrington Area Library, the Gail Borden Public Library District and the Palatine Township Library. Pace runs bus routes that connect the village to Elgin, Rosemont and other destinations.

Confirm the district for your exact address before you name any school in a listing.

What does Village Hall require before a Hoffman Estates sale can close?

The Village's transfer tax dates to 1987 and falls on the seller of any real estate sold or transferred inside Village limits. Payment and the stamp come before closing and recording, and the Village prints the cost as $3 per $1,000 of the selling price.

  • Allow 48 hours of notice so staff can process the stamp, and send applications or questions to transferstamps@vohe.org.
  • Bring the state transfer declaration (PTAX-203/EZ Dec) and the deed or other document going to the recorder.
  • Call the Water Department at 847-843-4824 at least five days before buying the stamp to order a final water bill.
  • Call 847-882-9100 or use that same email to confirm no liens or fines remain on the property and the garbage bill is paid.
  • An exempt stamp costs a $10.00 administrative fee, needs the fully executed deed carrying the exempt language and signature, and calls for a final water reading if ownership changes.

Stamps are sold at the Village Hall front counter at 1900 Hassell Road on weekdays during business hours, or by mail with a self-addressed stamped return envelope. Settle with your closing agent who will buy the stamp and on what day. Stamp questions go to 847-882-9100.

Where does a Hoffman Estates deed get filed, and what do Cook County and the state charge?

Most of the village sits in Cook County, so deeds go to the Cook County Clerk's recordings division at 118 N. Clark Street. The Clerk's fee page prices a deed at $107, which bundles the county recording fee, a GIS fee, a document storage fee, the State Rental Housing Support Fee and a non-government filer fee. Mail-in recording with return adds $5 per document.

In the Clerk's transfer fee table, the seller is liable for two more charges: .50 per $500.00 for the State of Illinois and .25 per $500.00 for Cook County. The statute behind the state tax is 35 ILCS 200/31-10.

Pick based on how much time and repair work you can take on.

  • Market the house openly. Exposure is greatest, though the sale then rides on the buyer's loan, appraisal and inspection.
  • Handle the sale yourself. You decide everything and also do the paperwork, stamp steps included.
  • Take a cash offer. Closing can be set to your date and the house is taken as is, which suits a tenant-occupied property or one with deferred repairs.

Count backward from closing day. The water bill request, the lien check and the 48-hour notice all precede the stamp, and the stamp precedes recording. Placing the water call first avoids the likeliest delay.

The Village prints $3 per $1,000 of the selling price, and the seller pays. An exempt stamp has a $10.00 administrative fee.

Cook County for nearly every parcel. A very small part of the village is in Kane County, so check the parcel first.

The Village asks for 48 hours of notice, and the final water bill request, at 847-843-4824, should come at least five days before you buy the stamp.

Which district will my Hoffman Estates children attend?

That follows the street. In the north, east of Huntington Boulevard is CCSD 15 for grades K to 8 and west of it is Barrington 220, while addresses west of Barrington Road mostly go to Elgin Area U46.

What are the fastest ways to sell in Downers Grove, IL?

Speed points to a direct cash sale in Downers Grove, while a top price points to a broker listing and a house staged for showings. Handling the sale yourself falls in between.

  • A broker suits a house in good shape that can wait through showings and a buyer's loan.
  • Selling alone suits an owner who already knows the local price range.
  • Cash suits estates, houses that need a roof or new systems, occupied rentals and owners relocating on short notice.

At a middle home value of $449,800, each extra month of holding a house means more tax, insurance and utility cost, so the time a direct sale saves deserves a place in your comparison.

What is Downers Grove like for sellers?

Downers Grove is a DuPage County village roughly 20 miles from the Chicago Loop, between I-88 and I-55. Pierce Downer settled the area in 1832, and the name refers to the old bur oak grove around it. Burlington trains arrived in 1864, and the village incorporated in March 1873.

Metra's BNSF Line stops three times in the village, at Belmont Road, Main Street and Fairview Avenue, and the Grove Commuter Shuttle feeds two of those stations. I-355, I-88 and Ogden Avenue (U.S. 34) run through or beside the community. The village's 2023 financial report ranks Duly Health and Care, Hearthside Food Solutions, Advocate Good Samaritan Hospital and Midwestern University as the largest employers, and Dover and Univar Solutions are among the corporate headquarters.

Grade School District 58 runs most of the elementary and middle schools. Center Cass District 66 operates Prairieview, Elizabeth Ide and Lakeview Junior High, and Community High School District 99 covers Downers Grove North and South.

Mid-19th-century houses cluster near the center, and every later decade is represented around them. The village has had one of the Chicago area's highest teardown rates, with small older houses replaced by much larger ones. If your house is dated, tell buyers it may suit a rebuild as well as a move-in purchase.

What local history and green space shape Downers Grove?

The Lyman Home, built in 1839 by the Rev. Orange Lyman and his wife, is believed to be the first house in the village and served as a stop on the Underground Railroad. In April 1947 a Burlington Twin Cities Zephyr struck a tractor that had fallen from a freight train and crashed into the Main Street Station, killing three people. The village has been named a Tree City USA 28 times by the National Arbor Day Foundation, and two forest preserves, Lyman Woods and Maple Grove, lie inside its borders.

The village covers about 14.5 square miles, a larger footprint than most DuPage towns except Bartlett, Aurora, Naperville and Bolingbrook. Its population rose from 47,833 in 2010 to 50,247 in 2020. The village's climate record shows a high of 105 degrees in July 2005 and a low of minus 26 in January 1985, and about 38 inches of precipitation in a typical year, with August the wettest month.

Education runs deep here: Midwestern University trains osteopathic physicians, pharmacists and dentists, and the private Avery Coonley School, founded in 1906, has been at its present site since 1929. The village's wastewater is treated by the Downers Grove Sanitary District.

Why do teardowns and stormwater come up in Downers Grove?

Teardowns have been contentious because larger new houses cover more of each lot and push rainwater into neighboring yards and streets, and critics also say they thin out affordable housing. The village's permit page lists summaries of its stormwater and tree protection ordinance changes plus site-management forms such as a construction checklist and a notice to adjacent property owners.

Three practical effects follow for a seller:

  • A buyer planning to rebuild must follow the village's demolition, stormwater and tree rules, so ask Community Development which apply to your lot.
  • Drainage history on your lot matters, so disclose known water problems.
  • Open permits or unfinished work should be closed out before listing.

The permit page also carries residential re-roofing requirements, a contractor list, an encroachment license, a pool information sheet and a form for homeowners acting as their own plumbing contractor, so a buyer planning a new roof, a pool or DIY plumbing has a place to start. Sellers who made such changes should have their permit paperwork on hand.

The village runs a permit portal through its Customer Self Service system, and its Stormwater Utility and Utility Bill services are separate accounts to settle at sale.

How does DuPage County property tax work for a Downers Grove seller?

DuPage County collects in arrears, so the 2025 tax year was billed and paid in 2026. The Treasurer mailed 321,773 bills on April 29, each with two coupons, and the due dates were June 1 and September 1, 2026.

In the Treasurer's letter, the general homestead and senior exemptions are each listed at $8,000, and owners are urged to confirm that every exemption they qualify for appears on the bill. A yellow box means a mortgage company is paying, so a second check would be a duplicate. The Treasurer does not set values; the assessor named on your bill answers those questions. Call 630-407-5900 for payment issues.

At closing, your title company can explain how the year's tax is divided. The state's rate under 35 ILCS 200/31-10 is 50 cents per $500 of value or fraction, and the same company can say whether a county or local stamp also applies. For current recording fees, ask the DuPage County Clerk's recording division.

What should a Downers Grove owner prepare before an offer arrives?

Preparation prevents surprises at the table.

  1. Find the deed and confirm every name on it will sign.
  2. Print the newest tax bill and see which exemptions it shows.
  3. Ask the village about open permits and finish any unfinished work.
  4. Settle the village utility account before the house changes hands.
  5. Obtain a written payoff from each lender or lienholder.

If you inherited the house, gather the paperwork that shows who may sign early, since a title company will ask for it. List or sell directly, but judge each offer by the net after payoffs, taxes and closing costs, and get terms in writing.

Which county is Downers Grove in?

DuPage County. Property tax bills come from the DuPage County Treasurer and deeds are recorded with the county.

When do DuPage property taxes fall due?

They are billed a year behind. For tax year 2025 the installments fell on June 1 and September 1, 2026, on one bill with two coupons.

Can I sell a Downers Grove house to a builder who will tear it down?

Yes. Teardown buyers are common in the village. Share what you know about drainage or trees on the lot, and point them to the village's stormwater, tree protection and demolition requirements.

Which school districts serve Downers Grove?

Most of the village is in Grade School District 58, some areas are in Center Cass District 66, and the two high schools are in Community High School District 99. Check your tax bill to see which districts your parcel pays.

How can I avoid paying my tax bill twice?

Check for the yellow box on your bill. It says when a mortgage company is paying, and in that case you should not send another payment.

Which sale route suits a Plainfield homeowner best?

A Plainfield owner can put the house on the market through an agent, handle the sale personally, or hand it to a buyer paying cash who accepts it unrepaired. Price, effort and speed pull in different directions, so start from the shape the house is in and the date you must be out.

Plainfield has grown quickly, so a newer subdivision house competes against many near-identical neighbors, while a home near the old downtown draws a different crowd. Rank these goals before you pick:

  • Getting the highest possible price, which usually means repairs, staging and showings.
  • Closing on your own schedule, which often favors a direct sale with no financing contingency.
  • Avoiding repairs on a house with deferred maintenance, storm damage or a failing system.
  • Handling an inherited house, a divorce sale or a move that cannot wait for a long listing period.

Because a cash purchase skips the lender's appraisal, one common cause of failed contracts disappears. Even so, set any offer next to what a listing might realistically bring, and have the terms put in writing before you sign anything.

How do Census figures describe Plainfield homes and owners?

Plainfield skews toward expensive, owner-held housing. Census estimates for 2020 to 2024 show 88.0 percent of homes lived in by their owners, far above the share in Illinois's larger downstate cities such as Rockford or Rock Island.

Plainfield village, Illinois, selected figures from Census Bureau QuickFacts

People counted in the 2020 census44,762

Middle monthly rent, taxes and utilities included$2,119

Average household size3.17
Average one-way commute33.3 minutes

The village grew from about 4,500 residents in 1990 to nearly 45,000 by 2020, and the estimate for 2025 is higher again. That pace means much of the housing stock is under thirty years old, so buyers will ask about roof age, HVAC replacement dates and any homeowner association rules.

A median across the village hides a wide spread. A downtown cottage and a newer four-bedroom on a cul-de-sac sit in different price brackets, so use these numbers as background and not as an offer on your own address.

How do Plainfield's counties, roads and location affect a sale?

Plainfield sits in northwestern Will County, and the village limits reach west into Kendall County. That split means some addresses are recorded, assessed and taxed through Kendall County offices even though the mailing address says Plainfield. Check the parcel record before you assume which county handles your deed.

Location is a real selling point for commuters. The village lies roughly midway between Naperville to the north and Joliet to the south, with Romeoville to the east and Bolingbrook to the northeast. The roads buyers care about are:

  • Interstate 55 along the eastern edge, with two exits serving the village.
  • U.S. Route 30 through the center of town, running toward Joliet and Montgomery.
  • Illinois Route 59, which runs north toward Naperville and south toward Shorewood.
  • Illinois Route 126, which crosses US 30 in the center and heads west toward Yorkville.

The land is flat, a legacy of an ancient glacial lake bed, and the DuPage River runs through the village center. Ask your title company whether any part of your lot touches a mapped flood area, because that affects insurance and a buyer's lender.

Which school districts serve Plainfield addresses?

Most of the village falls inside Plainfield Community Consolidated School District 202, but not every Plainfield address does. Parts of the village are served by Oswego Community Unit School District 308 and Indian Prairie Community Unit School District 204, and in Kendall County most of the Plainfield land lies in the Oswego district.

Buyers often search by district first, so confirm yours before you write a listing or describe the house to anyone. District 202 serves parts of Joliet, Crest Hill, Bolingbrook and Romeoville as well as the village. Its enrollment peaked in the 2010 to 2011 school year at 29,254 students and has declined since, reaching 24,737 for 2022 to 2023.

If you have children in a district and need to move quickly, say so up front to whoever you sell to. A buyer who knows your timeline can often accommodate a rent-back period, which lets you finish a school year before handing over keys.

What village rules and history should a Plainfield seller know about?

The Village of Plainfield runs its building permit process through an online permitting and licensing portal, and its Building and Code Enforcement department takes complaints by phone, email or an online form. If you have open work, an unfinished deck or a basement finished without a permit, resolve it before a buyer's inspector finds it.

Plainfield also has a Preservation Commission and a historic preservation ordinance. The village includes Greek Revival homes and Upright and Wing cottages, a school built in 1847, and three buildings on the National Register: the Plainfield Halfway House, the Flanders House and a 1928 Standard Oil gas station. If your house is in the older core around Lockport Street, ask the village planning staff whether exterior changes need review.

The 1990 tornado is part of local housing history. The F5 storm crossed Plainfield on August 28, 1990, damaged or destroyed more than 1,100 homes and destroyed the only high school at the time. A boom of new subdivisions followed in the 1990s and 2000s, which is why so many Plainfield houses share a similar age and construction era. Buyers of those homes often ask about roof age, siding and the sump pump.

How is a Plainfield deed recorded and what does the transfer declaration require?

Whichever county contains the parcel handles the recording: Will County for most of the village, Kendall County for the western part. Each county sets its own fees and document standards, so ask that recorder's office for the current schedule.

Illinois law also requires a transfer declaration. Under 35 ILCS 200/31-25, it must be presented with the deed, or within three business days after the transfer, whichever is earlier, and signed by at least one seller and one buyer or their attorneys or agents. The form asks for the property's value, parcel number, legal description, deed date and type, street address, type of improvement, lot size, any homestead exemptions on the latest tax bill, and whether the transfer is between related parties.

A deed will not be accepted for recording without that declaration, unless an exemption applies under section 31-45. The county collects state transfer tax through revenue stamps. Section 31-15 prints the price as 50¢ for each $500 of value, rounding up for any fraction, and it scheduled paper stamps to end by December 31, 2025 in favor of electronic ones. Whoever runs your closing normally prepares both the declaration and the stamps.

What must a Plainfield seller disclose to a buyer?

Illinois sellers of residential property must fill in every item of the state disclosure report and hand it to the buyer ahead of signing a contract, according to 765 ILCS 77/20.

Section 25 of the same act says a seller must disclose material defects the seller actually knows about, and is not required to hire anyone to investigate. A seller is not liable for an error if the seller did not know of it, believed a defect had been fixed, or relied on information from a public agency or a qualified professional. Fill the report out carefully and keep copies, including any repair invoices that support what you wrote.

  • List known roof, foundation, basement water and drainage problems.
  • Note any past repairs and who did them.
  • Say what you know about nearby issues such as construction, traffic or highway noise.

Frequently asked questions

Must a Plainfield seller fix things before selling?

No. An as-is sale is allowed, whether to a cash buyer or on the open market, but the Illinois disclosure report still has to list defects you know about. A buyer will price the unrepaired items into the offer.

Which county records my Plainfield deed, Will or Kendall?

It depends on where the parcel sits. Most of the village is in Will County and the western edge is in Kendall County. Look at the parcel number on your tax bill or ask your title company, then contact that county's recorder for fees and format rules.

Does Plainfield have a historic district that limits what I can change?

The village has a Preservation Commission and a historic preservation ordinance. Whether your house is covered depends on its location and designation, so ask village planning staff before you list a house in the older downtown area.

What paperwork do I sign at a Plainfield closing besides the deed?

You will sign the Illinois transfer declaration along with the deed, plus a closing statement and the title company's affidavits. The disclosure report should already have gone to the buyer before the contract was signed.

How large is Plainfield?

The Census Bureau's 2025 estimate is 50,043 people, compared with 44,762 counted in 2020. The village spans Will and Kendall counties, southwest of Naperville.

Should a Glenview owner list the house or take a quick sale?

A quick as-is sale suits a Glenview house that needs work or an owner on a short clock, while a listing suits a house that shows well and can wait for the strongest bid. The choice comes down to condition, calendar and how much of the process you want to run yourself.

  • Listing: expect photos, showings, a buyer's inspection and possibly a repair list, with a closing date that follows the buyer's lender.
  • Do-it-yourself sale: you price the house, field inquiries and hire an attorney to review the contract.
  • Direct cash sale: no lender, no appraisal gap, and the house changes hands in its present state.

Inherited homes, houses with deferred upkeep and properties with a tenant you want to move on from tend to fit the third path best.

What is Glenview like beyond its price tags?

Glenview is a Cook County village about 15 miles northwest of downtown Chicago, with roughly 14 square miles of land. Residents settled on the name by vote on May 7, 1895, and the village incorporated in 1899. Much of the land stayed in farming until after World War II, when builders laid out the suburban streets that dominate today.

A large share of the modern village comes from the former Naval Air Station Glenview. The base closed in 1995 and became The Glen, a 1,121 acre mixed-use district that makes up about 15 percent of Glenview, with homes, offices, a town center, a lake, trails and the North Glenview Metra station. The Park, founded in 1894 around a common green, is among the oldest neighborhoods.

Astellas, Abt Electronics and Glenbrook Hospital topped the village's 2021 list of employers. Metra's Milwaukee District North Line stops at Glenview and North Glenview, trains run to Chicago Union Station, and Amtrak's Borealis, Empire Builder and Hiawatha also call at Glenview station.

Which school districts matter for a Glenview address?

More than half of Glenview sits inside District 34, the main kindergarten through eighth grade district in the center of the village. Its schools are Henking, Westbrook, Lyon, Hoffman, Glen Grove and Pleasant Ridge elementary schools, plus Attea Middle School and Springman Junior High.

  • The southeast and east parts of the village are served by Wilmette District 39 and Avoca District 37.
  • Northeast Glenview falls in Northbrook/Glenview District 30.
  • The northwest corner belongs to West Northfield District 31.
  • A small strip south of Central Road is in East Maine District 63.

For high school, most addresses attend Glenbrook South in District 225. Anyone on or east of Harms Road is in New Trier District 203. Buyers often ask for this detail first, so confirm it for your street before the first showing.

What parks and landmarks surround Glenview homes?

The Glenview Park District runs the Park Center on the shore of Lake Glenview, a prairie-style community center with an indoor pool, fitness rooms, a preschool and a senior center. The Grove, a 123 acre prairie with an interpretive center, nature trails and the 1856 Kennicott House, is a National Historic Landmark. Wagner Farm, an 18.6 acre working farm, shows farm life as it was in the 1920s. Portions of the Forest Preserves of Cook County also lie within the village, with Harms Woods among them.

Mention whichever of these sits closest to your house. Buyers comparing suburbs often ask what is within walking or biking distance.

What does the Census Bureau report about Glenview homes?

The Census Bureau put Glenview at 47,711 residents on July 1, 2025, compared with 48,642 at the April 2020 estimates base. Housing here is expensive and mostly owned by the people who live in it.

Glenview housing and income, five-year figures for 2020 through 2024, from Census Bureau QuickFacts

Homes lived in by their owners78.9%

Roughly 68 percent of adults hold at least a bachelor's degree, and about 22.6 percent of residents were born outside the United States.

What does the Village ask of a seller at closing?

The Village asks sellers to arrange a final water meter reading, and that is the only local task. Glenview states that it has no transfer stamp, so nothing has to be purchased from Village Hall before the deed goes to the county.

  • Water Billing takes the request at (847) 724-1700.
  • The Village suggests booking 7 to 10 business days ahead so a crew is free.
  • The person leaving pays the last bill, and the account itself stays with the address.
  • Bills arrive quarterly, dated the first of the billing month and due on the 25th, and a late balance picks up a 10 percent penalty.

Water comes from Lake Michigan by way of Wilmette, and the Village resets its fixed and usage rates each year. Request the current rate sheet from Water Billing if you want the figures for your own closing statement.

How do Glenview property taxes reach a sale?

Cook County prepares the bill, and the Village gets a thin slice. Out of a typical bill for the 2024 tax year, about 5.5 percent went to the Village. School districts, the library, the community college and other bodies took the rest. The Village's extended 2024 levy came to $27,255,379.

Questions about a valuation start with the township, and the Village lists four: Maine at (847) 297-2510, New Trier at (847) 446-8202, Niles at (847) 673-9300 and Northfield at (847) 724-8300. The Cook County Assessor's Office is at (312) 443-7550. How the year's bill is divided between you and the buyer is settled on the closing statement, so ask your attorney or title officer to walk through it before you sign.

What goes on a deed recorded in Cook County?

The Cook County Clerk's recordings office accepts Glenview deeds and publishes a checklist of required items. Missing any one of them gets a deed turned away.

  • Names and addresses of both the person conveying and the person receiving title.
  • The street address, the Property Index Number and the full legal description.
  • Return-mail and preparer details.
  • A finished MyDec filing for the state and county tax stamp.
  • An exemption line or affidavit, only if the transfer qualifies as exempt.

The state statute puts collection of the transfer tax with the county recorder, at 50 cents per $500 of value. Your closing agent will work out the exact total for your sale.

Does Glenview weather change what buyers look at?

Yes, the weather gives inspectors a short list of places to check. Glenview has a continental climate. January afternoons average 32 degrees with lows near 17, July highs reach about 86, and yearly precipitation totals roughly 38 inches, with August the wettest month at almost 5 inches.

Roofs, gutters, grading and basements therefore get close attention. Receipts for a new roof, a working sump pump or drainage repairs are worth gathering. If the house needs those jobs and you would rather skip managing contractors, a buyer who takes the property in its current state removes that burden from you.

You pick the closing dateClose in as little as 7 days or on the date that works for you, with no fees or commissions.Get My Cash Offer →

Frequently asked questions

Is there a Glenview transfer stamp to buy before I close?

No. The Village of Glenview says it has no transfer stamp. The state and county declaration is still filed through MyDec when the Cook County Clerk records the deed.

How far ahead should I schedule the last water read?

Call (847) 724-1700 about 7 to 10 business days before the closing date. The seller covers the final bill, and the new owner opens a fresh account on the same property.

Who records the deed for a house in Glenview?

The Cook County Clerk's recordings office. Its checklist asks for a Property Index Number, a legal description, return-mail and preparer details, and the MyDec declaration.

Will anyone buy a Glenview house that needs big repairs?

Yes. Buyers who purchase as-is accept the present condition, though they factor the repair work into what they offer.

What share of a Glenview tax bill funds the Village?

About 5.5 percent for tax year 2024. Schools, the library, the community college and other districts receive the rest.

What has to happen before an Elmhurst house can close?

Elmhurst requires a passed sump pump inspection and a purchased transfer stamp before a sale inside city limits can close, and those two steps control the timeline more than anything else. The city says it requires a sump pump inspection for every residential and commercial property prior to closing, with some exceptions for condo complexes. A sale of a house in Elmhurst therefore starts with a phone call to the city, well ahead of the contract date.

  • Book the sump pump inspection at least two weeks before closing, because same-week slots are rare.
  • Submit the transfer stamp application on the city's online portal.
  • Settle every city account: utilities, inspection fees, building permit fees, fines and parking tickets.
  • Have the signed sales contract, the deed and the state MyDec declaration ready before the stamp is issued.

Addresses in unincorporated Elmhurst, which include a letter in the street number such as 16W212, do not need the city sump inspection or the city stamp.

What does the Elmhurst sump pump inspection check?

The inspection checks that the pit has a cover and that only stormwater drains to it. Bathrooms, washers and utility sinks may not drain into a storm pit. If the pump discharges overland, it must drain toward the middle of the front or back of the lot and cannot reach a neighbor's yard, the city sidewalk or the parkway. If it drains underground, it must connect to the storm sewer and never the sanitary sewer, since a sanitary connection counts as illegal.

A passing result earns a certificate of compliance on site, and an approved inspection is good for six months. A failed inspection means repairing the problem and rebooking before stamps are issued, and the city says it will not accept a legal letter in place of a pass. Someone over 18 must be present, and the city asks you not to leave inspection requests on voicemail. The number is (630) 530-3030. An inspection done through RJN does not count.

  • The pit needs a cover.
  • Only stormwater may drain to the pit.
  • Overland discharge must not reach neighbors, the sidewalk or the parkway.
  • Underground discharge must connect to the storm sewer.

Flooding is part of the local background: the city has tended to flood after large rainfalls and is working on mitigation. A 59-acre quarry west of downtown holds stormwater, and a tunnel from Salt Creek diverts water into it during floods.

How much is the Elmhurst transfer stamp?

For most sales, the stamp costs $1.50 per $1,000 of the sale price, rounded to the nearest thousand, and the seller is responsible for buying it. The city wants all information five business days before it issues the stamp. You apply through the online portal, and the application asks for the property address, owner and buyer names, closing and move-out dates, the full consideration and the seller's forwarding address.

Beginning January 1, 2026, exempt transfers also need a stamp. Examples the city lists include adding or removing a name after marriage or divorce, transfers to or from a trust, foreclosure or short sale, transfers with governmental bodies, and transfers with consideration under $100. The exempt stamp has a $30 administrative fee, and it requires a sump pump inspection if none was done in the last five years. A signed and notarized deed goes with the application.

City Hall's finance counter issues stamps Monday through Friday, 8:30 a.m. to 5:00 p.m., or the city can mail one if you attach a prepaid shipping label. Payment options are online by card or e-check, or in person by cash, check or card. Questions go to the finance department at 630-530-3117 or 3118.

Can I get an Elmhurst transfer tax refund?

Yes, in one situation. Under the Elmhurst Municipal Code, the payor of the tax can receive a refund if they previously owned and lived in an Elmhurst home and, within 180 days of that closing, buy and occupy a new residence in Elmhurst. The city posts a Transfer Stamp Refund Form on its transfer stamp page.

This helps local move-up and downsizing sellers, who sell one Elmhurst home and buy another. Keep proof of both closings and both periods of occupancy. If you plan to leave the city, no refund applies.

What happens with the final water reading and trash cans?

Once your sump pump inspection is approved and the stamp form is in, the city pulls your current and forwarding address information and sets the final water reading itself. You do not call to schedule it. The reading happens on the day of closing, and the final bill goes to the forwarding address listed on the transfer stamp request.

Garbage, sewer and water share one bill, so the city says there is nothing extra to arrange for those services. The trash and recycling carts belong with the address, so leave them for the buyer.

What do Census figures say about Elmhurst homes?

Elmhurst is a western suburb in DuPage and Cook counties with 46,111 residents estimated for July 1, 2025. The owner-occupied rate was 79.9 percent for 2020 to 2024, and the median value of an owner-occupied home was $545,400. Median household income reached $149,644, and 64.2 percent of adults 25 and over held a bachelor's degree or higher.

Population estimate, July 1, 202546,111
Median value, owner-occupied homes$545,400
Median selected monthly owner cost with a mortgage$3,217
Median gross rent$1,975
Owner-occupied housing rate79.9%
Same house one year ago91.8%

With nearly 92 percent of residents in the same house a year earlier, turnover is low. Land area is 10.22 square miles, so the city is compact.

Which schools, transit and history shape Elmhurst listings?

Elmhurst Community Unit School District 205 serves most of the city, and its high school is York Community High School. Villa Park District 45, Salt Creek District 48 and Hillside District 93 serve other parts, feeding into DuPage High School District 88 or Proviso West. Elmhurst University, a four-year liberal arts college, is also in the city.

The Metra Union Pacific West Line stops at the Elmhurst station, Pace buses run through town, and O'Hare is about 18 minutes away. The community began as Cottage Hill in 1845, took the Elmhurst name in 1869 and incorporated as a village in 1882. Several homes were designed by Mies van der Rohe, Frank Lloyd Wright and Walter Burley Griffin, which can set a house apart in a listing.

Deeds go to the DuPage County Recorder or the Cook County Clerk. DuPage's Recorder holds records going back to 1839, and Cook prices a deed at $107 on its schedule effective April 1, 2024, with state transfer tax at .50 per $500 and county tax at .25 per $500.

Frequently asked questions

Do I need a sump pump inspection to sell in Elmhurst?

Yes, for properties inside city limits. The city requires an approved inspection before it issues transfer stamps, with some exceptions for condominium complexes. Schedule it at least two weeks before closing, since same-week openings are unlikely.

How long is an Elmhurst sump pump certificate valid?

An approved inspection is good for six months, and the certificate shows its expiration date. Bring it to the City Hall finance counter when you collect your transfer stamps.

What is the Elmhurst transfer stamp rate?

The city lists $1.50 per $1,000 of the sale price, rounded to the nearest thousand, for non-exempt sales. Exempt transfers carry a $30 administrative fee. The seller is responsible for buying the stamp.

Is Elmhurst's sump rule the same in unincorporated areas?

No. The city says a sump inspection and city stamps do not apply to unincorporated Elmhurst addresses, which show a letter in the street number such as 16W212. Check your address before you book.

Who pays for the final water reading in Elmhurst?

The city schedules the reading for the day of closing once your inspection is approved and your stamp form is filed. Your final bill goes to the forwarding address you list. Garbage, water and sewer share one bill, so there is nothing extra to arrange.

How can you sell a house in Lombard?

Lombard sellers choose between a traditional listing, a for-sale-by-owner sale, and a cash purchase of the house as-is. The village, in DuPage County, runs permitting and code enforcement through its Community Development Department, and deeds are recorded by the DuPage County Recorder, so those two offices set most of the practical timeline.

The 2020 census counted 44,476 people in Lombard, making it the largest of the four Illinois places in this batch of pages, with a mid-2025 federal estimate of 44,399.

What is Lombard known for?

Lombard began as Babcock's Grove, named for early settlers on the DuPage River, and took its present name from a Chicago developer who mapped the settlement in 1868. The Galena and Chicago Union Railroad arrived in 1848, and the village incorporated in 1869. A farm family settled on 80 acres in 1837, and their house, since restored by the Lombard Historical Society, was added to the National Park Service's Network to Freedom list of Underground Railroad sites in 2011.

The village calls itself the Lilac Village. A colonel's estate left to the village in 1927 became Lilacia Park, with some 200 varieties of lilac, and the Lilac Time festival and parade have run since 1930 into mid-May. A house near the park or the downtown station can use that identity in its listing description.

What do Census numbers show about Lombard housing?

Lombard has the highest median rent and the highest median home value among the four places in this comparison, and the shortest commute. It also has the largest share of residents with a bachelor's degree.

The short commute reflects the Metra Union Pacific West Line station, the I-88 and I-355 corridors and Illinois Routes 38, 53, 56 and 64. What is the local economy doing for home values?

The village's fiscal year 2024 financial report cites a 9.79 percent increase in equalized assessed valuation, with new construction adding $5.06 million. Retail, manufacturing, hospitality and professional services anchor the economy, and redevelopment projects near Yorktown Center include Lilac Station, Yorktown Reserve and the Summit at Yorktown. Retail sales per capita reached $27,321 in 2022 on the Census table.

Assessed value is one input to property tax bills, so ask the DuPage County Treasurer and Supervisor of Assessments for your parcel's current numbers before you set a price.

Which Lombard schools do buyers ask about?

Lombard's public high schools belong to Glenbard Township High School District 87, shared with Glen Ellyn, and Glenbard East High School is in the village. Elementary and middle schools (kindergarten through grade 8) belong to Lombard School District 44 or DuPage School District 45, depending on the street. Private choices include Montini Catholic High School and the College Preparatory School of America.

Line up the elementary district for your address before the first showing, since it shapes which families look at the house.

What permits and code rules apply in Lombard?

The Building Division handles signs, fire, fill and grade, new buildings, additions, backyard chickens, accessory structures and alterations. Permits can be requested online through the village portal, fees are paid when the permit is ready for pickup, and some items such as residential driveways, fences and new roofs carry flat rates. The division's number is (630) 620-5750.

  • Fences and grading: a permit is required for all fences and for all grading.
  • Exterior upkeep: grass and weeds must stay under eight inches during the growing season, and litter must be cleared within seven days.
  • Vehicles: inactive vehicles must be garaged and RVs may not sit in the front yard from November 1 through March 31.
  • Rentals: owners who rent must supply heat at 68 degrees from September 15 through June 1.
  • Address numbers: they must be visible and legible from the street.

A walk-through for these items before listing can head off an inspector's note. Lombard is a non-home-rule municipality with a council-manager government, so check the village code for local rules before you assume a state rule is the only one.

Lombard's code guide also asks owners to keep waste containers covered, keep items on the parkway only within 24 hours of scheduled pickup, and park vehicles on an approved hard surface, not on grass. Commercial-size trucks are barred from residential districts. Tidy these before photographs, since a neighbor's complaint can bring an inspection.

Which landmarks and transit links shape a Lombard address?

Lombard's older core grew up around its railroad. Today the Metra Union Pacific West Line connects the village to Ogilvie Transportation Center and out to Elburn, and former interurban rail lines are now the Illinois Prairie Path and Great Western Trail. Stops on the old Chicago Aurora and Elgin line once sat at Stewart Avenue, Main Street, Brewster Avenue and Westmore and Meyers Road.

Landmarks give streets a recognizable identity. Cartoonist Harold Gray drew Little Orphan Annie in a restored Italianate house from 1881 on Main Street, the Maple Street Chapel (1870) served as the first town hall and library, and the Helen Plum library on the lilac estate was decommissioned in 2023. Big Idea, the company behind VeggieTales, started in Lombard. Mention the walk to the train, the trails and the park in your listing, because commuters and trail users are the buyers who value them most.

How does recording work with the DuPage County Recorder?

The DuPage County Recorder maintains the county's land records back to 1839, and recording is fee-funded. The posted fee for a deed (Document Class 1) is $86, which the schedule says includes $10 for document storage, $21 for GIS, $1 for the real property fee and $18 for the Rental Housing Support Program. The Recorder's office number is 630-407-5400.

The state transfer tax in 35 ILCS 200/31-10 runs fifty cents per $500 block of declared value, and 35 ILCS 200/31-25 requires a declaration signed by at least one seller and one buyer. Collection of the tax runs through the recorder, and the statute provides that paper revenue stamps phase out by December 31, 2025, with electronic stamps or other indicia after that. Ask your closing agent whether the village or county adds any local fee on your parcel.

When does a cash sale suit a Lombard owner?

A cash sale suits owners who need to sell a house with deferred repairs, a tenant situation or an inherited estate without staging and showings. With median rent near $1,948, landlords holding an older Lombard rental sometimes prefer a clean exit over renovating. Ask any buyer for a written closing date and a list of who pays each recording item before you sign.

The DuPage County Recorder, whose records start in 1839. The posted deed fee includes storage, GIS, real property and Rental Housing Support Program amounts. Call 630-407-5400 for questions.

Is a fence permit required in Lombard?

Yes. Lombard's code enforcement guide says permits are required for all fences so the homeowner knows the requirements before buying the fence. Fences are among the flat-rate permits.

Can I park an RV in my front yard in winter?

No. RVs are not permitted in the front yard from November 1 through March 31, and vehicles that are not street ready must be garaged.

Which high school serves Lombard?

Glenbard East High School in Lombard belongs to Glenbard Township High School District 87. Elementary students attend Lombard School District 44 or DuPage School District 45 depending on the street.

What is the Illinois transfer tax rate?

The statute at 35 ILCS 200/31-10 sets it, counted in $500 units of the value on the declaration. A mortgage that stays on the property is left out of the base.

How do owners usually sell a house in Buffalo Grove?

Most Buffalo Grove owners list with an agent, because the village's housing market is built around mortgage-financed buyers and long-tenured owners. A direct sale to a cash buyer is the alternative when a house needs work or the closing date matters more than the top price.

The village adds one local step to every route. Buffalo Grove sells its own real estate transfer stamps, in person only, and holds them back if water or other village debts are unpaid. A seller who plans for that stamp early avoids a delayed closing.

  • Agent listing: more showings, more time, and the buyer's financing to wait on.
  • Owner sale: saves the commission, but you handle disclosures, the deed and the stamp visit.
  • Cash purchase: fewer contingencies and a closing set by you, usually at a lower price than a retail sale.

Which county is a Buffalo Grove house in?

Buffalo Grove is split by Lake Cook Road: the northern part, about three-quarters of the village, is in Vernon Township in Lake County, and the southern part is in Wheeling Township in Cook County. The village's own transfer tax page says that anyone changing the property record with Cook or Lake County needs a stamp.

So the deed is recorded with the Cook County Clerk's Recordings Division or with Lake County, depending on the parcel. Cook County Clerk's recordings office hours run 9 a.m. to 5 p.m., and the last customer is accepted at 4:45 p.m. Property tax bills, exemptions and appeals also follow the county, so check which assessor and treasurer cover your parcel.

The split shows up in services too. The Indian Trails Public Library District serves the Cook County part, and the Vernon Area Public Library District serves most of the Lake County part.

What does a Buffalo Grove transfer stamp cost and require?

The village charges $3 per $1,000 for its transfer tax, and it will not issue a stamp while water, fines, fees or other debts to the village are outstanding. Stamps can only be bought in person at Village Hall, 50 Raupp Boulevard.

What do water and sewer bills mean for a Buffalo Grove closing?

Water and sewer balances must be paid before the Village will issue a stamp, so a final bill needs to be settled ahead of closing. The Village's rate page lists $7.14 per 1,000 gallons for water and $1.77 per 1,000 gallons for sewer as of January 2026, a combined $8.91.

Lake County residents also pay a sanitary sewer pass-through fee of $5.26 per 1,000 gallons as of December 2025. If your house is on the Lake County side, that line item appears on your bill and will not appear for Cook County neighbors across Lake Cook Road.

The property check from the Finance Department is the quickest way to learn what you owe. Ask for the figure a few days before the closing date.

What does the Census say about Buffalo Grove housing?

Census Bureau figures put the median owner-occupied home value in Buffalo Grove at $412,300, and 79.8 percent of housing units are lived in by their owners. The 2020 census count was 43,212, and the July 1, 2025 estimate is 42,812, a decline of 0.9 percent from the 2020 base.

  • Median household income: $129,395 (2020-2024).
  • Bachelor's degree or higher among adults 25 and older: 68.6 percent.
  • Median gross rent: $2,037.
  • Mean commute: 26.3 minutes.
  • Share in the same house a year earlier: 88.6 percent.

The numbers describe an established village where population has been flat for years. Pricing a house against recent sales on your own street matters more than the village-wide median, which blends very different subdivisions.

How did Buffalo Grove grow, and where do its residents work?

Buffalo Grove incorporated in 1958 with 164 residents after a builder wanted his new development out from under Cook County planners. Developers filled the farmland with single-family houses, and the 1970s brought roughly 80 percent growth, along with home rule status and the village's high schools, park district and libraries.

About 20,000 daytime workers in ten million square feet of commercial and industrial space. The 2019 largest employers it names include Siemens Building Technologies, about 1,800 employees, and Plexus Corp. Woodman's Markets, supported by a village tax agreement, anchors retail along Milwaukee Avenue. Buffalo Grove High School and Adlai E. Stevenson High School both opened in the 1970s.

For a seller, the timeline matters because most of the village was platted after the 1950s, so a buyer's inspector will compare your house against subdivisions of the same era.

What local amenities can a seller point to in Buffalo Grove?

Buffalo Grove's Park District runs dozens of recreation facilities. Willow Stream Park is the largest at 54 acres, with sports fields, bike paths and playgrounds, and Mike Rylko Community Park hosts a Sunday farmers market from June to October and the Buffalo Grove Days festival in September.

The Raupp Museum, dedicated in 1979, covers the village's history from the Potawatomi onward. Two golf courses and the Community Arts Center, which opened in 2014, round out the list. Mentioning these in a listing or a conversation with a cash buyer gives context that numbers alone do not.

What state rules sit behind the village stamp?

Illinois imposes its own transfer tax at 50 cents per $500 of value, collected by the county recorder, and counties may add 25 cents per $500. Home rule municipalities such as Buffalo Grove can layer their own tax on top, which is why the village stamp exists.

The buyer and seller also complete the Illinois PTAX-203 transfer declaration, filed with the county where the property sits. The state's paper revenue stamps were scheduled for phase-out by December 31, 2025, after which counties issue electronic stamps, and the Village's own stamp is issued in person at Village Hall.

How does flooding and winter weather affect a Buffalo Grove house?

Buffalo Grove sits in a humid continental climate with about 28.93 inches of precipitation a year, cold snowy winters and hot summers. The village also uses open space for flood control: Buffalo Creek forest preserve functions as flood control, and the Buffalo Grove Golf Course is used as a floodplain.

Buyers near those areas often ask about basement dampness and drainage. Gather any sump pump service records and permits for roof or foundation work, since those papers answer the questions early.

Frequently asked questions

How much is the Buffalo Grove transfer tax?

The Village charges $3 per $1,000. Its Real Estate Transfer Tax page also says the closing date and a forwarding address are required when you buy the stamp.

Can I get a Buffalo Grove transfer stamp online?

No. The Village says stamps can only be obtained in person at Village Hall, 50 Raupp Boulevard, after a property check with the Finance Department at 847-459-2500.

What blocks a stamp from being issued?

Delinquent water charges, outstanding fines or fees, or any other debt owed to the Village. All debts must be paid before even an exempt stamp is issued.

Is Buffalo Grove in Cook County or Lake County?

Both. Lake Cook Road divides the village, with about three-quarters in Lake County's Vernon Township and the rest in Cook County's Wheeling Township. Your parcel determines where the deed is recorded.

Do I need a deed to get the stamp?

You need the deed or the most recent tax bill for the property. If you lack the deed, the Cook County Clerk or Lake County recording office can supply a copy.

What are the ways to sell quickly in Moline?

Moline owners have three choices: an agent, a buyer found without one, or a purchaser who pays cash and takes the house as found. That last choice closes soonest, with an offer shaped by the work needed.

Moline is a Quad Cities city, and the buyers who show up here are shaped by that. Some are workers tied to the large employers along the river, some are investors, and some are families moving within the Illinois and Iowa sides of the metro. Knowing which group your house suits helps you choose the route.

What follows is local: housing figures, neighborhoods and school boundaries, the city's building office, and the filing rules at the Rock Island County Recorder.

What does Census data say about housing in Moline?

No other city in Rock Island County is bigger. Moline logged 42,985 people in 2020 and an estimated 42,362 in July 2025, a dip of 1.4 percent from the estimates base.

The 2020 to 2024 profile sits well below Chicago-area levels. The median owned home is valued at $146,300 and median rent is $900. Owners live in 67.3 percent of homes, across 18,289 households of about 2.29 people. Household income at the median is $67,701, and the average drive to work is just 18.0 minutes.

  • At these prices a repair bill takes a larger bite of the sale price, so get quotes before you decide to renovate.
  • A short commute and a large employment base make renting out a house a realistic option for some owners, and buyers who rent houses out may bid on yours.
  • The estimate has slipped a little since 2020, so buyers can be choosy, and a house needing work may wait longer on the open market.

Which Moline neighborhoods and school districts do buyers ask about?

Moline sits on a bluff between the Mississippi and Rock rivers, and deep ravines cut the high ground into natural neighborhoods. Neighborhood associations work with the city, and the downtown area is known as Moline Centre.

Other neighborhood names in common use include Floreciente, Olde Towne, Uptown, Overlook, Karsten's Park, Wharton, Hamilton Heights, Wildwood, Prospect Park, Tartan Oaks, Park Hill, Forest Hill, Highland, Villa Park, Green Acres, Rockview Estates, Homewood, Heritage Park, Stewartville, Deerview and Walton Hills. A listing that names the neighborhood reads more clearly to local buyers than a street address alone.

Moline School District No. 40 covers most of the city, with about 7,500 students in twelve elementary schools, two middle schools named for John Deere and Woodrow Wilson, and Moline High School. Pieces of the city on the east side belong to East Moline District 37 and United Township High School District 30, and a southwest piece belongs to Rock Island-Milan District 41. Verify the district for an address before you advertise one.

How do Moline's roads, river and employers shape demand?

Interstate 74 runs straight through the city and splits it into two roughly equal halves, and Interstate 280 circles the Quad Cities. The new I-74 bridge over the Mississippi opened with a ribbon-cutting on December 1, 2021. Moline is about 165 miles west of Chicago.

Deere and Company keeps its corporate headquarters in Moline, and Kone's U.S. division is based in the city as well. Black Hawk College and the Quad Cities campus of Western Illinois University are both in Moline, and Quad Cities International Airport sits on the south edge of town. South Park Mall and a string of big-box centers make the city the retail hub of the Illinois side.

The downtown arena, Vibrant Arena at The MARK, and John Deere Commons draw events that fill nearby restaurants and hotels. Houses within a short drive of these destinations tend to be pitched to commuters and renters, so say so in your listing.

Does Moline's climate affect what a buyer will inspect?

Summers run hot and humid, winters cold. In an average year Moline sees 23 days of 90 degrees or more, 43 days when the high never climbs above freezing and 11 days below zero, plus 31.6 inches of snow a season.

Buyers will check the roof, the furnace and the air conditioner, because a house here works both systems hard. The freeze-thaw cycle also tests sidewalks, driveways and foundation walls. The long-run record puts freezing temperatures from about October 10 to April 24, so exterior work is easiest to schedule outside that window.

Houses on bluffs and ravine edges also deserve a look at drainage and grading. If a lot slopes toward the foundation, expect an inspector to flag it.

Which city office handles permits and code questions?

The Building and Inspections Division is at the City Services Center, 1830 6th Avenue, and visitors use the north entrance on 6th Avenue. It handles building permits and plan reviews, building inspections, contractor registration, food establishment licensing and code enforcement.

Code complaints about housing, nuisance, vegetation, zoning and signs go through the City's Neighborhood Improvement Officer, who also works with the neighborhood groups. If your house has an open complaint or a citation, resolve it or ask the city what a closing needs, because a title company can discover it.

  • Pull permit records for any remodel, deck, roof or mechanical work done in your years of ownership.
  • Ask the division how to close out any permit that was opened but never finished.
  • Ask the water and sewer divisions about final billing before the closing date.

The city publishes its Code of Ordinances online for anyone who wants to check a rule before listing.

How does a Moline deed get recorded?

Recording for a Moline address takes place in neighboring Rock Island, at the Recorder's second-floor office at 1504 3rd Avenue (309-558-3360). Counter hours are weekdays, 8 a.m. to 4:30 p.m.

The county lays out format rules: white letter-size paper, a clear 3 by 5 inch box at the top right of page one, no staples or tape, black ink and type of at least 10 points. The document must name its preparer and a return address, and a deed adds the grantee's address and a spot for the tax bill mailing address.

Under 35 ILCS 200/31-15 the state charges fifty cents for every $500 of value. Whether a county or city stamp is added is a question for the Recorder.

What should a Moline seller have ready before an offer?

Start with the disclosure report. State law, 765 ILCS 77/20, has the seller complete each item and hand the report over ahead of the signed contract.

Then pull together the closing file: parcel number, newest tax bill, any loan payoff figure and the permit history. A rented house also needs its leases and tenant contacts, which a buyer will want to read.

Weigh at least two offers by what you would net, not by the headline figure. Ask each buyer who covers transfer stamps, which repairs they expect and how fast they can close.

Do houses sell quickly in Moline?

It varies. The Census median home value of $146,300 is modest, and the population estimate has eased since 2020, so a house needing repairs may linger on the market. A purchase by a cash buyer is usually the quickest way out.

Which office files a Moline deed?

The Rock Island County Recorder, whose second-floor counter at 1504 3rd Avenue opens weekdays, 8 a.m. to 4:30 p.m. Call 309-558-3360.

What formatting does Rock Island County insist on for deeds?

Letter-size white paper, an empty 3 by 5 inch area in the upper right of page one, black ink at 10 points or larger, nothing attached, and lines naming the preparer and where to send the document back. Deeds also carry the grantee's address and the address for tax bills.

Who approves building work on a Moline house?

The city's Building and Inspections Division reviews plans, issues permits, runs inspections and registers contractors. Contact it at the City Services Center on 6th Avenue before starting a project.

What paperwork must a Moline seller give the buyer?

A finished residential disclosure report, in the buyer's hands before the contract is signed (765 ILCS 77/20). The state transfer tax, fifty cents per $500, is paid when the deed is recorded.

No city transfer tax applies here. The city's resident information page says Crystal Lake has none, and the McHenry County Recorder adds that no municipality in the county charges its own.

The city sits in McHenry County about 45 miles northwest of Chicago and is the county's most populous city. It takes its name from a lake 1.6 miles southwest of downtown. The 2020 census counted 40,269 residents and the 2025 estimate is 42,288, growth of 5.0 percent, while Cicero, Chicago and Danville all shrank in the same Census table. About 18.92 square miles of land hold roughly 2,129 people per square mile.

Census figures for 2020 to 2024 describe a market of owners. Roughly 77.6 percent of homes are lived in by their owners, with a middle value of $311,400, and households earn a middle income of $108,418. The city has 14,806 households of about 2.72 people, and 42.0 percent of adults over 25 finished a bachelor's degree.

How does the sale process work step by step in Crystal Lake?

A Crystal Lake sale follows the standard Illinois sequence, with only a few city-level touchpoints. You sign a contract, deliver the disclosure report, clear title, pay off any mortgage, sign the deed and have it recorded with the McHenry County Recorder.

The Recorder's page says a new deed is required to change ownership and suggests an attorney. Deed forms are free at the office. The PTAX-203 or MyDec form filed with the deed shows the full consideration, which is the base for the state tax of fifty cents per $500 in Article 31 of the Property Tax Code.

What city rules apply when you sell or hand over a Crystal Lake house?

Mostly utility, permit and street rules, since the city's resident information page lists no point-of-sale inspection. City Hall stands at 100 W. Woodstock Street, with weekday hours of 8:00 AM to 5:00 PM and a main line of (815) 459-2020.

  • Permits: the Building Division issues building, electrical and plumbing permits and enforces the building, housing, pollution control and fire codes. If you started a project and did not finish it, call before you list.
  • Water and sewer: the buyer sets up service by contacting Water Billing, and the city offers a Direct Debit Program.
  • Garbage: the city's residential contractor is Lakeshore Recycling Systems, which provides weekly curbside collection and one bulk item per week.
  • Street parking: parking on city streets is prohibited from 2:00 AM to 6:00 AM year-round, which matters for open house guests.

Open permits and unfinished work tend to surface in inspection and title review, so closing them out before listing avoids a later argument.

Which neighborhoods and landmarks shape home values in Crystal Lake?

Buyers sort Crystal Lake by neighborhood and school boundary more than by city name. Downtown surrounds Crystal Lake Central High School and has the widest range of house sizes and ages. Directly south is the Coventry neighborhood, and southwest of downtown is the sprawling Four Colonies area, which covers nearly 2.5 square miles. South of that are The Villages, named for Village Road.

North of downtown, the area near Prairie Ridge High School has large houses on widely spaced lots, and Burtons Bridge sits at the northeast edge next to the Fox River. The city was settled in the 1830s, and its first train station was built in 1856. Two villages, Nunda and Crystal Lake, were both incorporated in 1874.

Outdoor recreation helps listings. The separate Crystal Lake Park District runs more than 40 parks, including 140-acre Veteran Acres Park and 305-acre Lippold Park. Old gravel quarries on the south side have filled with water, forming the Vulcan Lakes area, and its two northern lakes became the Three Oaks Recreation Area in autumn 2010.

How do schools, roads and commuting affect a Crystal Lake sale?

Crystal Lake buyers frequently commute, so schools and the Metra station are the first questions. Community High School District 155 runs the high schools, and Crystal Lake Community Consolidated School District 47 operates the elementary and middle schools. Part of the northeast side is served by Prairie Grove Consolidated School District 46.

The three main high schools are Crystal Lake Central, whose first class graduated in 1924, Crystal Lake South, which opened in 1978, and Prairie Ridge, which opened in fall 1997. McHenry County College, a community college, is also located here.

The Metra Union Pacific Northwest Line runs to Chicago's Ogilvie Transportation Center, with stops at Crystal Lake and Pingree Road. U.S. Route 14, Illinois Route 176 and Illinois Route 31 serve the city by road, and O'Hare International Airport is about a 45-minute drive. Census data show a mean commute of 29.3 minutes, shorter than Chicago's 33.1 minutes.

What does an Illinois seller have to disclose in Crystal Lake?

Illinois law has the seller fill in a residential disclosure report and hand it over ahead of signing. The duty is in Section 20 of the disclosure Act, and Section 35 holds the form.

The report covers flood hazard insurance, flooding or recurring leakage in the basement or crawl space, whether the property is in a floodplain, and defects in the foundation, roof, walls, electrical, plumbing and heating systems. It also asks about wells, septic and sanitary sewer systems, radon, asbestos, lead, mine subsidence, termites, underground fuel tanks and boundary disputes. The form requires an explanation for any answer of yes or not applicable, except on the first question.

Answers rest on what you actually know, with no special investigation required. The form calls itself a disclosure rather than a warranty and leaves room for a buyer's own inspection.

Should a Crystal Lake owner take a cash offer or list on the market?

Condition, deadline and appetite for effort decide it. Cash makes sense for a house needing repairs, a firm move-out date or a wish to skip showings, and a listing suits a house that is ready to show.

  • List the repairs a buyer's inspector would flag and get bids for them.
  • Add the cost of carrying the home while it is listed, including taxes, utilities and insurance.
  • Ask what closing date the buyer will commit to in writing.
  • Confirm any open permits are closed or that the buyer accepts them.

Tax bill information is on the McHenry County Treasurer's site. Ask the title company to show the prorated tax lines on your settlement statement, and keep your latest bill handy.

Frequently asked questions

Does Crystal Lake charge a transfer tax when I sell?

No city tax exists, according to the resident information page, and the McHenry County Recorder says no municipality in the county levies one. The state tax still applies.

Is a city inspection required before a Crystal Lake sale?

The resident information page lists none. Call the Building Division at (815) 356-3605 to ask about open permits on the property.

Where is the deed recorded for a Crystal Lake property?

It is recorded with the McHenry County Recorder. The Recorder's page says a new deed is required to change ownership and recommends using an attorney.

How do I end water service when I sell?

Contact the city's Water Billing office at (815) 459-2020. Ask about the final reading and how the closing date will be handled.

Can I sell my Crystal Lake house as-is?

Yes, provided the Illinois disclosure report reaches the buyer first. The form itself recognizes that parties may agree to an as-is deal.

What are your options for a quick house sale in Romeoville?

Romeoville sellers choose between a conventional listing, a sale without an agent, and a direct sale to a buyer who pays cash. The cash route shortens the timeline most, though the village's clearance letter and transfer stamp process applies to every sale. What is Romeoville like for a house seller?

Romeoville is a village in Will County, about 26 miles southwest of Chicago, on the Gateway Wetlands just west of the Des Plaines River and Historic U.S. Route 66, now IL-53. It sits between Bolingbrook and Joliet near Interstates 55 and 355. The village was incorporated on January 19, 1895, after residents of the river port of Romeo voted to change the name, and it covers about 20 square miles.

The area earned the nickname Stone City because of its limestone quarries, and stone from Romeoville was used to build the Illinois State Capitol in Springfield. Lewis University was founded on the edge of town in 1934. In 1950 the village had roughly 46 homes. The Hampton Park Subdivision began in 1957 on more than 600 acres of wetland along IL-53, and the 1990 opening of the Weber Road interchange on I-55 set off two decades of rapid building. Population rose from 21,153 in 2000 to 39,680 in 2010.

Romeoville's ZIP codes are 60446 and 60491, and its land falls across four townships: DuPage, Lockport, Plainfield and Wheatland.

For college, Lewis University has its main campus on the village's edge, and Joliet Junior College and Rasmussen College both run campuses in Romeoville. Since district lines cross the village, confirm the school assignment for a specific address before quoting it to a buyer.

What must happen at the Village of Romeoville before a closing?

Romeoville's Real Estate Transfer Tax is the buyer's responsibility, but the seller has to clear the property first. To get a transfer stamp, the property must be clear of all debts to the village, including the most current water bill. You request a clearance letter, which starts the process and orders a final water reading. Clearance letters are valid for five business days. A final meter reading is not required for an exempt transaction if the water account is in good standing and the name stays the same.

The village prints its tax as $3.50 per $1,000 of the full consideration price for nonexempt transactions, or a $40 processing fee for exempt ones. Payment can be made online by credit card or e-check, or in person. After payment, you get a receipt with space for the stamp, and the physical stamp can be handed over or mailed. A lost stamp must be repurchased at full price.

A refund is available only to residents who sell the home they live in and buy another Romeoville home as a new principal residence, within 12 months of each other. The Finance Department is at 1050 W Romeo Road, phone 815-886-7212.

How does the final water bill work in Romeoville?

The final water bill is part of the clearance. The village mails it to the forwarding address you provide after closing. The seller's account stays in the seller's name until a final on-site meter read is complete, so give the Water Billing office your closing date and mailing address in advance.

Any unpaid balance blocks the stamp, which in turn blocks recording. Paying the account in full the day the reading posts keeps the closing on schedule.

What state and county stamps does a Romeoville deed need?

State law sets the Illinois stamp at 50 cents per $500 of value or fraction, sold through the county recorder (35 ILCS 200/31-15). A deed will not be accepted for filing unless those stamps have been purchased from the recorder of the county where it is filed (35 ILCS 200/31-20). Romeoville is in Will County, so the recording office there handles the filing. Ask the Will County Clerk's recording office for its current fee schedule and the county stamp amount, because those figures are set by the county.

Your title company normally prepares the state transfer declaration and delivers the deed with the village stamp attached.

How does Will County bill property tax, and what does a seller owe?

Will County mails bills on May 1 for the previous tax year, and the Treasurer's levy calendar for bills paid in 2026 shows a first installment due June 1, 2026 and a second due September 1, 2026, both with postmarks accepted. Late payments accrue interest under state statute: 1.5% per month on the first installment starting June 2, with the rate stepping up in later months.

For a seller, the practical step is to check whether both installments are paid and to settle the proration on the closing statement. The calendar changes yearly, so ask the Will County Treasurer for the schedule that applies to your sale.

The buyer is responsible for Romeoville's Real Estate Transfer Tax. The village prints $3.50 per $1,000 of full consideration for nonexempt transactions and a $40 fee for exempt ones, but the seller must still clear village debts first.

How long is a Romeoville clearance letter good for?

Five business days. The letter starts the clearance process and orders the final water reading, so request it close to your closing date.

Do I need a final water reading when I sell in Romeoville?

Usually yes. A final reading is not required for an exempt transaction if the account is in good standing and the name on it stays the same. For a normal sale the seller's account stays open until a final on-site read, and the last bill is mailed to your forwarding address.

Can I get a transfer tax refund in Romeoville?

Only if you live in the home, sell it, and buy another Romeoville home as your new principal residence within 12 months. Owner-occupants who sell and buy outside the village do not qualify.

Will County. The deed goes to the Will County recording office with the state and county stamps and the village stamp. Your title company usually files it.

Illinois Route 59 is the main north-south road, with a large retail area at Route 59 and Stearns Road. The village's Building Division issues permits for work from decks and pools to driveways and new construction, and inspections by building staff run Monday through Friday only. You can reach the division at 630.540.5920.

The village's guidance on new driveways is specific and worth reading before you list a house with a worn drive.

  • The apron, the part of the driveway that meets the street, is the homeowner's responsibility, and the village does not maintain or replace it.
  • Public works inspects the public sidewalk and utilities inside the driveway during permit review, and if the sidewalk needs repair the village will do it, which can take up to four weeks and delay the permit.
  • No apron extension is approved when a parkway tree stands within 10 feet of it, and the village will not remove parkway trees for that purpose.
  • If a concrete contractor repairs the public sidewalk, Public Works will reimburse part of the cost, and the number to ask is 630-837-0811.

Sprinklers and invisible fences placed in the village right-of-way are also the homeowner's problem if sidewalk work damages them.

Apart from the downtown, Bartlett's retail is concentrated at Illinois Route 59 and Stearns Road. Census figures for 2022 show $196.5 million in retail sales, or $4,897 per resident, along with $117.7 million in health care receipts and $89.3 million in transportation and warehousing receipts.

The Bartlett Public Library opened in 1973 and was renovated in 2015 with new study rooms, conference rooms and an art room. The village has a large Little League program, including a Challenger division for players with special needs, and holds an Independence Day festival near the community center and an arts fair on the last weekend of June.

These facts help when you write a listing or talk to a buyer, since families often ask about recreation within a few minutes of the house.

County recorders sell the revenue stamps that pay Illinois' transfer tax, according to the Department of Revenue. Home rule municipalities may add their own tax, so ask the title company whether the village charges one.

The PTAX-203 declaration goes to the county of the parcel. In Cook County the Clerk's deed fee is $107 on the schedule that began April 1, 2024, a sum covering recording, GIS, storage, the state rental housing support fee and a filer fee. Parcels in DuPage or Kane have their own fee lists, so call that recorder.

$107 on the schedule effective April 1, 2024. It rolls together the county recording fee, a GIS fee, a storage fee, the state rental housing support fee and a non-government filer fee. DuPage and Kane parcels follow those counties' fees.

Elgin Area School District U46, the second largest in Illinois, serves the entire village. Some residents' children go to South Elgin High School instead of Bartlett High School.

What is the city of DeKalb like?

DeKalb lies in northern Illinois, roughly 65 miles west of downtown Chicago and 30 miles southeast of Rockford, where the South Branch of the Kishwaukee River flows north through town. The 17-square-mile city was named for Baron Johann de Kalb, a Revolutionary War general.

Platted in 1853 as Huntley's Grove, the town grew with the railroad that arrived that year. Northern Illinois University, founded in 1895 and enrolling about 20,000, is the largest employer. Northwestern Medicine, General Electric, the school district and the retail strip along Route 23 add jobs, and distribution centers for several national brands sit near I-88 and I-39.

Route 23 carries traffic north and south, and Route 38, once the Lincoln Highway, carries it east and west. I-88 passes just south of the city. DeKalb Public Transit connects the campus, Sycamore and Kishwaukee College, and the closest Metra station is at Elburn, 15 miles east, reached by bus.

DeKalb Community Unit School District 428 covers most of the city, with eight elementary schools, Clinton Rosette and Huntley Middle Schools and DeKalb High School, home of the Barbs.

Who lives in DeKalb, and what does the census count show?

The 2020 census tallied 40,290 people in 15,259 households and a median age of just 27.7. One-person households made up 34.5 percent of the total, and 27.2 percent of households included children. Of 16,629 housing units, 8.2 percent stood vacant; the homeowner vacancy rate was 1.9 percent and the rental rate 7.9 percent.

The DeKalb Park District runs 44 parks covering more than 700 acres, including Annie's Woods, Huntley Park, Liberty Park and Hopkins Park, and Ellwood House, the former home of barbed-wire entrepreneur Isaac Ellwood, is a local landmark. Commercial flights leave from O'Hare, about 43 miles away, while DeKalb Taylor Municipal Airport serves general aviation on the east side of the city.

Do weather and river history matter when selling a DeKalb house?

Both matter. NOAA normals for the city list 37.25 inches of precipitation and 33.1 inches of snowfall in an average year, and the wettest months are May and June.

The Kishwaukee crested at 15.27 feet on August 24, 2007, the second time it had topped 15 feet in the recorded history of the gauge, and flooded parts of town. If your house is near the river or has ever taken on basement water, say so up front and keep your repair receipts. Buyers' inspectors in this climate look first at roofs, gutters and sump pumps.

How do DeKalb's housing numbers compare?

40,467 residents in mid-2025, up 0.3 percent from the 2020 base of 40,326. Renters outnumber owners.

DeKalb housing figures, Census QuickFacts, 2020-2024 estimates
ItemDeKalb
Middle value of homes their owners occupy$204,700
Owner-occupied share of housing units42.1%
