Bachelor's degree or more among adults 25 and over33.7%

With owners living in just 42.1 percent of units, a large part of the stock is rental. An investor buyer will likely want copies of leases, a rent roll and proof of city registration.

Which city rules govern DeKalb rentals and property upkeep?

Landlords must register each rental with the city every year. Chapter 10 of the municipal code, revised in October 2022, built the Crime Free Housing Program into that requirement.

  • Registration comes with a security plan aimed at preventing unlawful activity on the premises.
  • Each lease carries a crime free lease provision.
  • Owners attend a class once, then a refresher every year after that, and the city posts the refresher slides online.

Upkeep falls to the Building and Code Compliance Division at 164 East Lincoln Highway, reachable at 815-748-2070. Inspectors apply the International Property Maintenance Code through Chapter 24, mostly by viewing properties from public ground and answering complaints about weeds, trash, snow and ice, and inoperable cars. The city posts annual violation listings, so a seller can learn whether a parcel was cited before a buyer finds out.

Selling a rental? Ask the Crime Free Housing Bureau what your current registration status is and what the next owner has to file.

Where are DeKalb deeds recorded, and how does the tax bill work?

Deeds go to the DeKalb County Clerk and Recorder on the second floor of the Administration Building, 110 East Sycamore Street, Sycamore, open weekdays from 8:30 in the morning until 4:30 in the afternoon. Recording questions go to 815-895-7156. Since August 3, 2026, title companies, attorneys and lenders can also record electronically, and mailed or hand-carried paper still works.

The Recorder's fee page lists $74.00 for a standard letter-size deed and $94.00 for a larger page. It names transfer stamps at 50 cents per $500 of value for the State and 25 cents per $500 for the County, and sends filers to MyDec for the state declaration. A deed must show who prepared it, where to return it, where to send tax bills, the PIN and the street address.

The Treasurer mails a single bill around May 1 with two coupons. Due dates land near June 1 and September 1, and the 2025 bills fell on June 3 and September 3, 2026. Each month of delay adds 1.5 percent, and taxes still open after the second installment can be sold, with redemption handled by the County Clerk at 815-895-7149. A buyer who receives a bill in a former owner's name can download a copy from the county's online portal, and a seller no longer holding title should pass the bill along. Treasurer's office: 815-895-7112.

What paperwork should a DeKalb seller collect?

A brief checklist keeps the closing on schedule.

  1. Find the PIN and street address that must appear on the deed.
  2. Download your newest bill from the Treasurer's portal.
  3. Ask the city about unresolved rental registration or violation notices.
  4. Assemble leases, deposit records and tenant phone numbers for an occupied house.
  5. Ask each lender or lienholder for a payoff letter.

Once a contract is signed, the title company searches the record, drafts the deed, files the state declaration and sends the deed to Sycamore.

Frequently asked questions

Do I register my DeKalb rental before selling it?

Registration is a duty while you own and lease the unit under Chapter 10. Ask the Crime Free Housing Bureau whether yours is current and what a buyer who keeps tenants must file afterward.

Where does a DeKalb deed get recorded?

The DeKalb County Clerk and Recorder, 110 East Sycamore Street in Sycamore, second floor. Title firms may file electronically, and paper filings remain accepted.

How much is transfer tax in DeKalb County?

The fee page shows 50 cents per $500 of value for the State plus 25 cents per $500 for the County. Filing happens through MyDec, and your closing agent buys the stamps.

When are DeKalb County tax bills due?

Near June 1 and September 1. For the 2025 tax year the dates were June 3 and September 3, 2026, and late payments add 1.5 percent each month.

Can I sell a DeKalb rental with tenants inside?

Often yes, since investors buy occupied rentals. Hand over the lease, deposit records and contact details, and ask your closing agent how the deposit and current rent will be credited.

What is Belleville's housing stock like for a seller?

Belleville is the St. Clair County seat in the Metro East, and its housing stock reflects almost two centuries of building. The first homes were simple brick cottages that locals called German street houses or row houses, and later decades added Foursquare, Italianate, Queen Anne and Victorian styles. A seller with a pre-war house here is often selling a property that has had many owners, many repairs and several rounds of wiring and plumbing updates.

The city dates to 1814, when its founder donated an acre for the town square plus 25 adjoining acres so the county seat could move over from Cahokia. It became a village in 1819 and a city in 1850. After the 1848 revolutions in the German states, a wave of educated settlers arrived, and by 1870 an estimated 90 percent of residents were German-born or of German descent. That heritage still shapes the older neighborhoods around the square.

Belleville has three locally designated historic districts: Old Belleville (1974), Hexenbuckel (1991) and Oakland (1995). A separate National Register district, listed in 1976, has 73 contributing properties. If your house sits inside one of them, ask the city's building staff what rules apply to exterior work before you sign a repair-heavy contract with a buyer.

How big is Belleville and what do Census numbers say about its homes?

The 2025 Census estimate for Belleville is 40,237 people, a 5.0 percent decline from the 42,358 in the 2020 estimates base. Fewer people competing for the same stock tends to mean longer waits for conventional buyers, so pricing matters more here than in a growing suburb.

Home values near $141,300 and rents near $1,019 put a premium on condition, so the next two sections cover the city rules that can hold up a closing for owner-occupants and landlords alike.

Does Belleville require an inspection or occupancy permit when a house sells?

Belleville requires a Residential Certificate of Occupancy before a residence can be legally occupied, and the city's Health, Housing and Building Department issues it after an inspection of the dwelling. Its process sheet tells sellers to call for a housing inspection as soon as they decide to sell, because a passed inspection can shorten the closing timeline and help the new owner get the occupancy permit.

  • The inspection covers electrical and plumbing systems, exterior and interior structure and other readily visible areas, checked against the city's housing code.
  • Defects found must be corrected before occupancy is allowed, and a failed inspection means no permit until the violations are cleared and a reinspection is done.
  • All sewer bills for the property must be paid and current before an inspection can be scheduled or a permit issued.
  • The permit step for a new occupant lists a $55 fee as printed on the city's sheet, and the sheet lists $65 per dwelling unit for rental inspections.
  • The number of people allowed in a unit depends on bedroom square footage, so check the allowed count before finalizing a sales contract.

The department is at 2300 West Main Street, Building M, Suite M113, and takes calls at 618-233-6817 (option 1 for inspections). Its sheet gives weekday counter hours from 8 in the morning to 5 in the evening. Its fee figures carry a June 2022 revision date, so ask the department for current amounts. Any new occupant still needs the permit after a renovation, which is worth raising when you compare offers.

What rules apply if the Belleville house is a rental?

Belleville has run a Crime Free Housing program since November 1, 2013, and any owner who leases a unit must register it. The city's process sheet prices registration at $30 per dwelling unit, with renewals due by October 31 each year and fees doubling when a renewal is late.

Owners and managers must also complete the Crime Free Housing class, which the city now offers online, then email the department for a certificate. A leased unit needs a passed inspection, a nationwide background check on the tenant, the crime-free lease addendum and a signed lease before the tenant can obtain an occupancy permit. With a tenant in place, gather the registration receipt, the last passed inspection report and the lease so a buyer's lender or inspector can see the paperwork is in order.

A second failed reinspection carries a $50 fee on the city's sheet. Vacant, tired rentals that would need work to pass are a common reason owners look at an as-is sale instead of fixing everything first.

What do Belleville schools, jobs and roads mean for a sale?

Buyers ask about commutes and schools first, so have the facts ready.

  • High schools: Belleville Township High School District 201 runs Belleville East and Belleville West. Althoff Catholic High School is the Diocese of Belleville option, and parts of the city fall in East St. Louis District 189, Mascoutah District 19 and Freeburg District 77.
  • Grade schools: Districts 118, 119 (Belle Valley), 175 (Harmony Emge), 181 (Signal Hill), 115 (Whiteside) and 70 (Freeburg) all serve parts of Belleville, so the district depends on the street.
  • Transit and roads: Three St. Louis MetroLink stations sit in the city (Memorial Hospital, Belleville and College), and Illinois routes 15, 158, 159, 177, 13 and 161 pass through. Interstates 64 and 255 are adjacent.
  • Employers: Memorial Hospital, Illinois American Water, Empire Comfort Systems and Permobil are among the larger names listed for the city.

Southwestern Illinois College's main campus sits just outside the city limits, and the city's bicycle trail runs from Southside Park to the college and toward the base.

How do St. Clair County recording and transfer steps work in Belleville?

Belleville deeds are filed at the St. Clair County Recorder of Deeds, whose office is at the county building on Public Square. The county's fee table, current for deeds received after July 1, 2023, lists $55.00 with the Rental Housing Support Program fee and $36.00 without it, with transfer tax added when applicable. The office takes cash, check or money order payable to Recorder of Deeds. Mail goes to PO Box 543, Belleville, IL 62222, and overnight carriers use 10 Public Square, 5th Floor.

Buyer and seller also complete the state's PTAX-203 transfer declaration, which goes to the county office. The state says counties may levy a 25-cent-per-$500 transfer tax and home rule municipalities may add another, so ask your closing agent which charges attach to a Belleville address. Illinois Department of Revenue's Tax Rate Database lists the rates.

Sellers who hold title through an estate or a family transfer should confirm the deed type with the title company before the closing date, since an exempt transfer is recorded differently from a sale.

How are Belleville property taxes assessed, appealed and paid?

Property in St. Clair County is reassessed every four years, and any change must be published in a county newspaper and mailed to the owner. If you think your value is out of line with neighbors, the county's first step is an informal review with the County Assessor's office. Most cases end there, but you can also file an appeal for a hearing before the Board of Review. Bring an exterior photo of your house and photos of at least three similar nearby properties, property record cards, or a recent appraisal, contract, settlement statement or deed. Evidence must reach the Board at least five days before the hearing or the assessment stands unchanged.

The Treasurer sends bills to the owner even when a lender escrows the taxes, and the owner stays responsible for penalties and interest. Unpaid taxes can lead the county to sell a lien. A principal dwelling with no more than six units can be redeemed for two and one-half years, and other property for two years. The Treasurer also runs a monthly payment plan for homeowners with the Homeowner Occupied Exemption, and online card payments carry a 2.5 percent convenience charge. Before closing, get this year's installment dates and a payoff figure from the Treasurer's office.

Frequently asked questions

Can I sell a Belleville house with failed occupancy inspection items?

Yes, a sale is still possible, but the new occupant cannot get a Residential Occupancy Permit until the violations are corrected and the unit passes reinspection. Ask the Health, Housing and Building Department for the written inspection report, then decide whether to repair, credit the buyer or sell to someone who plans the work.

Who records the deed after a Belleville sale?

The St. Clair County Recorder of Deeds files it. The county fee table lists deeds at $55.00 with the Rental Housing Support Program fee or $36.00 without, with transfer tax added when it applies. Your title company or attorney normally handles the filing.

Do Belleville landlords have to register rentals before selling?

Yes while the unit is leased: the city's sheet requires registration of each leased dwelling unit and an annual update by October 31. Keep the registration, inspection report and lease together so the buyer can see the unit was compliant.

What if my Belleville assessment looks too high?

Start with an informal review at the County Assessor's office, then file with the Board of Review if needed. Submit comparables or an appraisal at least five days before your hearing, because late evidence results in the appeal being upheld with no change.

Is the Belleville population shrinking, and does that affect my price?

The 2025 estimate of 40,237 sits 5.0 percent under the 2020 base of 42,358. At a typical value near $141,300, condition and price both matter, so get two or three offers or a local agent's opinion before choosing a route.

What is the quickest way to sell a house in Oswego, Illinois?

A direct cash sale gives the shortest wait before closing, while a listing takes longer and favors a house that shows well. Selling on your own is the third route and suits owners with time and a good title company.

Oswego is a village on the Fox River in Kendall County, with a small part in Will County, and it is the largest municipality in Kendall County. The Census Bureau counted 34,585 people in 2020 and its 2025 estimate is 39,948, an increase of 15.4% from the 2020 base.

  • Hire an agent if the roof, windows and mechanical systems are in good order and you can handle showings and a financing timeline.
  • Handle the sale yourself if you can price the home from recent nearby sales and coordinate the paperwork the village requires.
  • Take a cash buyer if the house needs work, is vacant, or belongs to an estate. Weigh the offer against a listing price after commission, repairs and the months of taxes and utilities you would carry.

How did Oswego grow from a river town into a large suburb?

Oswego grew slowly for more than a century and then expanded quickly after 1990. Settlers arrived in 1833, the village was incorporated in 1852, and in January 1837 residents settled on the name Oswego by a single vote after the place had been called Hudson and Lodi.

Caterpillar and Western Electric built plants nearby in the mid-1950s, which helped the Boulder Hill area develop, and the home-building boom of the mid-1980s pushed the village limits west of the Fox River. The census counts tell the rest: 3,876 people in 1990, 13,326 in 2000, 30,355 in 2010 and 34,585 in 2020. A drag strip on Route 34 ran from 1955 to 1979 and is still a topic of local nostalgia, though the site is closed to the public.

Downtown has older buildings, including the Little White School Museum, built in 1850, plus brick pavers and landscaping from a streetscape project. Hudson Crossing Park opened on the river in October 2004, and the Waubonsee Creek Promenade completes the downtown work.

What does the transfer stamp mean for an Oswego sale?

Oswego voters approved a real estate transfer tax on June 28, 2022, and the buyer pays it at $3 per $1,000 of the sale price. A stamp from the village is required before the deed can be recorded with Kendall or Will County, even when the buyer is exempt from the tax.

The seller still has a part in the process, because open village bills block the stamp. Here is how the village describes it:

  • The buyer or a representative sends a MyDec or PTAX-203 declaration at least three business days before closing, online or at Village Hall.
  • The village then prepares a Statement of Open Accounts, and any open invoice tied to the property must be paid in full before the stamp is released.
  • After review, the buyer brings the deed to Village Hall at 100 Parkers Mill, open weekdays from 8 a.m. until 5 p.m., and the tax is calculated while they wait.
  • Payment is accepted by credit card, cash or certified check.

A person who has owned a primary residence in Oswego for at least a year is exempt from the tax when buying another Oswego home, but still obtains a stamp. The village's own example shows a $300,000 sale carrying a $900 charge at the $3 rate. The village states the money must go to the water and sewer fund, tied to the Lake Michigan water connection through the DuPage Water Commission. Questions go to TransferTax@oswegoil.org or (630) 554-0864.

Which schools serve Oswego homes?

Oswego Community Unit School District 308 serves most of the village, and portions of Oswego fall within Yorkville Community Unit School District 115. District 308 operates 22 schools, including one early learning center, 14 elementary schools, five junior high schools, two high schools and one opportunity school.

Because the district also reaches Boulder Hill, Montgomery, Plainfield, Aurora, Yorkville and Joliet, a house's attendance zone is not always obvious from the village name. Confirm the district for a specific address before listing, and mention the nearest elementary and junior high on the flyer. The Census Bureau puts persons under 18 at 26.3% of Oswego's population.

What permits does Oswego require for home improvements?

Oswego handles residential permits through its Building and Permits department, and a long list of projects needs one. The village's application list includes basement remodels, decks, driveways, fences, fireplaces, garages, hot tubs, HVAC, irrigation systems, patios, pergolas, permanent pools, sheds, solar, sump pumps and downspouts, and window and door replacement.

Roof, siding, radon and water heater permits go through an online portal called Civic Access, and the other applications are emailed to the department. If you did work on the house, gather the permit and final inspection records for the buyer.

Floodplain rules apply along the river and creeks. Any change to a structure in the floodplain may need a permit, and the substantial improvement rule generally limits an addition to less than fifty percent of the structure's value. The village has a floodplain map where you can check an address, and the village asks owners to contact it before designing a project.

How are Kendall County property taxes billed?

Kendall County mails one bill a year that is paid in two installments, and the 2026 due dates were June 9 and September 9. Those dates have passed, and the county says a late payment is charged 1.5% of the installment per month.

The Collector's office is at 504 S. Main Street in Yorkville, open weekdays from 8 a.m. until 4:30 p.m., with the telephone at 630-553-4124. The county will not take estimated or partial payments, so the exact amount on the bill is required. It also accepts payment online, by phone, by ACH, by mail, at most Kendall County banks, and in person, and a drop box outside the office is available at any hour. Ask the Collector for your schedule and for a copy of the bill, and ask your closing agent how the year's tax is prorated between you and the buyer.

How does the weather affect an Oswego house?

Oswego has a hot-summer humid continental climate with four seasons, and a buyer's inspector will focus on the roof, gutters, sump pump and heating system. NOAA climate normals for 1990-2021 give an average of 39.53 inches of precipitation and 29.1 inches of snow a year.

January's mean daily high is 30.5 degrees and July's is 84.0. Spring and summer can bring severe weather, including tornadoes, according to the same climate summary. Keep receipts for any sump pump, downspout or drainage work for the buyer.

What do Census numbers say about Oswego?

Oswego has a young, family-heavy profile, with 87.9% of homes occupied by their owners and a median household income of $123,792.

Frequently asked questions

Who pays the Oswego real estate transfer tax?

The buyer. The tax is $3 per $1,000 of the sale price, and a village stamp is needed before the deed is recorded. The seller's part is clearing any open village invoices on the property.

How early must the transfer declaration reach Oswego?

At least three business days before closing. Send a MyDec or PTAX-203 to the village online or at Village Hall, and the village will then prepare its Statement of Open Accounts.

Is anyone exempt from the Oswego transfer tax?

Yes. Owners of an Oswego primary residence for at least one year are exempt when they buy another home in the village, though they still need a stamp. Other exemptions are listed in Ordinance 22-54.

When are Kendall County property taxes due?

The 2026 installments were due June 9 and September 9. Kendall County issues one bill, payable in two parts, and charges 1.5% per month on late payments.

Do I need a permit to replace a roof in Oswego?

Yes. Roof permits are filed through the village's Civic Access online portal. Keep the permit and final inspection record to hand to the buyer.

Which selling routes make sense in Urbana?

Listing through an agent, selling alone and accepting a cash buyer's as-is price all work in Urbana. Tenants change the picture, because the city runs a rental registration program, and the University of Illinois next door keeps the rental market busy.

Urbana belongs to Champaign County, shares its western edge with the city of Champaign, and holds most of the university campus. Residents numbered 38,336 on census day in 2020. The mid-2025 estimate of 39,719 is 1.9% above the 2020 base.

What do Urbana housing and households look like?

Five-year survey results portray a young, renter-heavy city where home values sit far under those in the Chicago suburbs.

  • Only 37.3% of homes are lived in by their owners, so renters hold most of the stock
  • Middle value among owned homes: $184,900

Why is Urbana mostly rentals, and what does the city require of landlords?

The city says it has more than 10,000 rental units, nearly two-thirds of its housing, and the University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign enrolls more than 50,000 students annually. The city adopted a Rental Registration and Inspection Program, described on its program page.

  • Every rental property must register each year and pay a fee from the city's schedule of fees.
  • The program year runs from October 15 to October 14, matching the leasing calendar.
  • It covers single-family homes, duplexes and multi-family buildings, including room rentals where the owner also lives there.
  • Nursing homes, hotels and motels, housing authority units and university-certified housing are excluded.
  • The city aims to inspect every rental on a cycle of three to five years, and results appear in its open data portal.

Landlords register through an online Citizenserve account, and the Building Safety Division answers questions at 217-384-2443. Owners of a rental should make sure the registration is up to date before listing, and ask the division what the inspection record shows.

Who collects the property tax on an Urbana house?

The Champaign County Treasurer and Collector bills and collects it, from the Bennett Administrative Center at 102 E. Main Street in Urbana, phone 217-384-3743. The county mails a single bill for the full year with coupons for two equal installments, and does not send a second bill. The collector handles more than 77,000 real estate bills for 156 taxing districts, which include school districts, cities and villages.

Champaign County real estate tax calendar for 2026 bills
DateWhat happens
May 1Bills are mailed
June 3First installment due
September 3Second installment due
September 30, 4:30 p.m.Last day to pay by check, e-check or card; later payments are cash, money order or cashier's check
October 1A $10 cost is added to each unpaid parcel for notices and publication
December 1 to 31Advance payments accepted, from 50% of the prior year's total up to 10% over it

The treasurer's pages state that postmarks do not apply to the late-payment dates. All of the 2026 dates above have passed, and the same pattern repeats with new dates each year. If the county does not have your current mailing address, call the Supervisor of Assessments at 217-384-3760.

What exemptions and tax programs can an Urbana owner use?

The Treasurer's tax page lists the programs and the office that handles each one. Most go through the County Assessment Office at 217-384-3760, which is also the number for corrections to bill information.

  • Owner-occupied exemption
  • Over-65 exemption for real estate, and the Senior Assessment Freeze
  • Disabled persons exemption and various veterans exemptions
  • Natural disaster homestead exemption
  • Tax deferral for owners over 65, run by the County Treasurer

Before you sell, ask the assessment office what is on file for the parcel, so the buyer's first bill is not a surprise. Champaign County has also elected to acquire delinquent real estate taxes as trustee for the taxing districts, beginning with the 2025 taxes payable in 2026 (Public Act 104-0553), so the county, as trustee for the taxing districts, takes the delinquent taxes at the sale in place of private tax buyers. If back taxes are owed, get a payoff from the Treasurer before a closing date is fixed.

What shaped Urbana, and what do its neighborhoods offer?

Europeans first settled the area in 1822, calling it Big Grove. When Champaign County was organized in 1833 the county seat was set on 40 acres, and the name came from Urbana, Ohio. The Illinois Central line bypassed the town and ran two miles west, where West Urbana, later Champaign, grew around the depot.

The Urbana Free Library, founded in 1874, sits downtown. The Lincoln Square area hosts the Market at the Square each Saturday morning from May to November, running since 1979. East of downtown, the Candlestick Lane neighborhood, centered on Grant Place and parts of Fairlawn and Eastern Drives, lights its yards from the third Saturday in December through New Year's Day. Urbana uses a mayor-council form with seven wards.

NOAA normals for 1981 to 2010 show about 41 inches of precipitation and 23 inches of snowfall across a year, with extremes from 109 degrees in July to minus 25 in winter.

Sell as-isNo repairs, no cleaning and no showings. We buy Urbana houses in any condition.See My Cash Offer →

What do Urbana schools, roads and buses offer a buyer?

Urbana School District elementary schools are Leal, Dr. Martin Luther King Jr., Dr. Preston L. Williams Jr., Thomas Paine and Yankee Ridge, with an early childhood school on the Prairie Campus next to Williams. Urbana Middle School served 897 students in grades 6 to 8 as of 2024, and the current Urbana High School building dates to 1914. University Laboratory High School is a publicly funded lab school on campus and sits outside the district.

South of I-74 lies most of the city, with Lincoln, Cunningham and University exits. University Avenue is US 150 and Vine Street and Cunningham Avenue carry US 45. Local buses run through the Champaign-Urbana Mass Transit District, and University of Illinois Willard Airport serves the area.

Does an inherited Urbana house need the usual seller disclosure?

Not always. Illinois expects residential sellers to give the buyer a disclosure report ahead of signing (765 ILCS 77/20), but Section 15 exempts several kinds of seller, including a fiduciary administering a decedent's estate, a transfer from a decedent by will or intestate succession, and transfers made under court order.

Who signs the deed decides whether an exemption applies, so check with the closing attorney. The Champaign County Recorder can tell you the current deed requirements and fees before you schedule a signing.

Frequently asked questions

Does the city of Urbana inspect a house before it sells?

The city's permit and rental pages describe permits and a rental inspection cycle. Call the Building Safety Division at 217-384-2443 to ask whether anything applies to a sale at your address.

What dates apply to Urbana property tax installments?

There are two installments, with bills going out May 1. For 2026 they fell on June 3 and September 3, and the pattern repeats yearly.

What should the owner of an Urbana rental do before listing?

Confirm that registration is current, because the program year runs October 15 to October 14 and fees are annual. The Building Safety Division can explain the inspection history, which also appears in the city's open data.

Where can an Urbana owner pay property tax in person?

Pay at the Champaign County Treasurer's Office, 102 E. Main Street in Urbana. A 24-hour drop box sits in front of the guard shack in the parking area, and cash, checks, money orders and cards are accepted, with cards and checks only through September 30.

How fast can a cash sale of an Urbana house close?

Once the title work, payoff letters and deed are ready. A cash closing depends on the buyer's funds, the title company and the county's recording of the deed.

Where does Carol Stream sit in DuPage County?

Carol Stream is a village in DuPage County, Illinois, in the western Chicago suburbs. It was incorporated on January 5, 1959, and 39,854 people lived there at the 2020 census.

The village covers 9.44 square miles, of which 9.12 are land and 0.32 are water. That is a compact footprint for nearly 40,000 people. The village dates only from 1959, so the housing stock is young by Chicago-area standards.

  • County: DuPage, with deeds recorded at the DuPage County Recorder
  • Village government: a mayor and six trustees, with an appointed village administrator
  • Parks: 36 parks run by the Carol Stream Park District

How did Carol Stream get started?

Developer Jay Stream began buying unincorporated farmland outside Wheaton in 1957, after a frustrating run-in with red tape on a Naperville subdivision, and named the new community for his daughter Carol.

The first village board meeting took place on February 12, 1959. The population was 836 in the 1960 census, then climbed to 4,434 in 1970, 15,472 in 1980 and 31,716 in 1990. It peaked near 40,438 in 2000, slipped to 39,711 in 2010 and stood at 39,854 in 2020.

A former Gretna railway station was renamed Carol Stream in 1962 and now serves as a museum for the Carol Stream Historical Society. The pattern of fast growth followed by a flat decade is useful to a seller: most neighbors bought within the same few decades, so comparable sales tend to be houses of similar age.

Which employers shape the Carol Stream housing market?

Carol Stream's jobs lean toward warehousing, food production and printing rather than one anchor company. The village's 2022 annual financial report, as summarized in the encyclopedia entry for the village, lists these largest employers:

  • Hearthside Food Solutions, 650 employees
  • FIC America Corp., 494
  • Grunt Style, 400
  • FedEx, 369
  • American Litho, 350
  • Tyndale House Publishers, 260

The United States Postal Service also runs a sectional hub here for ZIP codes beginning 601 and 603. Because the employer base is spread across several industries, a layoff at one plant is unlikely to empty the neighborhood, though it can affect a seller who has to move on a short timeline.

Which school districts serve homes in Carol Stream?

Carol Stream's village limits do not match school district lines, so the district depends on the street address. Buyers ask about this early, and a seller who can answer it removes one question from the showing.

  • Most homes: Community Consolidated School District 93 for kindergarten through eighth grade, then Glenbard Township High School District 87 and Glenbard North High School
  • Northwest corner: Elgin Area School District U46, with Spring Trail Elementary in the village
  • Part of the west side: Benjamin School District 25, then Community High School District 94 and West Chicago Community High School
  • Some southern and southeastern blocks: Community Unit School District 200 in Wheaton, or Glen Ellyn School District 41 with Glenbard North for high school

District 93 runs eight schools in the village, including Jay Stream Middle School, named for the founder, and Stratford Middle School.

What roads and transit connect Carol Stream?

North Avenue runs east and west near the middle of the village and is the main corridor, with Army Trail Road and Geneva Road as the other major east-west routes. Gary Avenue runs north and south toward Bloomingdale and the Stratford Square area, and County Farm Road is a major commercial route. Schmale Road serves a small commercial pocket in the southeast, and Kuhn Road runs north and south as a lesser route.

Pace operates Route 711 between Carol Stream and Wheaton. The Great Western Trail crosses town, and the Steve Ravanesi Trail links it to Red Hawk Park, the dog park and Glenbard North High School. A house within a short walk of the trail or a park district facility has an easy item to put in a listing description.

What does Carol Stream require before a sale can close?

The village charges its own transfer tax, and the stamp has to be obtained before closing paperwork goes to the recorder. The rate printed on the Finance Department page is $3.00 for each $1,000 of the selling price or fraction thereof.

Carol Stream transfer stamp checklist, from the Village of Carol Stream Finance Department page

Where stamps are issuedFinance Department at the village's main offices

Contracts can be emailed to the Finance Department, with a 25MB file limit and no zip files. Call the Water Billing division at 630-871-6222 to set the meter reading. Most readings are taken by radio, so the village does not usually need to enter the house.

Who pays the village tax, and can it be refunded?

The seller, or grantor, normally owes the village tax. When a property passes through a sheriff's sale or a tax deed, the buyer owes it instead.

The village allows a refund only when every one of four conditions is met. The seller must have lived in the house for a year within the last three, must not have rented out any part of it, must have bought and now occupy a replacement home inside the village, and must apply within one year of paying the tax. A seller who moves out of Carol Stream will not qualify for this refund.

Do permits matter when I sell a Carol Stream house?

Yes, since an unclosed permit is a question a buyer's agent or the closing attorney may raise. Permit applications go through the Community Development Department, either online or in person, and the village notes a card fee of 2.9 percent online and 3.5 percent at the counter.

  • Inspections need about 24 hours of advance notice and are scheduled at 630-871-6230 between 8 a.m. and 5 p.m.
  • Plumbing inspections are done by a consultant on Monday, Wednesday and Friday afternoons, 1:30 to 3:30 p.m.
  • A re-inspection fee can apply if work fails or is not ready, and it must be paid before the next visit

If you remember a finished basement, deck or water heater swap from a previous owner, ask Community Development whether the permit was closed out. A cash buyer purchasing as-is absorbs that question, while a retail buyer's lender may want it settled.

What state and county steps apply to a sale here?

The state adds its own levy on title transfers under 35 ILCS 200/31-10, at half a dollar for each $500 of declared value. The declaration is filed through the state's MyDec system, and the Carol Stream stamp requires a copy of it.

Your deed is filed with the DuPage County Recorder, whose land records reach back to 1839. The recorder's office can be reached at 630-407-5400, and it also provides deed copies if you need one for a tax appeal or an exemption.

You pick the closing dateClose in as little as 7 days or on the date that works for you, with no fees or commissions.Get My Cash Offer →

How do listing, selling yourself and a cash offer compare in Carol Stream?

Listing with an agent puts the house in front of the widest group of buyers, which suits a house in good shape and an owner who can wait through showings, inspection requests and a buyer's mortgage approval. Selling it yourself saves the agent's fee but leaves the contract, disclosures and the village stamp paperwork on your desk.

An as-is cash sale fits a house that needs work, has a tenant in it, came through an estate or faces a tight deadline. The trade-off is that a cash offer is usually below what a fully repaired house might bring on the open market. Weigh the offer against the repair bill, the carrying costs while the house sits, and the time you have.

Frequently asked questions

Do I pay the Carol Stream transfer tax as the seller?

Usually yes. The village page says the tax generally falls on the grantor, the seller, with an exception for sheriff's sales and tax deeds, where the buyer pays. The rate shown is $3.00 per $1,000 of the price or fraction thereof.

How soon before closing should I book the water meter reading?

Book it at least two working days before closing. Call the Water Billing division at 630-871-6222. The final bill, and anything else owed to the village, must be paid before the stamp is issued.

Which school district is my Carol Stream house in?

It depends on the address. Most homes are in District 93 and Glenbard North, while parts of the village fall in U46, District 25, District 200 or District 41. Check the boundary with the district before you advertise the house.

Can I sell if a past owner skipped a permit?

Yes, you can still sell, but the issue may come up in an inspection or title review. Ask the Community Development Department at 630-871-6230 about the permit history. An as-is cash buyer may take the risk on, while a financed buyer may ask you to resolve it first.

Where is the deed recorded after the sale?

With the DuPage County Recorder, the county's land records office. The state transfer declaration and the village stamp are completed before recording. Call 630-407-5400 with questions about recording.

Which way of selling fits a Quincy homeowner?

Quincy owners usually choose between a standard listing, a private sale, and a direct offer from someone paying cash for the house exactly as it stands. Age of the structure, the work it needs and your calendar decide which of those makes sense.

Quincy has several historic districts, and many of its brick homes date to the German immigrant building boom of the late 1800s. Those houses charm some buyers and put off others who dread the cost of updating them. Think through which of these describes your situation:

  • The condition is sound and months of waiting for the right buyer would not hurt, which favors a listing.
  • A roof, furnace or foundation needs money you would prefer not to spend.
  • A parent who lived there for decades has died and you are settling the estate.
  • A tenant, a code complaint or a lien is getting in the way of a conventional sale.

In the last three situations a direct sale can shorten the process, since no lender appraisal has to be passed. With any route, get the price, the closing date and the split of costs written down before you commit.

What do Census estimates reveal about Quincy housing?

Quincy prices sit low and renters make up a sizable share of households. Just 63.6 percent of occupied units are lived in by their owners in the 2020 to 2024 estimates, which gives landlords and investors a real presence among buyers.

The city has lost a little population since 2010, when the census counted 40,633 residents. The population peaked decades ago, and about one in five residents is 65 or older. Plenty of sellers are longtime owners downsizing or heirs clearing out a parent's place. Commutes average about 14 minutes, which is a point to mention to buyers.

How do the bluffs, river and neighborhoods shape a Quincy sale?

The city rises on bluffs above the Mississippi River at Quincy Bay, with a floodplain across the river in Missouri and the Quincy Hills to the east. Houses on sloping lots near the river deserve a close look at drainage, retaining walls and basement moisture before you list.

The city is compact, at about 15.8 square miles, and buyers tend to think in terms of areas. Downtown is a historic district, and the South Side German Historic District holds the brick homes built by German immigrants in the late 1800s, including the Dick Brothers Brewery buildings from 1857. North Quincy lies beyond a rail line and a large creek, and Hickory Grove sits to the east along Interstate 172.

  • Illinois Route 104 (Broadway) runs from the river bridges east to Interstate 172.
  • Illinois Route 96 doubles as the Great River Road, and Illinois Route 57 links U.S. 24 downtown to Interstate 172.
  • U.S. Route 24 crosses the river on the Quincy Memorial Bridge and the Bayview Bridge.
  • Interstate 72 passes about 12 miles south of town.

A house inside or beside a historic district should be described in terms of its architecture. Brickwork, original trim and period details are what shoppers in those areas tend to look for.

What drives Quincy's economy and demand for homes?

Quincy's largest employers anchor steady demand for housing. Blessing Hospital, Quincy Public Schools and Titan International are named as the area's top three employers. Niemann Foods, Gardner Denver, Kohl Wholesale and Knapheide Manufacturing are among the companies headquartered in town.

Higher education adds renters and buyers as well. Quincy University, John Wood Community College, Gem City College and the Blessing-Rieman College of Nursing and Health Sciences are all in or near the city, and the public school district is Quincy Public School District 172. Employers and campuses of that size keep a base of local buyers and renters in the market.

Census figures put health care and social assistance receipts in Quincy at about $1.3 billion for 2022. The Quincy and Hannibal area forms a combined statistical area of roughly 116,000 people, so some buyers come from across the river in Missouri.

What city rules should a Quincy seller check?

Quincy's Office of Inspection, on the second floor of City Hall at 730 Maine Street, handles building permits and minimum housing complaints. The city runs a complaint-driven system for rentals, where a tenant files a Minimum Housing Complaint Form and an inspector visits. If you are selling a rental, ask the Office of Inspection whether any registration or inspection requirement applies to your address.

The complaint form's checklist shows what inspectors measure against the International Property Maintenance Code. Working smoke detectors in each bedroom and hallway, carbon monoxide alarms in homes with fuel-burning appliances or an attached garage, handrails on stairs with more than four risers, a watertight roof and a heating system that holds 68 degrees are among them. A buyer's home inspector will likely check the same points, so repair them before you list.

The city has also had a Small Rental Rehabilitation Program for owners of small rental buildings west of 18th Street, but its program page carries a note that the city is not offering it. Do not count on that money when pricing a repair-heavy house.

What local history helps explain Quincy's older housing?

Quincy was founded by John Wood and took its name in 1825, when the settlement became the seat of Adams County and honored the newly elected president. It was incorporated as a city in 1840 and grew into the second-largest city in Illinois, passing Peoria in 1870. Riverboats and rail service made it a transportation center in the 1800s.

The 2020 census counted 39,463 people, below the high of 45,288 recorded in 1970. Housing built for a larger population now serves a smaller one, with 10.4 percent of the 19,028 housing units vacant in 2020 and a rental vacancy rate of 11.6 percent. Sellers should expect buyers to compare their house with others on the market and to ask pointed questions about condition, so a clear repair history and recent utility bills help.

How does a Quincy sale get recorded in Adams County?

Adams County files deeds through its Clerk and Recorder office at 507 Vermont Street in Quincy. According to the office, a deed or trust document has to arrive with an Illinois Department of Revenue Real Estate Transfer Declaration or a Statement of Exemption.

The posted fees start at $80.00 for land records under 50 pages on standard paper, rise to $92.00 for documents that miss the 55 ILCS 5/3-5018 format standards, and add $80.00 per extra book and page reference. The table says it includes the Rental Housing Support Fee increase that began July 1, 2023. Fees move over time, so confirm the amount with the office before closing.

State law adds a duty on the seller's side: a completed residential disclosure report goes to the buyer ahead of a signed contract (765 ILCS 77/20). The following section limits that duty to material defects the seller actually knows about, with no obligation to investigate. Hold on to invoices for any work done on the house.

Frequently asked questions

Does an older brick house take longer to sell in Quincy?

Often, because buyers want evidence that the wiring, plumbing and foundation are sound. A listing can reach people who prize historic detail, and a direct sale suits an owner who wants to skip the repairs.

What are the recording fees for a Quincy deed?

Adams County posts $80.00 as the minimum for land records under 50 pages that meet the paper standards, and $92.00 for those that do not. Call the office to confirm the schedule before closing.

Does Quincy require a rental registration for landlords selling a house?

The city's housing complaint process is tenant-driven, and an inspector visits after a complaint. Ask the Office of Inspection at City Hall whether any registration applies to your property before you list a rental.

Who inspects Quincy houses for code problems?

The city's Office of Inspection, at 730 Maine Street, reviews minimum housing complaints and building permits. A tenant files the complaint form and an inspector schedules a visit.

How big is Quincy?

Census Bureau estimates for 2025 give 38,918 people, down from 39,463 in the 2020 count. Quincy is the Adams County seat, on the Mississippi River.

Where is Park Ridge and how did it develop?

Park Ridge is a city in Cook County about 15 miles north of downtown Chicago, close to O'Hare International Airport. It covers roughly 7 square miles and touches three Chicago community areas on the Far Northwest Side: Edison Park, Norwood Park and O'Hare. The Des Plaines River separates it from Des Plaines to the west.

The ground itself shaped the early town. Clay deposits fed a brickworks that George Penny established in 1854, and locals called the settlement Brickton, after an earlier name of Pennyville. The city was incorporated in 1873. Population then jumped from 10,417 in 1930 to 32,659 in 1960 and peaked at 42,614 in 1970 before settling near 39,656 in the 2020 census. Much of the housing stock traces to that mid-century boom, so a buyer's inspector will look closely at the age of the wiring, plumbing, roof and foundation.

  • The city belongs to the Oakton Community College district.

The city's 2020 financial report lists Advocate Lutheran General Hospital as its largest employer, with 3,693 employees, followed by the high school district, the Park District and District 64.

Do you need a permit for repairs on a Park Ridge house?

A permit is required for most construction. The city lists new buildings, additions, garages, driveways, HVAC, electrical and plumbing work, pools, fences, patios, decks, sheds and siding. It does not require one for window replacement unless the opening is enlarged, or for residential roof replacement, although roofing contractors must be licensed with the city. Routine maintenance that leaves existing systems and structural walls alone also needs none.

Timing matters if you plan fixes before a sale:

  • Reviews usually take up to two weeks, and the standard time is two weeks for every permit during the May to September busy season.
  • Residential permits stay valid for one year, and a renewal after expiration costs 50 percent of the original permit fee.
  • Applications go through the Civic Access online portal, and inspections are booked by morning or afternoon block with a one to two business day lead time.

Questions go to the Community Preservation and Development department at 847-318-5291. A separate tree removal permit is required for trees larger than 10 inches in diameter, so check before clearing a lot.

What does the Park Ridge transfer tax cost and who files it?

The city charges its own real estate transfer tax, and the seller pays it. The city's FAQ prints the rate as $2.00 per $1,000 of value or fraction thereof. Cook County Clerk's municipal list shows the same rate for Park Ridge, notes that it includes foreclosures, and lists the exempt-transfer fee as $25.00.

To get the transfer tax certificate, send the Finance Department:

  • The PTAX-203 or MyDec form.
  • A photo of the water meter for the final reading.
  • The closing date.
  • A contact name, phone number and email address.

Documents go to transferstamp@parkridge.us or to the Finance Department at 505 Butler Place; questions go to 847-318-5222, option 4. The certificate is issued once the tax and any other amounts owed to the city, including the final water bill, are paid, and the certificate is attached to the deed at recording. Cook County adds its own state rate of 50 cents per $500 and county rate of 25 cents per $500.

How do water bills and closing dates work in Park Ridge?

The city bills water every other month, with bills issued on the last day of the month and due by the 20th. Email the meter photo no earlier than five days before closing, with the service address and closing date. Water is not shut off during a transfer, and the account moves automatically into the buyer's name.

Final payment is accepted as cash, credit or debit card, certified check, money order or attorney's check. Homeowners are responsible for repairs to the water service pipe between the buffalo box and the house, which is worth knowing if a buyer's inspection turns up a leak. The city also says property assessment is a Cook County function, so appeals and exemptions go to the county assessor, not City Hall.

Are there landmark or preservation rules to know about?

Park Ridge has a Historic Preservation Commission. According to the city's FAQ, a house becomes a local landmark only with the owner's consent, and a designation can be rescinded, though the Commission encourages owners to look at alternatives first. If your house is already landmarked, tell buyers early.

What are your options for selling quickly in Park Ridge?

With a median owner-occupied value of $551,200 and owners who tend to stay put, a standard listing is the usual route when a house is in good shape. A cash buyer is more useful when the house needs work that would take months to finish, when a probate or move deadline is close, or when you want to avoid showings.

Before you accept any offer, line up the transfer tax certificate steps above, because closing cannot be completed without the city's certificate and the final water reading. Ask your closing attorney or title company to start those steps as soon as the contract is signed.

Frequently asked questions

How much is the Park Ridge transfer tax?

The city's FAQ prints it as $2.00 per $1,000 of value or fraction thereof, paid by the seller. Cook County's clerk list matches that rate. The state adds 50 cents per $500 and the county adds 25 cents per $500.

Do I need to pay my final water bill before closing in Park Ridge?

Yes. The transfer tax certificate is issued after the tax and any other amounts owed to the city, including the final water bill, are paid. Email a photo of the meter to the Finance Department no earlier than five days before closing.

Can I replace my roof or windows in Park Ridge without a permit?

Usually yes. The city says residential roof replacement and window replacement do not need a permit, unless the window opening is enlarged. Roofing contractors must be licensed with the city, and other projects such as decks, fences and electrical work still require permits.

Who handles Park Ridge property tax appeals?

Cook County does. The city says assessment is a county function and refers owners to the Cook County Assessor's office, which handles appeals, exemptions and the required forms.

Does the water account transfer when a Park Ridge house sells?

Yes. The city places the account in the buyer's name automatically, does not shut off service during the transfer, and bills every other month afterward. Sellers settle the final reading through the transfer tax process.

Does Wheeling, Illinois have a transfer tax on home sales?

No. The Village of Wheeling states that it has no real estate transfer tax of its own. It does, however, require every seller to obtain a Real Estate Transfer Stamp on the original deed, and the stamp carries no fee. The catch is that the stamp is only issued after the final water, sewer and garbage charges, plus any outstanding tickets and penalties, are paid in full.

The state tax still applies. Under 35 ILCS 200/31-10, Illinois taxes the privilege of transferring title at 50 cents per $500 of value stated in the declaration, and the county where the parcel sits can add its own.

How does the Wheeling transfer stamp process work?

The rule took effect August 24, 2015 and sits in Section 15.10 of the Wheeling Municipal Code. The seller presents the original deed at the Finance Department counter in Village Hall, or mails it in, and the stamp is placed on that deed. The village asks for 10 business days of notice before closing so it can schedule a final meter reading and prepare the stamp.

Sellers should be ready to give the village a forwarding address and the final reading date. Buyers then supply new resident registration information, and if registration is incomplete the village warns that water service may be discontinued.

Why does condominium ownership matter for Wheeling sellers?

Condo owners pay for water, sewer and garbage through monthly assessments, but the village still treats them as owners who need a stamp. A condo seller therefore has two sets of paperwork: the association's payoff and resale documents, and the village's stamp. Ask the management company early for its timeline, because the association's letter and the village's 10 business day notice both feed the closing date.

  • Order the association paperwork as soon as a contract exists.
  • Submit the village's transfer stamp application at the same time.
  • Keep a copy of the original deed, since the village stamps the original.

What does the Census count for Wheeling housing?

Owners occupy 62.7% of Wheeling homes for 2020 to 2024, which leaves a large share of rentals. Typical owner-occupied value is $266,200, rent is $1,663 and household income is $85,205 across 15,171 households, per the Census Bureau. The July 2025 estimate is 38,391 residents, 2.0% below the 2020 base.

  • Foreign-born residents make up 45.4% of the population.
  • A language other than English is spoken at home by 61.8% of residents age 5 and over.
  • Monthly owner costs are $1,909 with a mortgage and $892 without.
  • The village covers 8.67 square miles of land, about 4,513 residents per square mile in 2020.

Because a large share of homes are rented, investors and landlords are an active part of the buyer pool here, and a seller with tenants in place should expect questions about lease terms.

How are Wheeling property taxes assessed and billed?

Most of Wheeling lies in Cook County, in Wheeling Township, with a smaller part in Lake County. Cook County reassesses one-third of the county each year, and the north suburbs, Wheeling Township included, were reassessed in 2025. Initial values came out August 18, 2025 and appeals had to be filed by September 30, 2025. Wheeling Township takes in all or part of Wheeling, Arlington Heights, Des Plaines, Glenview, Mount Prospect, Northbrook, Palatine, Prospect Heights, Rolling Meadows and Buffalo Grove, so neighbors across a municipal line share the same assessment cycle. Owners in the Lake County portion should ask the Lake County treasurer and assessor for their schedule.

The Assessor's release put the township's median 2024 single-family sale price at $457,000 against a median market value estimate of $429,000. The Cook County Assessor also said that second-installment bills reflecting the reassessment would be issued September 1, 2026, with an October 1 due date. Your closing agent prorates the unpaid tax, so request a copy of the most recent bill before you list.

What is Wheeling like for a house sale?

Wheeling is a village in Cook and Lake counties about 23 miles northwest of downtown Chicago, in Wheeling and Vernon townships. Settlers arrived in the 1830s, and residents voted to incorporate on June 18, 1894, by 43 to 3. The first Village Hall from that year is now the Wheeling Historical Museum in Chamber Park. Since 1970 Wheeling has run a council-manager government as a home-rule village.

Metra's North Central Service stops in Wheeling on weekdays only, and Pace buses connect to Des Plaines and Buffalo Grove. Chicago Executive Airport, shared with Prospect Heights, is the fourth busiest airport in the state. Public schools are run by Wheeling Community Consolidated School District 21 and Township High School District 214, which operates Wheeling High School. The Wheeling Park District manages parks including Chamber Park, Heritage Park and Mark Twain Park, and Indian Trails Public Library District serves most residents.

What else shapes the Wheeling market?

Wheeling's winters are usually very cold and snowy and summers are hot and humid, so buyers look closely at roofs, gutters and furnaces when they walk a house. Precipitation is spread through the year, which keeps drainage and basement moisture on most inspection lists.

The village's economy employed 21,671 people at the 2020 Census, and the community includes the Korean Cultural Center of Chicago and Camp Ramah. The Wheeling International Festival at the Heritage Park Performance Pavilion celebrates that mix each summer. Buyers from many backgrounds shop here, so clear photos and a straightforward disclosure report help any listing, whether it is sold to a family or to a cash purchaser.

How should a Wheeling seller get ready for a quick sale?

Start with the village paperwork, because it has the longest lead time. Then gather the Illinois disclosure report required for one to four unit homes before a contract is signed under 765 ILCS 77/20, and a recent tax bill. An investor who pays cash and takes the house as-is still needs the stamp, the final water reading and the paid utility balance, so those steps do not shorten with a faster closing.

  • Call Water Billing at (847) 459-2607 about 10 business days before the closing date.
  • Pay any outstanding tickets and penalties with the village.
  • Have the original deed available, since a copy will not be stamped.
  • Have the closing agent confirm the county's recording charges.

Does the Village of Wheeling charge a transfer tax?

No. The village says it has no real estate transfer tax, but it requires a transfer stamp on the original deed. The stamp has no fee, and all water, sewer, garbage charges, tickets and penalties must be paid first.

How much notice does Wheeling need before closing?

The village asks for 10 business days of notice. Its FAQ says the electronic final water reading happens 2 business days before closing, so the longer notice gives staff time to prepare the stamp.

Do condo owners in Wheeling need a transfer stamp?

Yes. The requirement applies to condominium owners even though they pay water, sewer and garbage indirectly through monthly assessments. It also covers refinances, quit claim deeds and transfers into a trust.

Which agency assesses a Wheeling house for tax?

The Cook County Assessor handles most of Wheeling, since the village lies mainly in Cook County. Wheeling Township was reassessed in 2025. Owners in the Lake County portion deal with Lake County offices instead.

The Census Bureau reports $266,200 for owner-occupied homes for 2020 to 2024. The July 2025 population estimate is 38,391, and median gross rent is $1,663.

What are a Streamwood owner's options for selling?

Three doors are open to a Streamwood seller: a broker's listing, a sale you manage alone, or a buyer who pays cash and takes the house untouched. Repairs, renters and the date you need funds usually settle the question.

  • Broker's listing: rewards a house in good order, provided you can sit through inspections and a lender's schedule.
  • Going alone: saves the commission and hands you the pricing, advertising and contract review.
  • Cash, untouched: no buyer repair demands, which suits a worn, inherited or tenant-occupied house.

Rented houses carry a Streamwood-specific wrinkle. The village licenses every rental property, single-family homes and condominium units included, so a landlord who sells should ask what happens to the license at transfer.

Where is Streamwood, and how has the population changed?

Streamwood is a Cook County village in the northwest suburbs of the Chicago area. It belongs to the Tri Village area with Bartlett and Hanover Park, and it was first incorporated on February 9, 1957. The village covers about 7.83 square miles.

The curve was steep, then flat. The census counted 4,821 residents in 1960, 18,176 in 1970, 30,987 in 1990 and 39,858 in 2010. The 2020 count came to 39,577, and the Bureau's mid-2025 estimate of 38,277 is 3.3 percent under the 2020 base.

Climate matters for condition. NOAA's 1991 to 2020 normals list a mean January high of 32.3 degrees, a mean July high of 86.9 degrees, 38.02 inches of precipitation and 34 inches of snowfall in a year. Expect inspectors to focus on roofs, gutters and basements.

Which schools, libraries and trains serve Streamwood?

Elgin Area School District U-46, the state's second largest, serves most of the village. A small area east of Barrington Road is served by District 54 for kindergarten through junior high and Township District 211 for high school, and the whole village falls in Elgin Community College District 509.

  • Libraries: the Poplar Creek Library District serves most residents; people east of Barrington Road use the Schaumburg Township District Library, and people west of Route 59 use Gail Borden Public Library in Elgin.
  • Parks: the Streamwood Park District covers most of the village, and the Schaumburg Park District covers the east edge.
  • Rail: the nearest Metra station is in Bartlett, on the Milwaukee District West Line to Chicago Union Station.
  • Bus: Pace Route 554 runs from Streamwood to Schaumburg.

Because boundaries split near Barrington Road and Route 59, tell buyers which district, library and park district apply to your address.

What does the Village of Streamwood require at a sale?

Streamwood has its own real estate transfer stamp, issued by the Finance Department. Its rate is printed as $3.00 per $1,000 of value for each transfer, and three items must reach the village before a stamp is issued.

  • A copy of the deed.
  • A copy of the state's Illinois Real Estate Transfer Declaration.
  • Payment of all outstanding water and sewer charges, including any assessments or penalties owed to the village.

A transfer that changes the deed with no money exchanged needs an exempt stamp instead, priced at $10, and that application requires a signed, notarized deed. Send completed forms to finance@streamwood.org, or call the Finance Department at (630) 736-3810. The closing attorney or title company normally files these, yet the water and sewer clearance is one the seller should expect.

The village's licensing rule for rentals is separate. A single-family or condo rental license costs $155 per building per year, includes the required inspection, and expires December 31. Landlords must finish a free online Crime Free Housing seminar of about an hour before applying.

What does Streamwood's rental program mean for a landlord who is selling?

A landlord should treat the license as part of the house's paperwork, because the village ties renting to inspection and training. Each single-family or condominium rental needs an interior and exterior inspection before the one-year license is issued, and the license must be renewed and paid for every year.

  • The tenant, or the landlord acting for the tenant, signs an inspection consent form before the village schedules the visit.
  • Landlords must show a certificate from the Crime Free Housing seminar, and the village will accept one issued within the last five years by a community in Cook, DuPage, Kane, McHenry or Will County.
  • A sample Crime Free addendum for leases is posted on the village page.

A buyer who plans to keep the tenants should ask for the license record and the latest inspection result. A buyer who wants the house empty will want to know the lease end date before closing. A cash buyer can take a rented house, but the lease still has to be read first.

Who assesses and bills Streamwood property taxes?

The village does not provide property tax services. Assessment is handled by Hanover Township through the Cook County Assessor, and the Cook County Treasurer collects the tax. Current bills are a question for the Treasurer at (312) 443-5100, and past years or delinquent taxes go to the Cook County Clerk at (312) 603-5645.

Cook County reassesses each property once every three years, on a township schedule. The 2026 cycle covered the south and west suburbs, while north suburban townships such as Hanover are reassessed only where something about a property has changed. The Assessor's 2026 calendar still lists Hanover with notices dated October 22, 2026 and a last file date of December 7, 2026 for appeals to the Assessor.

  • Start by looking up your parcel number and notice on the Assessor's website.
  • Find out from the Assessor which exemptions are attached to your parcel.
  • Have your closing attorney explain how the year's bill is divided with the buyer.

What does Cook County require on a Streamwood deed?

Deeds for Streamwood property are recorded by the Cook County Clerk. Its checklist for deeds includes the common address, the Property Index Number, a legal description, mail-to and prepared-by names, grantor and grantee details and a completed MyDec form for the state and county stamps. It also lists the municipality's real estate transfer tax, which is where the Streamwood stamp comes in.

For an exempt transfer, the deed needs exemption language citing 35 ILCS 200/31-45 and Cook County Ordinance 93-O-27, or a grantor and grantee affidavit. Section 31-15 of the Property Tax Code sets the state rate at 50 cents per $500 of value, and your title company can confirm the county amount.

Frequently asked questions

Does Streamwood charge its own transfer tax?

Yes. The village's Finance Department states a rate of $3.00 per $1,000 of value, and it issues the stamp after receiving the deed, the state transfer declaration and proof that water and sewer charges are paid.

Should a landlord keep the Streamwood rental license while selling?

Streamwood requires a license for every rental, at $155 per building per year with an inspection. Keep it in force while the house is rented, and ask your attorney how a tenant's lease passes to the buyer.

Which office assesses a Streamwood home?

Hanover Township does the local assessing through the Cook County Assessor, and the Cook County Treasurer collects the tax. The village itself does not handle assessments or bills.

What happens to water and sewer balances at closing?

Pay them first. The village will not issue the transfer stamp until all outstanding charges, assessments and penalties are cleared.

How many people live in Streamwood?

The Census Bureau estimated 38,277 residents on July 1, 2025, down from 39,577 counted in April 2020.

Where is Carpentersville and what is the village like?

Carpentersville is a village in northern Kane County, Illinois, on the Fox River and part of the Chicago metropolitan area. The 2020 census counted 37,983 residents in 8.09 square miles, of which 7.88 are land.

The village runs under a council-manager form of government: an elected president and six trustees appoint a professional manager who runs daily operations. For a seller, the practical point is that Carpentersville handles its own permits, water billing and rental licensing, so most of the paperwork stays at Village Hall rather than moving to a county office.

  • County: Kane, with deeds recorded by the Kane County Recorder in Geneva
  • Green space: Carpenter Park, the Carpentersville Dam area and Raceway Woods Forest Preserve
  • Housing units in 2020: 11,777, of which 2.9 percent were vacant

How did the Fox River settlement become Carpentersville?

In 1837 the Carpenter brothers were heading for the Rock River when spring floods stopped their oxcart journey on the east bank of the Fox River. They stayed and called the place Carpenters' Grove. Julius Angelo Carpenter built the first store, bridge and factory, and he later served two terms in the Illinois House.

The Illinois Iron and Bolt foundry anchored early industry, and an electric interurban line reached the foundry in 1896. For about a hundred years the town grew slowly. Until the 1950s it was a street grid along the river centered on Main Street, which was the only highway bridge across the Fox between Algonquin and Dundee.

Then the suburbs arrived. The population went from 1,523 in 1950 to 17,424 in 1960, the fastest jump in the village's history. Older homes near the river and the post-1950 subdivisions are very different housing, and a seller should know which type they own when pricing.

How has the population changed since 1950?

The census counts show one great leap in the 1950s, a flat stretch through the 1980s and steady growth into the 2000s. Growth since 2010 has been small, up 0.8 percent between 2010 and 2020.

The 2020 census recorded a homeowner vacancy rate of 0.9 percent and a rental vacancy rate of 5.0 percent. A homeowner vacancy rate that low suggests few for-sale houses sit empty, which is generally favorable to a seller who prices the house sensibly.

The village's income section lists a median household income of $73,105 and a median family income of $79,102, with a per capita income of $26,770. Those figures help frame what a buyer who needs a mortgage can afford, and they are one reason some owners prefer a cash buyer who does not depend on lender approval.

What landmarks and shopping areas shape the village?

The Meadowdale Shopping Center opened in May 1957 and had grown to as many as 53 stores a year later. A November 1963 fire destroyed 25 stores and an ice rink, and the mall reopened in November 1964 without the rink. A competing mall opened 2.5 miles west in 1980, and Meadowdale shrank through the 1980s. Part of it was demolished in 1989, and a Walmart opened on the east end in 2016.

From 1958 to 1969 the Meadowdale International Raceway, a 3.27 mile track west of Illinois Route 31, ran here. The site is now a township park and county forest preserve. Since the 1990s, growth has moved west along Randall Road, where newer subdivisions and shopping centers sit.

The Dundee Township Historic District appears among the village's related places. If your house is in the older river-side grid, ask Village Hall whether any local review applies before you plan exterior changes.

How do people get around Carpentersville?

Illinois Route 31 runs past the older river-side grid, and Randall Road is the corridor where the newer subdivisions and shopping centers were built. Pace buses connect the village to Crystal Lake, Elgin and other destinations. A Chicago and North Western line between Elgin and Crystal Lake served Carpentersville from 1904 to 1932.

A buyer comparing Carpentersville with its neighbors will look at bus access and drive times, so mention both in a listing.

Does Carpentersville charge a transfer stamp on a sale?

No. The village's transfer stamp page says Carpentersville does not have a transfer stamp requirement for real estate transactions. This puts it among the simpler closings for a seller in the northwest suburbs.

The seller still has one task. Call the Water Billing Department at 847-551-3476 to schedule a final reading on the water meter. The new owner then opens service in person at Village Hall with a settlement statement or deed, a completed water application and picture identification.

State tax still applies. Illinois taxes the transfer of title at 50 cents per $500 of value or fraction thereof under 35 ILCS 200/31-10, based on the declaration filed for the sale.

What permits and inspections come up when selling in Carpentersville?

The Community Development Department issues permits for construction, and the village's permit page says even a new water heater or a shed needs some kind of permit or approval. It also links a list of work that does and does not need one.

  • Past work: if the previous owner added a deck, finished a basement or replaced a furnace, confirm the permit was closed
  • Open work: a buyer who takes the house as-is takes the open permit with it
  • Rental houses: the village runs a rental licensing program with an initial inspection and an annual license

The village's rental licensing checklist, last revised in 2011, describes a temporary certificate after an application, then an inspection, then a follow-up inspection if violations are found, and a Crime Free Housing seminar the owner must attend. Ask Community Development for the current version before you rely on it. If you plan to sell a tenant-occupied house, note that the owner is responsible for getting tenant consent for inspection visits.

Where is the deed recorded for a Carpentersville sale?

The Kane County Recorder in Geneva keeps the land records for the village. The recorder's website provides a records search, and the office describes services including recording, copying, scanning and a tract department.

The recorder has also announced a free Property Watch service aimed at deed fraud, which the office says targets homeowners at risk of foreclosure. An owner of a vacant or inherited house may want to look at it.

How do a regular listing and a cash sale compare in Carpentersville?

A listing makes sense when the house is move-in ready and you can wait out showings and a buyer's financing. A cash sale as-is makes sense when repairs, a tenant, an inherited estate or a deadline would make a listing slow or costly.

In either case the village side is light: no municipal stamp, a final water reading and the permit review above. That leaves the seller's time and repair costs as the real variables, so compare the net result of each route rather than the headline price.

Do I need a village transfer stamp to sell in Carpentersville?

No. The village states it has no transfer stamp requirement for real estate sales. You should still schedule a final water meter reading by calling Water Billing at 847-551-3476.

What does the buyer need to start water service?

The new owner brings a settlement statement or deed to Village Hall in person, fills out the water application and shows picture identification.

Is a permit needed for a water heater or shed in Carpentersville?

Yes, in general. The village's building page says work from a new water heater or shed up to a full building requires some type of permit or approval. Check the village's list of work that does and does not need a permit before you start.

Which county records the deed?

Kane County. The Kane County Recorder in Geneva records deeds and offers an online records search.

How much did Carpentersville grow in the last census decade?

Slightly. The population rose from 37,691 in 2010 to 37,983 in 2020, a gain of 0.8 percent.

What should I know before selling a house in Hanover Park?

The biggest local step is the Village transfer stamp, which every Hanover Park seller has to buy before closing. The second is working out which county records your deed, since the village straddles Cook and DuPage counties. Everything else follows the usual path of listing, selling on your own, or accepting an as-is cash offer.

  • Listing with an agent: the most exposure, with showings and buyer repair requests.
  • Selling on your own: you manage the marketing and the paperwork, often with an attorney reviewing the contract.
  • As-is cash purchase: fewer contingencies and a closing date you can usually choose, with the buyer accepting the house's condition.

Start the stamp request early, because the Village needs notice and every balance owed to it has to be settled first.

How does the Hanover Park transfer stamp work?

All residents selling a home in Hanover Park must buy a Transfer Tax Stamp from the Village before the closing. The homeowner, realtor or lawyer calls the Finance Department at 630-823-5790 at least three business days before closing, and walk-in requests are not honored.

  • Have the MyDec or PTAX-203 form ready.
  • Complete the Village of Hanover Park Real Estate Transfer Tax Declaration form.
  • Include the deed, and email the set to financedepartment@hpil.org if you prefer.
  • Pay everything owed to the Village first: tickets, invoices, liens, judgments and the final water bill.

A quitclaim deed also needs a stamp. In that case the Village asks for a copy of the signed, notarized deed plus its own declaration form. Ask Finance for the current stamp rate, since the amount depends on the value of the sale.

How do I close the water account when I sell in Hanover Park?

Water bills go out on the first of each month and are due by the 21st, whatever day of the week that falls on. A payment that is not received by then draws a 10 percent penalty, and a termination notice is mailed on the 22nd.

Because an unpaid final water bill blocks the transfer stamp, arrange the closing read with Water Billing early. You can email waterbilling@hpil.org with your property address in the subject line, and a representative replies with forms or instructions, so there is no need for a trip to Village Hall. Log in to your water account on the Village website to check the balance before you call.
