Which schools, roads and neighborhoods shape a sale in Elk Grove Village?

Interstate 290 splits the school boundaries. East of I-290, students attend Elk Grove High School in Illinois High School District 214 and Community Consolidated School District 59. West of I-290, students go to James B. Conant High School in Township High School District 211 and Mead Junior High in District 54. Name the right district in your listing, since buyers with children search by it.

The village is reached by I-90, I-290, I-355, Route 53 and IL-390, and the I-490 Western O'Hare Bypass is expected to serve it once complete. Pace Route 223 links to the Rosemont station. Early boundaries ran along Higgins Road, Arlington Heights Road, Landmeier Road and Wildwood Road, and the village doubled in size during the 1960s. The village sits directly beside O'Hare International Airport, and its location along the Golden Corridor is a selling point for commuters.

Deeds are recorded by the Cook County Clerk or the DuPage County Recorder. Cook lists state transfer tax at .50 per $500, county tax at .25 per $500 and a $107 deed recording fee under its April 2024 schedule. DuPage's Recorder keeps records back to 1839 and can be reached at 630-407-5400.

Frequently asked questions

How much is the transfer tax in Elk Grove Village?

The village rate is $3 per $1,000 of value, or fraction thereof, with the primary liability on the seller. State and county transfer taxes are separate charges set by the recording county. Ask your title company to list each one on the settlement statement.

Can I pay for an Elk Grove Village transfer stamp with a credit card?

No. Cash, a cashier's check, a money order, or an attorney's or title company's check to the village will work. It does not accept credit cards or personal or company checks.

How early must I schedule the final water reading?

The village's stamp page says at least two days before the closing date. Book the reading as soon as your closing date is set, and confirm the timing with the Finance Department.

Do I need an underground fuel tank disclosure?

Yes, if the house is north of Elk Grove Boulevard. The village requires sellers there to give buyers a disclosure form about possible underground fuel heating storage tanks. Fire Department staff answer questions about the tanks.

Which county records my Elk Grove Village deed?

Either Cook County or DuPage County, depending on where your parcel sits. Look at the tax bill for the county, and the title company files the deed there.

Where is Pekin and what is its housing like?

Pekin is the county seat of Tazewell County, on the Illinois River in central Illinois. It is the largest city in the county and the second most populous in the Peoria metropolitan area. A small part of the city lies in Peoria County, reached by a bridge over the river, which means some Pekin addresses are recorded and taxed in a different county than most of the city.

The Census Bureau counted 31,731 residents in 2020, down from 34,094 in 2010, and estimated 31,277 for July 2025. Housing here costs far less than in the Chicago suburbs: the median owner-occupied value in Palatine, for comparison, is $355,600. The table shows what the 2020 to 2024 figures look like for owners and renters.

What is Pekin's history and why does it matter to a seller?

A settler from Ohio built a log cabin on a ridge above the river in 1824, and a surveyor laid out the town site in 1827. One account says the name Pekin came from a nineteenth-century habit of naming towns after places thought to lie on the opposite side of the globe. The first post office opened in 1832.

Coal mining left a physical mark. At least four mines: the Pekin, Regal, Tazewell and Ubben mines. One of them, run by the Pekin Coal Mining Company until 1952, lay under what later became Broadmoor Junior High, Willow Elementary and Schramm School. The Regal mine crossed Broadway in the eastern part of town, below what is now Parkway Golf Course and Coal Miner's Park. Coal mining in Pekin had ended by 1951.

If a buyer asks whether your lot sits over old workings, the title company or the county recorder's records are the place to start. Do not guess at the answer in a listing.

Which employers and schools shape the Pekin market?

Pekin is home to the headquarters of Pekin Insurance and to the Federal Correctional Institution, Pekin, and it has its own hospital, Carle Health Peoria - Pekin Hospital. CityLink buses on Routes 17, 18 and 23 connect the city to downtown Peoria. The Census Bureau puts the average commute at 21.7 minutes.

Public schools depend on where the house sits:

  • Most of the city is in Pekin Public School District 108, which has six elementary schools, two intermediate schools, two junior highs and the Pekin Technical Education Center.
  • Parts of the Tazewell County side belong instead to North Pekin-Marquette Heights School District 102 or Rankin Community School District 98.
  • All of Pekin in Tazewell County feeds Pekin Community High School District 303.
  • The Peoria County portion is in Hollis Consolidated School District 328 and Limestone Community High School District 310.

Ask the district for the boundary of your address before a buyer does.

How do Pekin's weather and river location affect a house?

Pekin has a hot-summer continental climate. NOAA normals for 1991 to 2020 show about 37.4 inches of precipitation a year, spread through the seasons with late spring the wettest, January afternoons near 33 degrees and July afternoons near 86. Summers are humid, and winters can turn severely cold and snowy.

The river adds a flood question. The city takes part in the National Flood Insurance Program and says properties below the 1 percent annual chance flood level may be required by law to carry flood insurance. An owner who thinks the flood designation is wrong can ask FEMA for a Letter of Map Amendment, and lenders may still require insurance. Properties along the Illinois River are often subject to floodway rules. For a sale, find out your flood zone early, since it affects a buyer's mortgage and insurance.

What does Pekin require for permits and yard rules before a sale?

Pekin's Inspections Department says permits are required for electrical, plumbing, sewer, heating, ventilation and air conditioning work, and also for fences, sheds, new homes, additions, decks, signs and pools. A roofing permit applies to a complete tear-off or a second layer of shingles. Siding, windows, doors and interior remodeling need none unless the work changes structural walls, plumbing or electrical.

Other rules a buyer's agent may bring up:

  • A homeowner may do their own work but must still get a permit. The city defines a homeowner as the person who owns and lives at the residence.
  • Pools deeper than 24 inches need a permit and may sit only in the rear yard.
  • Chain link fences are not allowed in any front yard, and corner lots must keep sight lines clear.
  • Vehicles may not be parked in yards or the right of way, and must stand on a hard surface such as concrete or asphalt.

The Inspections Department takes questions at 309.478.5364. If you built a deck or finished a basement without a permit, ask whether it can be inspected before you list.

Which county records a Pekin deed, and who collects the taxes?

Most Pekin parcels are in Tazewell County, where the County Clerk and Recorder keeps real estate records. The office says everything in the Recorder's files is public record, that anyone may look through it free of charge, and that it supplies some forms at no cost. Ask the office for current recording fees and transfer stamp amounts before closing, since they change.

Parcels in the Peoria County portion go through Peoria County instead. That county's land records page says it participates in the state's MyDec system, which lets filers submit the PTAX-203 transfer declaration electronically before a deed is recorded. Check your tax bill or parcel number to see which county applies, and tell your closing attorney if the house straddles the line.

How do homeowners sell quickly in Pekin?

The median value of owner-occupied homes in Pekin is $120,700, so repair costs can take a large share of the price. A new roof or furnace is a bigger decision when the house is worth a fraction of what homes cost in Chicago's suburbs. For that reason many sellers weigh a cash purchase against listing and fixing the house first.

  • Pull any permits or inspection records so a buyer can see what was done.
  • Confirm your flood zone and your school district boundary.
  • Ask the title company which county records your parcel and whether any liens or unpaid taxes are on file.
  • Compare offers by what you keep after repairs, fees and carrying costs, not by headline price.

Frequently asked questions

Which county is Pekin in?

Pekin is the county seat of Tazewell County. A small part of the city extends into Peoria County, so parcels there are recorded and taxed through Peoria County. Check your parcel number to see which applies.

Do I need a permit to replace a roof in Pekin?

Yes, for a complete tear-off and replacement, or for adding a second layer of shingles. The city's Inspections Department says siding, window and door replacement do not need a permit unless structural, plumbing or electrical changes are involved.

Does Pekin have flood rules that affect a sale?

Yes. The city takes part in the National Flood Insurance Program, and properties below the 1 percent annual chance flood level may be required by law to carry flood insurance. New construction in a flood hazard area must set the lowest floor two feet above base flood elevation.

Can I do my own repairs on my Pekin house?

Yes, if you own and live in it, but you still need the permit. The city defines a homeowner as the person who owns and lives at the residence, and nobody may work on someone else's property unless licensed or registered with the Inspections Department.

Where do I get recording information for a Pekin sale?

Ask the Tazewell County Clerk and Recorder, whose office keeps real estate records open to the public at no charge and supplies some forms for free. For the Peoria County portion of the city, use the Peoria County land records office, which accepts the MyDec transfer declaration.

How did Algonquin grow, and where does it sit?

Algonquin is a Fox River suburb about 40 miles northwest of the Chicago Loop, and a sale there means working with two counties because the village straddles the McHenry and Kane line. Roughly 78 percent of the village area is in McHenry County and the rest is in Kane County, so the county printed on your tax bill decides who records the deed and who collects the tax.

The place grew slowly for a long time. The name became official on December 23, 1847, a railroad arrived in 1855, and the village was formed on February 25, 1890. Summer homes along the river made it a weekend getaway for Chicago families for much of the twentieth century. The population then climbed from 5,684 in 1980 to 11,663 in 1990 and 23,276 in 2000, which means most of the housing is relatively young. The 2020 count was 29,700, and Census estimators reached 30,824 for July 1, 2025.

  • Home value among owners, 2020 to 2024 survey: $351,000

Which parts of Algonquin shape what a buyer is willing to pay?

Location inside the village matters because Algonquin has distinct districts with different traffic and different housing. Old Town sits along Main Street (Illinois Route 31) near the original village hall at 2 South Main Street, and exterior changes to any building in its historic district need a Certificate of Appropriateness from the village.

The Randall Road corridor on the western side is the retail spine. Algonquin Commons, an outdoor mall of about 80 stores, opened in 2004, and the Algonquin Corporate Campus was planned across more than 1,000 acres between Randall Road and Square Barn Road. The manufacturing belt runs along Algonquin Road between Pyott Road and Route 31, west of Old Town, and it houses tool, die, mold and plastics shops.

Subdivision names that show up in school boundary descriptions include Willoughby Farms, Brittany Hills, Providence Point and Shenandoah. A buyer comparing a house near the industrial belt with one near the river will weigh noise and truck traffic differently, so an honest description in the listing or cash offer discussion saves time later.

Which school districts serve Algonquin houses?

Two districts split the village, and the boundary often decides which houses draw the most interest from families. Community Unit School District 300 covers the area generally along and east of Randall Road. Consolidated School District 158, headquartered in Algonquin, serves the far western side.

  • District 300 elementary schools serving the village include Neubert, Eastview and Algonquin Lakes, plus Lincoln Prairie and Lake in the Hills Elementary in neighboring towns.
  • Westfield Community School serves the Willoughby Farms area and feeds Jacobs High School. Algonquin Middle School serves Eastview and Algonquin Lakes and feeds mostly into Dundee-Crown High School.
  • District 158 runs Mackeben Elementary, Marion Conley Elementary and Bernice Heinemann Middle School on the Square Barn Road campus, with Huntley High School for high school.
  • St. Margaret Mary Catholic School and Foundations Montessori School are the private options.

McHenry County College generally serves residents in the District 158 boundaries, while Elgin Community College serves residents in District 300.

Do I need a village permit before repairing or selling an Algonquin house?

Algonquin requires a building permit before anyone erects, enlarges, alters, repairs, moves, improves, removes, converts or demolishes a building or structure. Small cosmetic jobs are listed as exceptions. The Community Development Department says permit review can take up to five weeks, so repairs you want done before listing should start early.

Anyone moving into a newly built home needs a certificate of occupancy before move-in. The village adopted the 2018 International Residential Code and the 2018 International Property Maintenance Code, among others. Questions go to Community Development at (847) 658-2700, option 3, or permits@algonquin.org. If a prior owner finished a basement or deck, ask that office whether the permit was closed before you list.

How do roads, fire districts and transit affect an Algonquin address?

The road network is the first thing out-of-town buyers check. Randall Road is the multi-lane north and south arterial and runs six lanes for the stretch between Harnish Drive and Corporate Parkway. Illinois Route 31 is the two-lane Main Street through downtown, and the intersection with Algonquin Road backs up at peak times. Illinois Route 25 runs along the eastern edge and ends at Route 62. Pace Route 550 runs along Randall Road between Crystal Lake and Elgin.

Fire and rescue come from one of three districts depending on the address: the Algonquin-Lake in the Hills Fire Protection District, the Huntley Fire Protection District or the Carpentersville Countryside Fire Protection District. The tax bill lists the districts that serve the parcel.

How is property tax billed for an Algonquin house in McHenry County?

McHenry County mails one bill and collects two installments. For the 2026 collection year, bills were mailed in early May and the installments were due June 9 and September 9. The county's payment office, 2100 N. Seminary Ave. in Woodstock, accepts payment at the window or drive-thru lanes between 7:30 and 5 on weekdays.

  • eCheck payments online carry no fee. Credit cards, debit cards and digital wallets add a 2.4% convenience fee.
  • Two 24-hour drop boxes, one walk-up and one drive-up, accept checks and money orders payable to the McHenry County Collector. No cash.
  • Write the parcel number (PIN) on any check, and ask the Post Office for a postmark when mailing close to a due date.
  • The VIP Taxpayer program sends email and text reminders and lets owners switch to e-billing.

Parcels in the Kane County part of the village are billed by Kane County, so look at the county name on the bill before you pay. At closing, ask the title officer to settle the current year's tax and any open installment between buyer and seller.

What does McHenry County want on a deed recorded for an Algonquin sale?

The County Recorder rejects documents that miss formatting or content rules, and a rejection can push back the date a buyer gets title. The Recorder's tips page asks for a white 20-pound page with a half-inch clean margin on every side and a clear 3 by 5 inch box at the top right.

  • A deed needs the grantor's signature, the grantee's address and the full McHenry County legal description.
  • A Plat Act affidavit must accompany the deed when the legal description is metes and bounds.
  • Either a completed exemption paragraph or the Illinois transfer declaration (PTAX-203 or MyDec) must accompany every deed. A MyDec filing must state "Closing Completed."
  • Every document needs "Prepared By" and "Mail To" lines with names and addresses.

The state transfer tax, set by Section 31-10 of the Property Tax Code, is 50 cents on each $500 block of value in the declaration. Ask the McHenry or Kane County Recorder, whichever holds your parcel, for any county stamp and for the Rental Housing Support Program surcharge details.

Which sale routes suit an Algonquin house?

Owners here usually weigh three paths: an agent listing, a private sale and a sale to a buyer who takes the house as it stands. A listing fits a house ready for move-in. Selling privately skips the agent but leaves the permit, deed and declaration work to the owner and the closing attorney. A sale as-is, to a buyer who accepts the house in its current state, fits a vacant, inherited or tenant-occupied property that needs work.

Whichever route you pick, an open permit or a missing certificate of occupancy will still come up at closing, so a call to Community Development early in the process keeps the schedule intact.

Frequently asked questions

Which county handles my Algonquin deed and tax bill?

It depends on the parcel. About 78 percent of the village is in McHenry County and the remainder is in Kane County. The county name on your tax bill tells you whom to ask.

Does Algonquin require a permit for a small roof repair?

Not for a repair of 200 square feet or less. Larger roof work, gutters and downspouts, and a garage service door do need permits.

When were McHenry County property tax installments due in 2026?

June 9 and September 9, 2026. Check the Treasurer's Office for the dates on the next bill, and pay online by eCheck to avoid the 2.4% fee charged on cards.

Does Algonquin Old Town have extra rules for exterior work?

Yes. A Certificate of Appropriateness is required for all exterior changes, additions and demolitions to buildings inside the historic district.

What must a MyDec filing say for McHenry County recording?

It must state "Closing Completed." The Recorder also needs the grantee's address, the legal description and a Plat Act affidavit if the description is metes and bounds.

Where is Highland Park, Illinois, and what shapes the housing here?

Highland Park is a city in Lake County on the North Shore of the Chicago area, about 25 miles north of downtown Chicago. Its 12.24 square miles of dry land are split between Moraine Township and West Deerfield Township, and mail goes through ZIP codes 60035, 60036 and 60037.

Lake Michigan defines the layout. A bluff about 100 feet high runs along 6 miles of shoreline, and wooded ravines cut up to a mile inland. Elevations range from 580 to 725 feet above sea level. A house beside a ravine or at the bluff edge sells differently from one on a flat street near a Metra stop, and buyers of every kind will ask about the lot as closely as the building.

In the 2020 count the city had 11,557 households spread over 12,405 housing units, and 6.8 percent of those units stood empty. A mid-2025 estimate puts the population at 30,767.

How did Highland Park grow, and why do so many older houses survive?

Two small lakefront settlements, St. John's and Port Clinton, came first. After the Chicago and Milwaukee Railroad built a depot, a plat was laid out in 1856. Highland Park was established as a city on March 11, 1869, and it annexed the village of Ravinia in 1899. St. Johns Avenue and Port Clinton Square still carry the old settlement names.

The housing stock reflects that early start. The Willits House is on the federal historic register, and the register also lists, designed by Frank Lloyd Wright, along with homes by John S. Van Bergen, Howard Van Doren Shaw, Robert E. Seyfarth and David Adler. Landscape architect Jens Jensen lived in the city and designed projects that are on the register as well.

Owners of an architect-designed house usually have the original plans, permits and drawings in a drawer somewhere. Gather them before you talk to any buyer, because documented history is the one thing that can set a house apart from its neighbors.

How common is homeownership in Highland Park, by the federal numbers?

The five-year survey figures cover 2020 to 2024. They give Highland Park 11,787 households, 83.8 percent of them owners, and a median home value of $607,300. Renters pay a median gross rent of $1,925. Roughly 87.5 percent of residents stayed at the same address through the previous year, and 24.3 percent are 65 or older.

Those numbers describe a city of long-time owners. Downsizing, estate settlement and relocation all produce sales with a firm deadline. Median household income is $168,094, and workers travel 27.5 minutes on average to get to a job.

  • Because most residents stay put, your listing may be the first on the street in years, so pull recent sale records before you pick a price.
  • Older construction makes for a long inspection report, and a buyer may ask to see original plans and permits.
  • Four Metra stations inside city limits make distance to the platform a selling point for downtown workers.

Which schools and commuting routes matter to Highland Park buyers?

Public schools come from two districts. North Shore School District 112 operates an early childhood center, seven elementary schools and two middle schools. Township High School District 113 operates Highland Park High School and also Deerfield High School in nearby Deerfield.

US 41 is the main highway and connects Chicago to Milwaukee. Four Metra stations sit inside the city limits: Braeside, Ravinia Park, Ravinia and Highland Park. All are on the Union Pacific North Line, which starts in Chicago and ends in Kenosha, Wisconsin. Pace buses add local routes, O'Hare is about 20 miles southwest, and the Skokie Valley Trail runs through town.

Ravinia, the open-air pavilion that seats 3,200, has been the summer home of the Chicago Symphony Orchestra since 1936. Three public beaches, Rosewood, Moraine and Park Avenue, round out the lakefront. Buyers of every type, cash buyers included, weigh the stations, schools and beaches when they set a price.

What must happen at City Hall before a Highland Park closing?

Chapter 97, Article X of the city code taxes real property transfers. The declaration form prints the rate as $5.00 per $1,000 or fraction thereof of full actual consideration, and it puts payment on the transferor when the sale contract says nothing different.

  • The declaration needs a signature from a transferor and a transferee.
  • A final water bill must be prepared and paid when the tax stamp is bought, and a final meter reading can be scheduled up to five business days before closing.
  • A copy of the deed headed for the Recorder of Deeds goes to the city, while an exempt transfer requires the original.
  • Consideration counts the mortgage amount and any liabilities the buyer assumes.
  • Section 97.1004 lists exempt deeds. Examples include tax deeds, partition deeds, deeds with consideration under $100, and foreclosure or in-lieu deeds to a mortgage holder.

The form says personal checks and credit cards are refused. Finance, at 1707 St. Johns Avenue, takes calls at 847.432.0800 and email at Finance@cityhpil.com.

What does the Lake County Clerk charge to record a Highland Park deed?

The Recording Division of the Lake County Clerk's Office handles deeds at 18 N County Street, 6th Floor, Waukegan, phone 847-377-2575. Its fee page sets $70 for a standard document and $82 for a non-standard one, and says state and county transfer taxes are the only added charges at recording.

The state levies its own tax under 35 ILCS 200/31-10, charged on the value stated in the declaration, and a mortgage the buyer takes over can be excluded when the deed says so. The closing agent will give you the county rate and a final total.

Which selling route fits a Highland Park owner in a hurry?

Three routes exist, and each trades price, certainty and effort differently.

  • Work with a listing agent. Exposure is widest, and a bluff, ravine or architect-designed property can justify a longer wait.
  • Go it alone. You control the contract and carry the showings, disclosures and negotiation.
  • Accept a cash offer. The closing date can follow your calendar and the house stays as it is, which helps with an estate home, a tenant-occupied unit or a house that needs work.

The city stamp, the final water bill and the deed filing apply on every route. Ask for the final reading early so closing does not wait on a meter.

When a cash buyer makes an offer, get in writing who pays each transfer charge named above. The sale contract is where the allocation is settled.

How many people live in Highland Park?

The April 2020 census found 30,176 residents, and the Census Bureau's mid-2025 estimate is 30,767.

Who owes the city transfer tax on a Highland Park sale?

The transferor does, as the city's form reads, when the contract has no clause to the contrary.

Does a Highland Park sale need a final water bill?

Yes. The form requires it to be prepared and paid when the stamp is bought, and a final meter reading can be booked up to five business days ahead of closing.

Which office files the deed after a Highland Park closing?

The Lake County Clerk's Recording Division in Waukegan. Its published fee for a standard document is $70.

Which school districts serve Highland Park?

North Shore School District 112 runs the elementary and middle schools, and Township High School District 113 runs Highland Park High School and Deerfield High School.

How do Gurnee owners usually decide between a listing and a fast sale?

Most weigh the condition of the house against the days they can afford to wait. A move-in-ready home can justify a listing, while a house that needs work or an owner facing a deadline points toward an as-is purchase. All three routes end the same way, with a deed recorded at the Lake County Clerk.

  • As-is cash sale: a shorter path to closing, with the buyer assuming whatever repairs remain.

Gather recent sales on your street first, because Gurnee houses are priced against their neighbors, not against the resort attractions nearby.

Where is Gurnee and how did it start?

Gurnee sits on the Des Plaines River in Lake County, roughly 40 miles north of Chicago and 50 miles south of Milwaukee, next to Waukegan. The village was founded in 1928 and carries the name of Walter S. Gurnee, a Chicago mayor who was also a railroad director. It covers a little over 13 square miles.

The first families came in the 1830s, and the crossroads was originally called Wentworth before the railroad station took the Gurnee name. A stagecoach stop on the old Milwaukee Road, known as the Mother Rudd House, now holds the Warren Township Historical Society.

Interstate 94 splits the village into an older east side and a newer west side. Pace buses link Gurnee with Waukegan and Grayslake, and a CPKC rail line between Chicago and Minneapolis runs through town.

Gurnee is a home rule municipality run by a council-manager system, with a Village President and six trustees serving four-year terms. Education levels are high: 56.7 percent of adults 25 and older hold a bachelor's degree or higher, and 67.9 percent of residents 16 and older are in the labor force. About 17 percent of residents were born outside the country, and 26.1 percent speak a language other than English at home, which can be worth remembering when you write a listing or an offer letter.

Why do so many visitors come to Gurnee?

Gurnee is a regional destination. Six Flags Great America opened in 1976 as Marriott's Great America, and its Hurricane Harbor water park arrived in 2005. Gurnee Mills, open since 1991, ranks as the fourth largest mall in Illinois, and the Great Wolf Lodge resort opened in 2007. Together they bring about 23 million visits a year and are among the village's biggest revenue sources.

Corporate employers include High Sierra Sport Company and PurposeBuilt Brands, which owns Goo Gone. In 2022, Census data show retail sales of about $1.4 billion, or $46,148 per resident. Buyers will want to know how close a house sits to the I-94 corridor and the attraction areas, so be ready to describe its location.

Gurnee Mills has drawn between 15 million and 20 million visitors a year since it opened, and Six Flags Great America alone had about 3 million guests in 2023.

Look up which side of town your address falls on before you describe the house. The Warren-Newport Public Library, with more than 270,000 books and a service area of about 60,000 people, is another amenity families mention.

What flood history should a Gurnee seller expect questions about?

The May 2004 storm brought the worst flooding in a century, closed schools and damaged dozens of homes and businesses. The Village names the low ground along the Des Plaines River and its tributaries as the most dangerous flood hazard area.

  • Look up your address on the Federal Insurance Rate Map and on the Village's inundation map.
  • Basements built more recently must have a sump pump ejection system, and the Village urges backups.
  • The Engineering Division, at 847-599-7550, keeps elevation certificates supplied by owners and historical flood records.
  • The Village's participation in the Community Rating System earns policyholders a 5 to 20 percent insurance discount.

A voluntary floodplain buyout program is also listed among the Village's flooding resources, along with a mailing list for flood updates.

Which permits and utility steps come up before a Gurnee closing?

Most construction, remodeling and improvement projects need a permit before work starts, and the Village notes that permits can help prevent issues in later property sales. Fences, reroofs, siding, water heaters, furnaces, driveways and window replacements go through an online One Stop portal. Larger projects such as additions and garages use a separate application. For inspections, call the Building Division at 847-599-7550 with 24 hours' notice and your permit number.

The Village sets a maximum U-factor of 0.28 for replacement windows in residential projects, so keep the contractor's paperwork if you replaced yours. Water arrives from Lake Michigan through the Central Lake County Joint Action Water Agency. The Village website has a Start, Stop or Make Changes page for your service, which is the place to end your account near the closing date.

How is a Gurnee deed recorded?

The Lake County Clerk's recording division in Waukegan takes the deed. According to the Clerk's packet, the grantor's signature must be notarized and the page must show the buyer's address, a full legal description, the preparer, a return address and where tax bills go. A PTAX-203 declaration or a signed exemption statement is also required.

The packet names six municipalities that require a local stamp before recording: Buffalo Grove, Highland Park, Lake Forest, Lincolnshire, Mettawa and North Chicago. Gurnee does not appear on that list, but confirm with the Village before closing.

The Lake County Clerk's recording division, in Waukegan. A notarized grantor signature, legal description and PTAX-203 or exemption statement are part of what it requires.

The Lake County Clerk lists six municipalities that need one, and Gurnee is not among them. A quick call to the Village confirms it for your closing.

Start with the Village's Engineering Division at 847-599-7550. It keeps flood maps, elevation certificates provided by owners and historical flood records.

East side addresses mostly fall in District 56 and west side addresses in District 50, with all feeding Warren Township High School. Check your exact address.

What if my Gurnee house has work done without a permit?

Ask the Building Division about your permit record. The Village says permits can help prevent issues in future sales, and an as-is buyer can take the house regardless.

Where is Niles and how did the village take shape?

Niles is a village in Cook County that sits against the far northwest edge of Chicago. It lies in Maine and Niles townships, covers 5.85 square miles, and has Skokie to the east, Morton Grove to the northeast, Glenview to the north and Park Ridge to the west. Milwaukee Avenue runs diagonally through the middle, and the North Branch of the Chicago River crosses the eastern part.

Settlers arrived in 1827, and the place was first called Dutchman's Point for the German immigrants who followed. The village was incorporated on August 24, 1899 with about 500 residents. Postwar housing did the rest: the census counted 3,587 people in 1950 and 20,393 in 1960, and the 1970 count of 31,432 remains the peak. The 2020 count was 30,912, and the Census Bureau's July 1, 2025 estimate is 30,443.

Former farms and nurseries were redeveloped into housing during that burst, so much of what sellers here own dates from the postwar years.

What taxes are due at a Niles closing?

Three transfer tax layers can apply to a Niles sale. The village's page prints its rate as $3.00 per $1,000 of price, and says the buyer pays it. The state and county rates come from the Cook County Clerk's transfer fee page.

LayerRate as printedParty liable

An exempt stamp, for a deed that is not a sale, costs a flat $25.00 and cannot be issued until all outstanding fines and fees are paid. To get either stamp, the village requires a completed Niles Real Estate Transfer Declaration Form and a copy of the Illinois Real Estate Transfer Declaration.

What does a Niles seller have to do before the transfer stamp is issued?

Call the Finance Department at 847-588-8030 ten days before closing. The village uses that call to arrange a final water reading and a property search for fines, fees or violations.

The village will not issue a stamp unless the property is free of liens and violations and has no outstanding bills owed to the village. Its page lists these practical points:

  • Stamps can be bought in person at the Finance Department in Niles Village Hall, or by mail to 1000 Civic Center Drive with a self-addressed, postage-paid envelope.
  • In-person transactions must reach the Finance Department before 4:30 pm with paperwork already complete.
  • Accepted payment includes a cashier's check, money order, title company check, attorney firm check, cash, or a credit or debit card with a processing fee.
  • Completed forms can be emailed to the village's real estate transfer stamp address, with the property address in the subject line. Water reading and property search requests must be phoned in, not emailed.

A lien, an unpaid water bill or an open code violation will stop the stamp, so ask the Finance Department for the property search result early enough to fix anything that turns up.

What happens to a Niles rental when it is sold?

If the transfer declarations show the new owner will not live there, the buyer must file a Rental License Application when buying the transfer stamp. The village's page also says rental licenses are non-transferable when a property is sold, so the license you hold does not pass to the buyer.

That affects a landlord selling to another investor and a family selling a house that will be rented out. Questions about the application go to Community Development at 847-588-8040. A seller who has a tenant in place should also check the lease and ask the buyer's side how it plans to apply for the license, since the application is filed when the stamp is bought.

Is there a transfer tax rebate for Niles residents who buy again in the village?

Yes, for a narrow group. The village's rebate form describes a rebate of $2 per $1,000 for a Niles resident who sold a principal residence and buys a residential structure in the village to use as a principal residence. The form says the rebate equals two-thirds of the amount paid for the transfer stamp on the new property.

The buyer files it after closing, with proof of the transaction, within one year of the sale of the old residence. The Finance Director reviews the claim, and commercial and retail property do not qualify. A homeowner who is selling in Niles to move up or down within the village should keep the closing statements from both deals.

What do Census figures say about Niles homes and households?

The Census Bureau's 2020 to 2024 and 2025 figures include:

  • Owner-occupied rate: 74.6%.
  • Median value of an owner-occupied home: $358,700.
  • Median monthly owner costs: $2,159 with a mortgage and $844 without.
  • Median gross rent: $1,336.
  • Households: 11,481, with 2.51 persons per household.
  • Median household income: $75,274, and 28.5% of residents are 65 or older.
  • Foreign-born residents: 42.0%, and 59.5% of residents age 5 and older speak a language other than English at home.

The July 1, 2025 population estimate is 1.6% below the April 2020 base.

What else do buyers weigh when they look at a Niles house?

Services and location carry a lot of weight in a village this compact. Niles started the first free ambulance service in Illinois in 1946, and it later added the free bus. It was named an All-America City in 1964.

The Tam O'Shanter Golf Course, owned by the Niles Park District, hosted the All American Open on the PGA Tour from 1941 to 1957 and the Western Open in 1964 and 1965. St. Adalbert Cemetery is the largest in the Archdiocese of Chicago by burials. Niles has four sister cities: Pisa in Italy, Nafplion in Greece, Leixlip in Ireland and Limanowa in Poland.

Retail is a strength as well. The Census Bureau lists 2022 retail sales of about $2.1 billion, or $70,862 per resident, a high per-capita figure for a village of this size.

Which schools, buses and employers define Niles?

Several elementary districts cover the village: East Maine District 63, Park Ridge-Niles District 64, Golf District 67, Niles District 71 and Fairview District 72. High school students attend Maine Township District 207 or Niles Township Community District 219, and Oakton Community College is the local community college district. Notre Dame College Prep and Northridge Preparatory School are Catholic high schools in the village's education listing.

Niles runs a free village bus, and Pace operates its Pulse Milwaukee and Pulse Dempster lines through town. U.S. 14 and Illinois routes 21, 43 and 58 cross the village. The Leaning Tower of Niles, a scaled replica of the tower in Pisa, is its best-known landmark, and Golf Mill Shopping Center opened in 1960.

The village's 2019 financial report, as summarized by Wikipedia, listed Woodward with 1,000 employees, Shure with 680, Bradford Exchange with 600 and Coca-Cola Bottling with 500 as leading employers.

Who pays the Niles real estate transfer tax?

The buyer pays the village stamp, at $3.00 per $1,000 of price or fraction thereof. The Cook County Clerk's table lists the state ($.50 per $500) and the county ($.25 per $500) as the seller's responsibility.

How early should I call the village before closing on a Niles house?

Ten days before closing. The Finance Department asks the seller to call 847-588-8030 so it can take a final water reading and run a property search for fines, fees and violations.

Can a Niles stamp be issued with an unpaid water bill or violation on the property?

No. The village says the property must be free of liens and violations and cannot have outstanding bills owed to the village. Exempt stamps are also held until all fines and fees are paid.

What does a Niles buyer need if the house will be a rental?

A Rental License Application, filed at the time the transfer stamp is bought. Rental licenses do not carry over to the buyer when a property is sold.

Does Niles refund any of the transfer tax?

Only to a Niles resident who sold a principal residence and buys another residence in the village, and only on the form filed within one year. The rebate is $2 per $1,000, calculated as two-thirds of the stamp price paid on the new property.

How does a McHenry homeowner go about selling?

Three paths are open. An agent can list the house, you can find a buyer yourself, or you can deal with a purchaser who accepts the house as it sits and brings no lender. Once a contract exists, every path ends at the same county filing: a transfer declaration plus a recorded deed.

Condition and calendar settle the choice. Patience plus a tidy interior favors open houses. Worn systems, a tenant, an estate in limbo or a hard closing date tilt toward a direct purchase.

What follows sticks to McHenry itself: Census figures, the permit rules at 333 S Green Street, how city water accounts change hands, and what the county recorder expects.

What is McHenry like as a place to sell?

East-central McHenry County holds the city, which the municipal history page measures at 55 miles from the Chicago Loop and 35 from O'Hare, spread over about 13 square miles of land and organized around two state routes, 31 and 120.

Its roots are a river-resort past. By the 1920s the Fox River and nearby lakes had made the town a summer destination, and summer cottages spread along the river. Subdivisions were annexed on every side from the late 1940s onward, and the city lists active ones such as Boone Creek, Glacier Ridge, Legend Lakes, Liberty Trails and Prairie Lakes.

Counting from 27,135 people in 2020, the Bureau puts McHenry at 29,217 by mid-2025, a 6.8 percent climb off its estimates base. Owners live in 74.4 percent of the 11,897 households. A typical owned home is valued at $266,500, rent runs $1,553 at the middle of the range, and household income sits at $86,315 (all figures 2020 to 2024).

Roughly three in four homes are owner-occupied, so the people you compete with are mostly neighbors. Getting to work takes 29.0 minutes on average.

How do McHenry's schools, roads and rail affect a sale?

Schools and the commute are usually the first questions. McHenry Community High School District 156 and McHenry School District 15 (five elementary and three middle schools) both serve the city.

  • Roads: Route 31 and Route 120 cross in the middle of town and carry most traffic in and out.
  • Rail: the city is the last stop on a Metra branch that offers weekday trains into downtown Chicago.
  • Trails and parks: the Prairie Trail runs through the center, while Moraine Hills State Park, anchored by 48-acre Lake Defiance, lies on the east side.
  • Airports: O'Hare and Milwaukee Mitchell are the closest public international airports.

Downtown is split into Green Street, Riverside Drive and Main Street, tied together by a 0.73 mile Riverwalk along Boone Creek and the Fox. Healthcare employs the most people in the city, at 5,136 jobs or 26 percent, ahead of retail at 3,139 and manufacturing at 2,418, according to the city's profile.

Does McHenry's climate change how the house should be prepared?

Winter is the main factor. NOAA normals reported for McHenry show about 34.5 inches of snow a year, 22 days with measurable snow, and a January average daily low near 13 degrees. The all-time low on record is 32 below zero.

Expect scrutiny of the roof, gutters, attic insulation, furnace and basement. Yearly precipitation totals close to 37 inches, peaking in May and June, so a basement that smells damp or a sump pump that cycles constantly will show up on an inspection.

Glacial lakes, Boone Creek and the Fox River give the area its character and also its drainage questions. If the lot lies near the water, find out its flood zone designation before you name a price.

Which permits come up when a McHenry house is on the market?

Most remodeling and home improvement jobs in McHenry need a building permit. Sort out any open or missing permits early. The Community Development Department answers at 815-363-2170 and sits in the Municipal Center, 333 S Green Street.

The city says most residential permit applications are processed within 10 business days, and the clock does not start until everything needed for review has been submitted. Some permits are issued faster:

  • Reroof, siding, and windows or doors.
  • Water heater and furnace or air conditioner replacement.
  • Sewer or water repair.

Those counter-based permits come back immediately for walk-in applicants and within a day for online ones. The permit fee already covers the inspections, which need a day's notice and are booked in three-hour windows (9 to noon or 1 to 4, except roofing and siding, which run 10 to 2). Same-day inspections are not offered.

If an earlier owner skipped paperwork on a deck or basement, the department can say what finishing it involves. Investors often absorb that cost; buyers with mortgages tend to raise it.

Where does a McHenry deed go after the closing table?

The county Recorder's Office handles it, not city hall. Per its FAQ, a document that meets state formatting rules and comes with the right payment is recorded the same day, then mailed back in roughly two working days. For fees, ring 815-334-4110.

Sale prices are visible through a PTAX-203 or MyDec form that can accompany the deed. The state levy is set in 35 ILCS 200/31-15 at fifty cents for every $500 of value, with revenue stamps as proof.

According to the Recorder, no McHenry County municipality adds its own transfer tax. For ownership by parcel number, the Assessor's number is 815-334-4290; for tax bills, the County Treasurer's is 815-334-4072.

What does a McHenry seller owe the buyer and the city utility?

Under 765 ILCS 77/20 the seller fills out every item of the statutory report and puts it in the buyer's hands before anyone signs a contract. Finish it while offers are still coming in.

City water and sewer bills arrive every two months, and accounts fall on even or odd billing months depending on the account number prefix. McHenry publishes a Water/Sewer Transfer Form that records the ownership date along with billing addresses for the outgoing and incoming owner. Submitting it fixes the date your final bill stops.

The title company will ask for a loan payoff figure if you owe on the house, along with the parcel number and your latest tax bill.

Which McHenry selling route fits which situation?

Set the three paths side by side before choosing.

  • Agent listing: the largest audience, in return for showings, an appraisal and inspection, and possible repair requests from the buyer.
  • Owner-handled sale: control over price and timing, with the paperwork and promotion landing on you.
  • Direct sale for cash: quicker, with fewer conditions, and priced around the repairs ahead.

With any offer, insist on a written copy and read each closing cost line.

Do roof and water heater swaps in McHenry need city sign-off?

Yes. Both jobs sit on the city's counter-based permit list, which means same-visit approval in person or a one-day turnaround online. Community Development at 815-363-2170 can say what your project requires.

Is there a McHenry city transfer stamp?

No. The Recorder's FAQ reports that none of the county's municipalities levy their own, so the state's fifty cents on each $500 (35 ILCS 200/31-15) is the charge described there.

Who records the McHenry deed?

The McHenry County Recorder, at 815-334-4110. Documents that conform and carry the right payment are recorded the day they arrive.

How does the city water account change hands?

McHenry bills every second month and provides a Water/Sewer Transfer Form noting the ownership date. File it at closing and each owner pays only for their own period.

Will anyone buy a McHenry house that needs work?

Yes. Illinois asks only that the disclosure report precede the contract; fixes are bargained over afterward. Mortgage-backed buyers lean on repair requests, while investors price the work into their offer.

Where is Huntley, Illinois, and why does it sit in two counties?

Huntley is a village in the northwest Chicago area that straddles McHenry County and Kane County. It lies along Interstate 90, covers about 14.29 square miles of land, and uses ZIP code 60142. Three townships divide it: Grafton, Rutland and Hampshire.

The village's own FAQ gives the township split. Land north of Kreutzer Road is in Grafton Township, and land south of Kreutzer Road is in Rutland Township, except the northwest end of Sun City, which is in Hampshire Township. The county and township matter to a seller because they decide which office handles your tax bill and your deed.

Huntley was founded in 1851 and incorporated in 1872, and it is named for Thomas Stillwell Huntley. Its census count was 5,730 in 2000, 24,291 in 2010 and 27,740 in 2020, one of the sharpest growth curves in the region.

What do the Census numbers say about Huntley homeowners?

The Census Bureau estimated 29,132 residents on July 1, 2025, up 5.0 percent from the April 2020 base. For 2020 to 2024 it reports an owner-occupied rate of 88.9 percent, a median value of owner-occupied homes of $334,300, and 12,213 households averaging 2.29 people. Median household income is $88,536, and the mean commute is 29.5 minutes.

The age profile is the most unusual part. 34.1 percent of residents as 65 or older and only 3.2 percent under 5. The 2020 census put the median age at 48.2.

  • A high share of older residents often means estate sales, downsizing and moves to be near family.
  • With 88.9 percent of homes owner-occupied, most sales here are owner-to-owner rather than investor deals.
  • Sun City, the age-restricted community reached by Del Webb Boulevard, is its own submarket and has its own garbage arrangement according to the village.

What drives the local economy and the roads around Huntley?

Growth in new businesses and distribution warehouses, especially along Illinois Route 47, has shaped the last decade. A small downtown keeps restaurants and shops. Route 47 is the main north-south road and runs nearly seven miles through the village. It was widened from two to five lanes in 2011, carries over 20,000 vehicles a day, and meets I-90 at a full interchange that was finished in November 2013.

Algonquin Road, a four-lane divided highway, runs east toward Algonquin and Lake in the Hills, and Main Street connects west toward Marengo and Harmony Road. Huntley-Dundee Road leads east to the Carpentersville and Dundee area. The Union Pacific Belvidere Subdivision passes through, and many local industries sit near the tracks.

Huntley once planned a stop on a proposed Metra intercity line from Rockford to Chicago, but it withdrew over concerns about its downtown. A listing can point to the I-90 and Route 47 access as a practical selling point.

Which schools and services come with a Huntley address?

Huntley Community School District 158 serves the village. Huntley High School is on Harmony Road, and the middle schools are Marlowe in Lake in the Hills and Heineman in Algonquin. Elementary schools include Leggee in Huntley, Martin and Chesak in Lake in the Hills, and Conley and Mackeben in Algonquin.

  • The Huntley Fire Protection District covers about 55 square miles and serves all village residents.
  • The Huntley Area Public Library is on Ruth Road. The Hampshire Township part of the village is served by the Ella Johnson Memorial Public Library.
  • The Huntley Park District runs the recreation center on Mill Street.
  • Residential garbage goes through a single village-wide hauler with Monday pickup, except apartments and Sun City.
  • Overnight parking on village streets is prohibited from 2 a.m. to 6 a.m., which matters when buyers or movers visit.

Huntley is a home rule municipality with an elected village president and a six-member board of trustees.

Does Huntley charge a transfer stamp, and what else applies at closing?

No. The village's FAQ says Huntley does not require a real estate transfer stamp, and it also says the village does not require village stickers.

State law still applies. Illinois also taxes the transfer of title itself under 35 ILCS 200/31-10, and a mortgage the buyer takes over can be left out of the taxable value if the deed says so. Ask the title company which county charges apply to a McHenry County parcel and which to a Kane County parcel.

Most home improvements in the village need a permit, and Development Services at 847-515-5252 can confirm whether a past project was permitted. If you finished a basement, deck or similar work, find the permit paperwork before you list.

What village rules does a buyer inherit with a Huntley house?

Buyers often ask about local rules before they make an offer, and the village FAQ answers several of them.

  • Watering follows a four-tier color-coded conservation program (red, yellow, orange and green), with signs posted around the village.
  • The village applies the McHenry County Open Burning Ordinance to all property inside its limits, and because lots are small, leaf burning is essentially illegal for most homeowners.
  • There is no village pet license, but McHenry and Kane counties both require rabies tags for dogs.
  • A garage sale needs no permit, though signs may go only on private property.
  • Recreational vehicle parking and storage fall under Zoning Code Section 156.106.
  • Yard waste is collected from April 1 to November 30, and the village runs a branch pick-up program twice a year.

Handing a buyer this short list in advance saves questions during negotiations, and it shows the house has been looked after.

How can you sell a Huntley house quickly?

Three routes are open, and the right one depends on how much work the house needs and how soon you must close.

  • Hire an agent and list. This tends to reach the most buyers, and Huntley's owner-heavy market suits it when the house is in good shape.
  • Sell it yourself. You keep the whole process in your hands, including the contract and the disclosures.
  • Take a cash offer. It can work for an inherited house, a rental, or a place that needs repairs you do not want to fund, and the closing date can be set around your plans.

Before choosing, confirm the county for the parcel, collect any permit records, and ask the water billing office about a final reading. With no village stamp to buy, Huntley sales can move on a short schedule once the contract is signed.

Where is New Lenox and how did the village grow?

New Lenox is a village in central Will County, about 36 miles southwest of downtown Chicago. Joliet lies to the northwest, Mokena to the east, Frankfort to the southeast and Manhattan to the south, and the village covers about 15.7 square miles of land.

Fur traders set up an outpost on Hickory Creek in 1829, and the Rock Island Railroad's arrival in 1852 turned the area from farm country into a rail town. The village was platted in 1858 and took the name New Lenox in 1863, after Lenox, New York. It was incorporated on October 4, 1946.

The census count was 1,235 in 1950, 9,627 in 1990 and 17,771 in 2000. It reached 27,214 in 2020, and the Census Bureau's July 1, 2025 estimate is 28,893, a gain of 6.1% over the April 2020 base. Growth on that scale means many sellers here own houses built from the 1990s onward.

Which New Lenox projects need a village permit?

Most of them do. The Village says permits are required for most construction and homeowner projects, including sheds, decks, pools, fences, roofs, lawn irrigation, siding, window replacement, room additions and basement remodels. Homeowners may do the work themselves, but any contractor must be registered with the Village before the permit is issued.

  • Small jobs such as fences, sheds, driveways, roofs and windows can be reviewed over the counter and issued the same day if the application is accurate. Larger reviews can take up to two weeks.

  • Online applicants should hear a status within two business days, and no work may begin until the permit is paid for and issued.

The Village's list of miscellaneous permits says private sidewalks, concrete or paver patios, dog runs and playhouses under 100 square feet do not need one. The Community Development Department answers questions at 815-462-6490, and Village Hall, at 1 Veterans Parkway, takes in-person applications from 8:30 am to 5 pm on weekdays.

How do inspections and winter rules affect a New Lenox sale?

If a permit was never closed out, the Village's inspection steps apply. The Village asks for 48 hours of notice for building inspections and 24 hours for water meter and plumbing inspections, and it charges a fee for a failed inspection, including one where the work is not ready when the inspector arrives.

Winter adds a second limit. From December 1 through March 30 the Village prohibits placing concrete flatwork, and it regulates timing and insulation for footings and foundations. Bonds are accepted in place of exterior concrete during those months. A seller with an unfinished driveway apron or public walk should ask the Building Department how that bond works before a closing date is set.

The Village also keeps a Vacant Property Registration form on its permits page. If the house will sit empty during a sale, ask Community Development whether that registration applies to you.

What does the Will County Recorder require for a New Lenox deed?

New Lenox deeds record with the Will County Recorder of Deeds at 158 N. Scott Street in Joliet, phone 815-740-4637. The fee schedule effective October 1, 2025 lists $90.00 for a standard document and $118.00 for a non-standard one, and the $19.00 Rental Housing Support Program surcharge is part of those totals.

The recorder's deed checklist asks for:

  • The preparer's name and mailing address, and a return address for the document.
  • The permanent index number and a legal description.
  • A notarized original deed, not a copy.
  • The grantee name and address, and the name and address for tax bills.
  • A completed transfer declaration or exemption under the Illinois transfer tax law.

The checklist also lists municipal transfer tax stamps for nine municipalities: Aurora, Bolingbrook, Channahon, Joliet, Naperville, Park Forest, Romeoville, University Park and Woodridge. New Lenox is not on that list. Ask the Village Hall whether any local stamp or payoff step applies to your closing.

Which schools, roads and hospitals are close to New Lenox homes?

New Lenox School District 122 runs the elementary and middle schools. High schoolers attend Lincoln-Way Community High School District, which serves New Lenox, Frankfort, Mokena, Manhattan and a small part of Tinley Park. Lincoln-Way Central and Lincoln-Way West are in New Lenox, Lincoln-Way East is in Frankfort, and Providence Catholic High School is also in the village.

U.S. Route 30 is the main east-west road, with Cedar, Gougar and Nelson roads running north and south. I-80 and I-355, the Veterans Memorial Tollway, both pass through. The Metra Rock Island District station is at U.S. 30 and Cedar Road, and a second station at Laraway Road is on the SouthWest Service line.

Silver Cross Hospital moved to a $400 million building off U.S. 6 near the I-355 extension on February 26, 2012.

What does New Lenox weather mean for a house in the listing?

Winters are cold enough to matter. January averages about 21 degrees Fahrenheit, July averages 73, and the village sees on average 137 days with lows at or below freezing and 86 days with highs above 80. Record readings run from 104 degrees down to minus 27.

Those swings are hard on roofs, gutters, driveways, and sump systems in basements. Keep receipts for roof work and the sump pump, since both are standard questions in any sale.

What parks and community amenities do buyers ask about in New Lenox?

The New Lenox Community Park District maintains 40 parks and athletic fields on nearly 600 acres. The 22-mile Old Plank Road Trail passes through the village and reaches Village Hall at the Commons, which opened in 2005 with a performing arts pavilion. The Hickory Creek State Nature Preserve adds a 2.8-mile trail, and the Hadley Valley Preserve has a 4.85-mile crushed-stone greenway trail.

Summer concerts and festivals such as Cruise the Commons and Christmas in the Commons run out of the same civic center.

Not to sell, but open permits and unpermitted work can come up in a buyer's review. The Village requires permits for most construction projects, so call Community Development at 815-462-6490 if you remodeled, added a deck or replaced a roof.

Which office records a New Lenox deed?

The Will County Recorder of Deeds in Joliet. Its standard document fee has been $90.00 since October 1, 2025, and the deed must be an original with a notarized signature, a legal description and a permanent index number.

Does New Lenox charge a municipal transfer tax stamp?

The Will County Recorder's deed checklist names nine municipalities that issue transfer stamps, and New Lenox is not among them. Ask Community Development at 815-462-6490 before closing, since that list is the county's summary of what deeds need.

Can I sell a New Lenox house with unfinished concrete work?

Yes, but winter timing matters. The Village bars concrete flatwork from December 1 through March 30 and accepts a bond in place of exterior concrete during that period, so ask the Building Department what the bond requires.

How old are most New Lenox houses?

No single answer fits, but most of the building came between 1990 and 2010. The census count rose from 9,627 in 1990 to 17,771 in 2000 and 24,394 in 2010, so houses from those years are common.

What is the quickest way to sell a house in Glen Ellyn, Illinois?

Speed in Glen Ellyn usually comes from an as-is purchase by a buyer with no loan to approve, although a well-prepared listing can also hit a fixed date. What slows most Glen Ellyn closings is not the buyer but the village paperwork: the transfer stamp, the clearwater inspection and the final water reading.

  • An agent listing suits a house in good shape when you want to see how high the price can go.
  • Sell privately if you are comfortable handling contracts and disclosures on your own.
  • A cash purchase as-is fits a house with deferred repairs, an estate behind it, or a closing date that cannot move.

Glen Ellyn is a village in DuPage County about 24 miles due west of downtown Chicago, in Milton Township. With a Metra station downtown, three school districts and a village sump pump rule, train access, school boundaries and basement drainage are the topics to prepare before you talk to buyers.

What does the Glen Ellyn housing market look like?

Glen Ellyn is a high-value suburb where most residents own: QuickFacts shows 28,750 people in mid-2025 against 28,846 in the 2020 count. Homes that owners occupy have a median value of $544,000 in the 2020 to 2024 data, owners hold 78.3 percent of the housing, and the village has 10,698 households.

Households in the village bring in a median of $140,938, rent runs a median of $1,433, and 68.2 percent of adults hold at least a bachelor's degree. The average trip to work takes 29.1 minutes, a figure to read alongside the train and expressway access described below.

The main campus of College of DuPage is in the village, and the 2021 financial report named it the top employer at 3,837 people. School District 41 listed 549 employees and School District 87 listed 485.

The area began as Babcock's Grove after two brothers staked claims near the East Branch of the DuPage River in 1833. The Galena and Chicago Union Railroad finished its line through the village in 1849, and the center of the community shifted to the area around the depot.

Which schools, trains and parks draw buyers to Glen Ellyn?

School district is the first fact to confirm for any Glen Ellyn address. Primary schools are part of Glen Ellyn School District 41 and Community Consolidated School District 89, and high school students attend Glenbard Township High School District 87.

Elementary schools in the village include Abraham Lincoln, Arbor View, Benjamin Franklin, Churchill, Forest Glen, Park View and Westfield, and Glen Crest Middle School and Hadley Junior High serve older grades. Confirm which school serves your address with the district, since district boundaries do not follow village lines everywhere.

Transportation is a second selling point. The Metra Union Pacific West Line stops at the Glen Ellyn station at 551 Crescent Boulevard, about 22.4 miles from Ogilvie Transportation Center. Pace routes 714, 715 and 301 run along Roosevelt Road, and Roosevelt Road also leads to Interstate 355 at the east end of the village.

The Glen Ellyn Park District, set up in 1919, maintains 30 parks and two lakes, and the Illinois Prairie Path bike trail runs through the village. Lake Ellyn was created in the late 1800s when a dam was built on a nearby stream.

How does the Glen Ellyn transfer stamp and clearwater inspection work?

The Village of Glen Ellyn charges a real estate transfer stamp of $3 for each $1,000 of property sales price, and the home seller pays it. The stamp is required to record the deed, and the village will not issue it until every inspection is passed and every fee is paid.

Glen Ellyn steps before a transfer stamp is issued (Village of Glen Ellyn)
StepWho handles itContact
Transfer stamp application, completed onlineVillage of Glen EllynOnline form
Clearwater inspectionPublic Works630-469-6756, choose clearwater appointments
Final water readingUtility Billing630-547-5235
Stamp tax of $3 per $1,000 of sales pricePaid by the sellerVillage

The clearwater inspection comes from Village Code 3-42-15. It is required any time a stamp is needed, including a sale, a title transfer, putting a deed into a trust or a refinance, and it applies to exempt transactions too. The inspector checks whether the building has a sump pump and whether the pump is illegally tied into the sanitary sewer.

The rule exists because rainwater in the sanitary system can overload it during a major storm and push sewage back into homes. Village Code 7-9-25 bars clearwater from sanitary sewers, and Code 8-1-10 bars directing sump pump, gutter or similar discharge into the public right-of-way. If the inspector finds a problem, fix it before closing. Public Works can explain acceptable options, which may include moving the discharge point or connecting to the storm sewer.

Some sellers may qualify for a refund of the transfer tax. The eligibility rules are on the village's refund application, so ask the village before assuming one applies.

What permits and contractor rules apply to a Glen Ellyn house?

Permit work in Glen Ellyn goes through the village's online permit system, and open work can complicate a sale. The Building Division reviews plans, issues permits, inspects construction and enforces the building, property maintenance, fire and zoning codes.

Applications are signed electronically with the owner's authorization, and supporting documents such as plans, a plat of survey and contracts are uploaded with them. Construction plans must be prepared and stamped by an Illinois registered design professional. Fees depend on the project type and construction cost, and refundable deposits cover possible damage to public property. All contractors must meet the license and insurance requirements in Village Code Section 4-1-11, and a contractor working in violation can be cited or have a stop work order issued.

  • Locate permit records and final inspection sign-offs for decks, additions and finished basements.
  • Ask Public Works about drainage if your lot has a history of standing water.
  • Keep a copy of your plat of survey, since many permit and closing steps ask for it.

Selling as-is to a cash buyer puts the cleanup of open permits on the buyer, as long as the contract spells out who takes on what.

How do DuPage County property taxes work for Glen Ellyn sellers?

How does selling a house in Lake in the Hills work?

Three paths are open to an owner: hire an agent, handle the sale yourself, or sign with an investor who pays cash and skips the repair list. Whichever route you pick, a sale in Lake in the Hills runs through the same local pieces: Village Hall for permits and contractor questions, the three fire protection districts and four school districts that overlap the village, and the McHenry County Recorder for the deed.

Lake in the Hills sits in McHenry County, northwest of Chicago, along the Randall Road corridor. The 2020 census counted 28,982 residents, and that number has barely moved since. A seller here is usually working with a house built after the 1990s growth wave, or with an older lakeside cottage in the east side of the village, and the two behave very differently at sale time.

How did Lake in the Hills grow into the village buyers see?

It is a former summer-cottage community that turned into a commuter suburb. A federal judge started the lakeside settlement around Woods Creek Lake in 1923, vacationers from Chicago slowly became year-round residents, and the village was formed on November 29, 1952. Growth exploded in the 1990s: roughly 17,000 people were added in that decade, and the village issued more than 1,000 residential building permits in 1995 alone.

Randall Road now splits the village into an older East Side and a newer West Side, and Algonquin Road marks the boundary with the village of Algonquin. Buyers tend to compare houses by subdivision, so it helps to know which one yours belongs to.

  • The Old Section: four older neighborhoods (Original, Indian, Tree and Presidents, named for their street themes) near the lake, with mixed architecture instead of tract styling.

  • Big Sky and Harvest Gate: early subdivisions west of Randall Road, split by Woods Creek and close to the village hall and Lincoln Prairie Elementary.
  • Spring Lake Farm: an early-1990s subdivision south of Miller Road with both single-family and multifamily housing.

Which school and fire districts cover a Lake in the Hills address?

Four school districts share the village, so the district tied to your street matters to many buyers. Consolidated District 158 covers most of the dense western half, District 300 covers the older eastern sections, and Elementary District 47 and Community High School District 155 reach a small central slice.

That means a seller on the west side may market Huntley High School, while a seller on the east side points to Jacobs High School in Algonquin, and the central pocket feeds Crystal Lake South and Crystal Lake Central. Elementary names in the village include Lake in the Hills Elementary, Lincoln Prairie, Glacier Ridge, Canterbury, Woods Creek, May Chesak, Hannah Martin, Mackeben and Marion Conley, depending on the boundary.

Fire service is also split. The village says three separate districts, the Algonquin-Lake in the Hills Fire Protection District, Crystal Lake Fire Rescue and the Huntley Fire Protection District, serve different parts of town, each with its own taxing authority. Check your tax bill or call the district before you describe the house in a listing.

If a past owner finished a basement or deck and you cannot find the permit, ask Village Hall what is on file for the address before a buyer's inspector asks. A buyer paying cash for the house as-is may accept that risk, but a lender-backed buyer often will not.

Which village rules show up on a showing day?

Winter and noise rules are the ones sellers trip over. The village plows most streets, aims to clear them 6 to 10 hours after snow stops, and bans on-street parking once an inch has fallen under Municipal Code Section 41.03. County crews handle roads such as Algonquin, Lakewood, Randall and Ackman, and the state handles Routes 31 and 47.

Property owners clear their own sidewalks and driveways, and snow belongs in the yard, not the street. Garbage cans go to the curb at 6 p.m. or later the evening before pickup and should be stored out of sight otherwise. Construction, lawn work and personal snow removal are exempt from the noise limits only between 7 a.m. and 8 p.m., which matters if you are rushing repairs before listing.

What happens at recording and transfer in McHenry County?

Deeds are filed with the McHenry County Recorder, and the state transfer tax under 35 ILCS 200/31-10 is fifty cents per $500 increment of the value written on the declaration. Under 35 ILCS 200/31-25 the paperwork is due with the deed or inside three business days of the transfer, whichever comes first, with a seller's and a buyer's signature (or those of their agents).

The county's own checklist for good recordings is worth reading before closing:

  • The online MyDec declaration must read "Closing Completed."
  • A deed needs the grantee's address and the full McHenry County legal description.
  • A Plat Act affidavit must accompany a deed that uses a metes and bounds description.
  • A signed exemption paragraph or a PTAX-203 or MyDec declaration must come with every deed.
  • Documents need a half-inch clean margin and a clear 3 by 5 inch space in the upper right corner.

Ask the McHenry County Recorder whether a county or village transfer fee applies to your parcel, since this brief covers only the state rate.

When does a cash offer fit a Lake in the Hills sale?

A cash sale makes sense when the house needs work a lender's appraiser would flag, when you inherited a home you cannot maintain, or when the calendar matters more than squeezing out the top price. Houses with deferred maintenance, an association dispute or a pending violation notice are typical examples, since each can slow a conventional listing.

What if my Lake in the Hills house has open permits?

Which office records my deed?

The McHenry County Recorder records deeds for Lake in the Hills. The county's recording checklist requires a completed transfer declaration, the grantee's address and the full legal description, and the MyDec record must show that closing was completed.

Do homeowner associations affect permits here?

Village approval is based on codes and zoning, not on your association. Many Lake in the Hills subdivisions still have their own rules, so get any needed association sign-off in addition to the village permit.

Who handles snow removal on my street?

It depends on the road. The village clears most local streets, county crews handle Algonquin, Lakewood, Randall and Ackman Roads, the state handles Routes 31 and 47, and some roads belong to property owner associations. Call 847-960-7500 for a specific street.

How is the state transfer tax stated?

The state sets the tax in 35 ILCS 200/31-10 and applies it to the value shown on the declaration. A deed that says it conveys the property subject to a mortgage lets the unpaid mortgage balance be left out of the base.

Which routes lead to a fast sale in Galesburg, Illinois?

Your options in Galesburg: hire an agent, handle the sale personally, or hand the keys to a buyer who accepts the place with every flaw. The right choice follows from the shape of the house and how firm your closing date is. Prices in the city run low, so repair bills weigh heavily against the sale price.

  • Agent listing: a good match for a house in decent condition when you can sit through showings and loan approvals.
  • Do-it-yourself sale: you skip the agent fee and take over the pricing, contract and paperwork.
  • As-is offer: suits inherited houses, empty properties, rentals with tenant trouble and homes with repairs put off for years.

The city is the seat of Knox County, about 45 miles northwest of Peoria. That puts the county Treasurer and assessment office, the two county offices that touch every sale, within a short drive of any Galesburg address.

What does the Galesburg housing market look like?

Galesburg is inexpensive and getting smaller. 28,581 residents in mid-2025, down 4.9 percent from 30,046 in the 2020 base. In the 2020 census, 10.9 percent of Galesburg's 13,939 housing units were vacant.

Across 12,628 households, owners live in 62.2 percent of the housing, and the middle value of those homes is $96,400 in the 2020 to 2024 figures. Rent has a median of $801, household income a median of $48,297, and the typical trip to work takes 16.6 minutes. Low prices and short commutes draw first-time buyers and small investors, so price a Galesburg house against recent Galesburg sales rather than suburban figures.

The railroads shaped the city. The Chicago, Burlington and Quincy placed major sorting yards here, and BNSF has been the biggest private employer since the Maytag plant shut in 2004. Knox College and Carl Sandburg College are both in town, and plans call for a National Railroad Hall of Fame. A 496-acre area is designated as the Galesburg Historic District on the National Register, which matters if your house lies in or beside it.

Which roads, rail lines and neighborhoods affect a Galesburg house sale?

Location in Galesburg is mostly about access and the age of the housing stock. Interstate 74 runs along the east side of the city, leading southeast to Peoria and north toward the Quad Cities. US 34 is a freeway through Galesburg with interchanges at West Main Street, North Henderson Street and North Seminary Street, and US 150 enters as Grand Avenue and runs through downtown as Main Street.

Amtrak offers four daily trains to Chicago Union Station, and Galesburg Transit operates four bus loops. A home near the rail corridor will hear freight traffic, since BNSF runs a large hump yard south of town and its lines through the area carry an average of about seven freight trains per hour. Be upfront about that when you show a house nearby.

Lombard Middle School stands on the site of the former Lombard College, which closed in 1930. Ask the local school district for the attendance area of your address so buyers get the same answer you do.
